chapters.title: Chapter 553: Training Ends—1
paragraphs: Soon, Seraphine and Ira stirred on their own.

Leon was already awake — had been for a while, not restless, just comfortable in the specific way that made getting up feel unnecessary. Both of them warm against him, the room quiet, the dimensional world doing its thing outside. He hadn’t been sleeping deeply. Just enjoying the particular peace of lying still between two people he genuinely wanted to be next to.
This is a good morning,he thought simply.
Then Seraphine moved, and Ira made the sound she always made when waking up — a short noise that was half protest and half acceptance — and the morning became practical.

They dressed quickly. Seraphine stepped into her new armor, the Stormveil Regalia fitting exactly as she’d hoped it would — moving with her rather than on her; every adjustment she made met with zero resistance from the material. She ran one hand along the new katana’s grip and said nothing, but the expression she made said she approved and wasn’t going to make an event of it.

Ira pulled the Ember Sovereign set on with considerably less ceremony, more interested in the spear than the armor, turning the Blazing Fang in her hands once before nodding to herself with the satisfied expression of someone whose instincts had confirmed what their eyes were telling them.
She’s going to push that spear past its current listings within a month,Leon thought, watching her exactlylike I expected.
He strapped his epic-ranked sword to his waist and checked the revival treasures — both equipped, both ready. He’d checked three times already. He checked again.
"Ready?" he asked.
"Yes," Seraphine said.
"Obviously," Ira said.
He teleported them.
The dungeon location was an ice field.

Snow fell steadily; the ground below was solid ice that caught and scattered the dimensional world’s ambient light in cold blues and whites. The atmosphere had weight to it — not normal cold, not the kind that made you reach for a jacket, but the deep bone-settling kind that found gaps in your awareness and settled into them. The world upgrade had clearly done something to this region; whatever it had been before intensified into something with genuine presence.

Around the giant swirling portal — which crackled with energy that was visible from a significant distance, the air around it warping slightly with the force of something about to open — nine hundred or so equipped fighters had gathered. Fully outfitted, the distribution of his clones was visible in how they were carrying themselves. Revival treasures, mana, and healing artifacts, the borrowed weapons and armor. Ready.
But it wasn’t just nine hundred.

Behind them, around them, spread across the ice field in every direction — nearly ten thousand people. The entire population of his dimensional world, or close to it. Ninety percent of them present, the red-skinned Pyrans dominant in number but the humans visible throughout, and the Pyrans in their human-style clothing now, the adjustment to the new wardrobe having happened gradually enough that it no longer looked like costume.

The cold that was bothering some of the humans wasn’t bothering the Pyrans. Fire affinity had practical advantages in an ice field that went beyond combat, and Leon could see the Pyrans managing it naturally while the humans around them were dealing with varying degrees of discomfort. What he also noticed was the Pyrans helping — small gestures, a hand on a shoulder, a brief warmth shared without fanfare. The integration that had seemed uncertain when the Pyrans first arrived had become something else over the months.
That’s good,he thought.
The person who stood out from all of it was Xyra.

Positioned closest to the swirling portal, standing alone in the way that certain presences naturally created space around themselves without requiring it — an ethereal quality in how she existed in the scene, the world spirit visibly separate from the world’s inhabitants even while standing among them. She was wearing different robes from what she usually wore around him, something more composed, less deliberately provocative.
Leon felt genuinely relieved about that.
The admiring looks directed at her from the crowd were considerable. He noticed them and said nothing.

Then he made his entry and the admiring looks redirected, which he also noticed and also said nothing about, though the awareness of it settled somewhere in the back of his mind with a quality he chose not to examine.

He could see Loriel standing at the forefront with the other participants, positioned near the front of the nine hundred. She caught his eye across the distance and gave a small wave that was more restrained than her usual, the dungeon atmosphere apparently having affected her energy levels.

His clone wasn’t present. Leon wasn’t surprised — same mind, same understanding. The clone was out exploring the vast unexplored sections of his rank three world, a task he’d been putting off for too long, given how much it had expanded during the upgrade. Its presence here wasn’t needed. Getting ten thousand people to an ice field was well within the clone’s operational authority.
He walked toward Xyra with Seraphine and Ira beside him.
He noticed Xyra’s eyes before he’d covered half the distance.

She was watching Seraphine and Ira with her silver eyes fully active, the glow in them carrying a specific quality that Leon recognized immediately and felt a chill about that had nothing to do with the ice field.
She’s been watching us again,he thought.Through her world spirit perception. She never gets bored of it. She’s never going to get bored with it.
He was certain of this the way he was certain of very few things.

Seraphine and Ira had both gone slightly stiff. He could feel it without looking at them directly — the subtle shift that happened when someone realized they were being watched by something significantly above their threat ceiling. They’d met Xyra during the training period, had received her advice and her guidance, and had recognized quickly that she was operating at a level well beyond what they could currently perceive the edges of.

Being watched by her with that specific intensity didn’t feel like appreciation. It felt like being the most interesting thing in the room to something ancient and powerful that had decided to pay full attention.
Apex predator,Seraphine was probably thinking. Leon knew her well enough to guess.
Why is she looking at us like that?Ira was probably thinking. Leon knew her well enough to guess that too.
He cleared his throat.
"How long until it opens?" he asked Xyra, injecting the question into the atmosphere with the specific intention of breaking whatever she was doing with her eyes.
Xyra’s silver gaze moved to him.

chapters.title: Chapter 554: Class Reawakening Dungeon Opens
paragraphs: "Now," Xyra said.

Behind her, the portal responded immediately — a sweeping fluctuation rolled outward from it, passing through the crowd like a wave of pressure that made people instinctively steady their footing even though it didn’t knock anyone down. The blackish-blue swirl of the gate shifted, the darkness bleeding out of it, the color becoming a clean, deep blue that pulsed steadily with the rhythm of something that had finished opening and was now simply open.
The Class Reawakening Dungeon was active.
Leon moved forward without announcing it.

He heard Ira start to say something behind him — the beginning of a question that hadn’t finished forming yet — and kept walking, his eyes on the portal. Seraphine said nothing. He could feel her trust in the silence she maintained, the specific quality of someone who had decided to wait and see rather than ask.

He closed the distance to the portal steadily, the blue light growing stronger as he approached, the energy radiating from it pressing against his awareness with a density that confirmed this was something real and significant rather than decorative.
He reached the threshold.
And stopped.

Not by choice. There was no decision to stop — his body simply didn’t move forward, the way a hand doesn’t move through glass. An invisible barrier, present and absolute, sat exactly at the point where one more step would have carried him through. He pressed against it without urgency, confirming what it was, and felt it hold without any indication that effort would change the outcome.
SSS ranked class,he thought.That’s why. The highest possible class rank, and the dungeon won’t accept it.

He’d suspected this. Had prepared for it mentally. But there was a difference between suspecting and confirming, and standing in front of a barrier that his class rank had placed between him and an opportunity that everyone else present could access produced a feeling he sat with briefly before setting it down.
He stepped back and returned to where Seraphine, Ira, and Xyra were standing.

Xyra’s expression didn’t change dramatically. But he caught the quality of the thought moving behind her silver eyes — the specific satisfaction of someone who had just had a conclusion confirmed that they’d already been confident in.
She knew,he thought.She was certain about my class rank, and this just proved it.
He didn’t comment on it and turned to face the crowd.

Nine hundred equipped fighters. Every one of them was looking at him with the focused attention of people who had been preparing for this moment and were about to walk through a portal that might not return them.
He spoke clearly, his voice carrying without effort.

"Some of you won’t come back," he said. "I’m not saying that to frighten you. I’m saying it because it’s true, and you deserve to know it before you go in rather than after you’ve already stepped through. The Class Reawakening Dungeon isn’t designed to be survived by everyone who enters it. Historically, ninety percent of participants or more don’t make it out."
The ice field went very quiet.
"If you want to step back, step back now. There’s no shame in it. You’re not a coward for recognizing that you’re not ready — you’re intelligent. Come back stronger and enter the next one."
He waited.
Nobody moved.

Good,he thought, looking across the gathered faces. The tension was real and visible — the specific tension of people who had heard something true and were holding it rather than dismissing it — but no one retreated. The items he’d provided, the months of training, the resources distributed through his clone — none of it had made them complacent. His words had cut through any complacency that might have been forming and replaced it with the honest weight of what they were walking toward.
He looked at Xyra.

She nodded once — understanding the look, confirming she was ready to do what they’d discussed. Her role during the dungeon’s duration was to maintain the world’s stability and keep watch over the entrance. She would know if something catastrophic happened. She would act if something required her to act.
"Enter," Leon said.
They began moving.

Two at a time, then small groups, the line flowing steadily toward the blue portal with the serious expressions of people who had made a decision and were executing it. Spatial rings on their hands carrying their items, new armor fitted and worn, new weapons either strapped or held. The preparation was visible in how they moved — not cocky, not terrified, somewhere in the honest middle ground between those two things that was the only place from which good decisions got made.
The line shortened minute by minute.

Leon watched each person go through. He didn’t know all of their names — he knew most of the Pyrans who had come through from the original realm, recognized many of the humans, could have identified all of them by the thread of connection his world provided to its inhabitants. But names were different from recognition, and he found himself wanting to know them properly rather than just identifying them by face.
When they come out,he thought.When they come out, I’ll know them.
He held that thought without pressing on it and kept watching.
Eventually, the numbers dwindled to almost nothing.
The ice field emptied steadily until only five figures remained standing near the portal entrance.
Seraphine. Ira. Loriel. Vyra.
And Leon.

The four of them stood looking at the blue portal with four completely different expressions that were somehow all variations of the same thing — readiness, each of them wearing it in their own particular way.
Seraphine was quiet and composed, her new katana at her hip, her amethyst eyes steady.
Ira was practically vibrating with contained energy, the Blazing Fang spear already in her hand, her red hair catching the light of the portal.
Loriel gripped her cane, her expression carrying the specific courage of someone who was frightened and had decided to go anyway, which was the most genuine kind.
Vyra was still and certain, the Sovereign’s Lance across her back, centuries of combat experience sitting in how she held herself.
Leon looked at each of them in turn.
Come back,he thought, though he didn’t say it.All four of you. Come back.

chapters.title: Chapter 555: Class Reawakening Dungeon Opens—1
paragraphs: Leon went to Loriel first.

She was standing slightly apart from the others, close to the portal but not facing it directly, as though looking at it head-on required more composure than she currently had available. Her hands were at her sides. One of them was trembling — not dramatically, just a fine continuous vibration that she probably didn’t know was visible.
Leon put his arms around her.

She went still for a moment, then leaned into it with the specific quality of someone who had been holding tension in their body for a long time and had just been given permission to set some of it down.
He kept his voice low, just for her.
"If you don’t want to go, you don’t have to. A higher-ranked class isn’t worth more than your life. Stay out here — there’s no shame in it, and I mean that completely."
He felt her breathing change as his words landed. The trembling in her hand slowed, then stopped. Her shoulders dropped slightly, the held tension releasing in stages.
He ended the hug and looked at her face.
She looked back at him for one moment with an expression he couldn’t fully read — something that had moved through several things quickly and arrived somewhere resolved.
Then she said, clearly and without hesitation: "I’m going in."
And stepped through the portal before anyone could respond.
Leon stood where he was for a second, looking at the space she’d just occupied.
What made her so resolute,he thought, genuinely surprised.This girl can’t handle a paper cut.

He didn’t have an answer. He respected the decision and let it be what it was. He’d done everything he could to prepare her — the Sanctuary Veil, the cane, the instruction, the foundation work. Whatever happened inside, she was going in with more support than most people entering a Class Reawakening Dungeon had ever had.
Come back,he thought.Please just come back.
"Leon."

He turned. Ira was standing in front of him with her arms spread wide, the Blazing Fang spear held in one hand, her expression carrying the particular brightness she had when she was nervous and choosing not to show it.
He stepped forward and hugged her. She wrapped her free arm around him hard.
"Be careful," he said. "Do your best in there."
"Obviously," she said into his shoulder.
She held on for another second — long enough that he understood it wasn’t casual — and then pulled back and looked at him with something in her eyes that was more serious than her usual register.
Then she turned and dashed straight through the portal without slowing.
That’s Ira,he thought, watching the portal swallow her.Full commitment, no hesitation, second thoughts prohibited.
He turned to Vyra.

She was already looking at him, and the moment his gaze met hers, something shifted in her expression — a memory arriving without warning, visibly, the kind that rearranged your face before you could manage it. Her eyes moved away briefly. Color rose on her skin, deep over the red that was already there; her cheeks genuinely flushed in a way he’d only seen a handful of times.
The hug,he realized.She’s thinking about the mountain.
He kept his expression completely neutral. This was not the moment.

She gathered herself with the speed of someone who had centuries of practice at gathering herself, straightened, and looked at him directly again with the composure she’d rebuilt in approximately two seconds.
"I’ll do my best," she said, her voice steady.
"I know you will," he said simply.

She nodded once — sharp, definitive — and walked through the portal with her back perfectly straight and her face still carrying the faintest trace of color that she was clearly pretending didn’t exist.
Leon shook his head slightly.
Then Seraphine was in front of him.

He pulled her in without preamble, arms around her waist, and she came without resistance, her hands finding their familiar position against his back. He held her properly rather than briefly, the way the moment deserved.
"Be careful," he said. "Watch your positioning when you don’t have your stats. Your instincts are good — trust them more than the system information."
"I know," she said.
"I know you know. I’m saying it anyway."
He felt her smile against his shoulder.

He let her go, and she stepped back and looked at him with the amethyst eyes that had learned a long time ago not to say everything they were thinking. She was excited — he could feel it underneath the composure, the real anticipation of someone who had been working toward this moment for a long time and was finally standing in front of it.
She stepped through the portal without looking back, which was exactly how Seraphine entered things she’d already decided about.
Leon stood in the empty ice field.

The portal pulsed steadily behind him, blue and patient, with all four of them now somewhere inside it. The crowd was gone — he’d already sent everyone back to the settlement with a single directed thought, the teleportation so automatic now it barely registered as an action. The ice field was quiet. The snow kept falling.
He thanked Xyra briefly, meaning it genuinely, and braced slightly for whatever she might decide to do with the gratitude.
She took it with a smug expression and disappeared. No additional requests. No spatial fluctuations were carrying him somewhere he hadn’t agreed to go.
Progress,he thought, with genuine relief.
He stood alone in the ice field for one more moment.

The tower,he decided.Floors to climb, aura ranks to push, and that armor still sitting in inventory that he hadn’t been strong enough to test properly. And the instance reward from floor two — the Legendary Instance Seed, still in his pocket, waiting to be planted in his world.
He had work to do and time to do it in.
He disappeared from the ice field, the snow continuing to fall into the empty space where he’d been standing.

sentences.text: Leon went to Loriel first.
She was standing slightly apart from the others, close to the portal but not facing it directly, as though looking at it head-on required more composure than she currently had available.
Her hands were at her sides.
One of them was trembling — not dramatically, just a fine continuous vibration that she probably didn’t know was visible.
Leon put his arms around her.

She went still for a moment, then leaned into it with the specific quality of someone who had been holding tension in their body for a long time and had just been given permission to set some of it down.
He kept his voice low, just for her.
"If you don’t want to go, you don’t have to.
A higher-ranked class isn’t worth more than your life.
Stay out here — there’s no shame in it, and I mean that completely."
He felt her breathing change as his words landed.
The trembling in her hand slowed, then stopped.
Her shoulders dropped slightly, the held tension releasing in stages.
He ended the hug and looked at her face.
She looked back at him for one moment with an expression he couldn’t fully read — something that had moved through several things quickly and arrived somewhere resolved.
Then she said, clearly and without hesitation: "I’m going in."
And stepped through the portal before anyone could respond.
Leon stood where he was for a second, looking at the space she’d just occupied.
What made her so resolute,he thought, genuinely surprised.This girl can’t handle a paper cut.
He didn’t have an answer.
He respected the decision and let it be what it was.
He’d done everything he could to prepare her — the Sanctuary Veil, the cane, the instruction, the foundation work.
Whatever happened inside, she was going in with more support than most people entering a Class Reawakening Dungeon had ever had.
Come back,he thought.Please just come back.
"Leon."
He turned.

Ira was standing in front of him with her arms spread wide, the Blazing Fang spear held in one hand, her expression carrying the particular brightness she had when she was nervous and choosing not to show it.
He stepped forward and hugged her.
She wrapped her free arm around him hard.
"Be careful," he said.
"Do your best in there."
"Obviously," she said into his shoulder.
She held on for another second — long enough that he understood it wasn’t casual — and then pulled back and looked at him with something in her eyes that was more serious than her usual register.
Then she turned and dashed straight through the portal without slowing.
That’s Ira,he thought, watching the portal swallow her.Full commitment, no hesitation, second thoughts prohibited.
He turned to Vyra.

She was already looking at him, and the moment his gaze met hers, something shifted in her expression — a memory arriving without warning, visibly, the kind that rearranged your face before you could manage it.
Her eyes moved away briefly.
Color rose on her skin, deep over the red that was already there; her cheeks genuinely flushed in a way he’d only seen a handful of times.
The hug,he realized.She’s thinking about the mountain.
He kept his expression completely neutral.
This was not the moment.

She gathered herself with the speed of someone who had centuries of practice at gathering herself, straightened, and looked at him directly again with the composure she’d rebuilt in approximately two seconds.
"I’ll do my best," she said, her voice steady.
"I know you will," he said simply.

She nodded once — sharp, definitive — and walked through the portal with her back perfectly straight and her face still carrying the faintest trace of color that she was clearly pretending didn’t exist.
Leon shook his head slightly.
Then Seraphine was in front of him.
He pulled her in without preamble, arms around her waist, and she came without resistance, her hands finding their familiar position against his back.
He held her properly rather than briefly, the way the moment deserved.
"Be careful," he said.
"Watch your positioning when you don’t have your stats.
Your instincts are good — trust them more than the system information."
"I know," she said.
"I know you know.
I’m saying it anyway."
He felt her smile against his shoulder.
He let her go, and she stepped back and looked at him with the amethyst eyes that had learned a long time ago not to say everything they were thinking.
She was excited — he could feel it underneath the composure, the real anticipation of someone who had been working toward this moment for a long time and was finally standing in front of it.
She stepped through the portal without looking back, which was exactly how Seraphine entered things she’d already decided about.
Leon stood in the empty ice field.
The portal pulsed steadily behind him, blue and patient, with all four of them now somewhere inside it.
The crowd was gone — he’d already sent everyone back to the settlement with a single directed thought, the teleportation so automatic now it barely registered as an action.
The ice field was quiet.
The snow kept falling.
He thanked Xyra briefly, meaning it genuinely, and braced slightly for whatever she might decide to do with the gratitude.
She took it with a smug expression and disappeared.
No additional requests.
No spatial fluctuations were carrying him somewhere he hadn’t agreed to go.
Progress,he thought, with genuine relief.
He stood alone in the ice field for one more moment.
The tower,he decided.Floors to climb, aura ranks to push, and that armor still sitting in inventory that he hadn’t been strong enough to test properly.
And the instance reward from floor two — the Legendary Instance Seed, still in his pocket, waiting to be planted in his world.
He had work to do and time to do it in.
He disappeared from the ice field, the snow continuing to fall into the empty space where he’d been standing.

chapters.title: Chapter 556: Mythical Armor
paragraphs: Leon arrived at the glass field.

The crystalline ground stretched in every direction, flat and empty, catching the dimensional world’s ambient light and scattering it in the particular way that had become familiar over the months of training here. Nobody else came to this location. He’d chosen it originally for exactly that reason and kept returning for the same one.
He didn’t take out the mythical armor yet.
One thing at a time,he thought, settling into the open space.Armor after training. Instance dungeon placement after that, close to the tower where it makes sense.

The mythical armor had been sitting in his inventory for months, patient and untouched, waiting for him to reach the point where attempting to equip it wasn’t a gamble with his life. He wasn’t certain he was there yet. But he was considerably stronger than he’d been the last time he’d seriously considered it, and the Cradle Seed had changed the relationship between him and every element he carried in ways he was still discovering.

The instance dungeon he’d plant near the tower — ten or so kilometers from the Pyran and human settlement, close enough to be accessible, far enough that whatever the instance produced wouldn’t interfere with daily life in the settlement.
But first: aura ranks.

He’d felt what level five aura actually meant when he’d broken through in ice and lightning. The difference wasn’t just quantitative — the element stopped being something he wielded and started being something he was. No mana activation required. No reaching for it. Just presence, the affinity existing in him at a depth that made the distinction between him and the element genuinely unclear.
He wanted every affinity he’d developed to that point.

He messaged Xyra through their connection — a simple request, familiar by now — and felt the time field activate around him. The familiar sensation of time thickening, the 1000x ratio settling into place, the outside world slowing to irrelevance.
He sat down, closed his eyes, and began.
The training consumed him completely.

He lost track of time in the way he only did when something was working — when the engagement was deep enough that the monitoring part of his mind went quiet and left only the doing. Wind aura, fire aura, water aura, life aura, light aura, time aura — working through each one in sequence, pushing comprehension downward into the element rather than upward into application, looking for the depth that had produced the breakthrough in ice and lightning.
Some came more easily than others.

Fire responded quickly — the long familiarity with it through combat and through Ira’s fire affinity producing a context that made the deepening feel almost natural. Water took longer but moved steadily. Wind had a particular quality that required a different approach, less direct pressure and more passive listening, the element responding better to attention than to effort.

Life element surprised him. The depth he found there was different from the others — warmer, more complex, carrying a quality that felt less like mastering an element and more like being recognized by one. He sat with it longer than the others and came out of it changed in a way he couldn’t immediately articulate.
Space aura, holy aura, and illusion aura hit a wall.

He pushed at all three repeatedly across what felt like months of internal time and found the same resistance each time — not the resistance of something that needed more effort, but the resistance of something that needed a different kind of development entirely. Real battle. Real stakes. The kind of experience that comprehension alone couldn’t substitute for.
I’ve been in this field,he thought.Space and holy and illusion need something I can’t find here.
He accepted it without frustration. He knew the difference between a wall that required more force and a wall that required a different door.
Dark aura was the unexpected breakthrough.

He hadn’t expected it to be the first of the remaining affinities to reach level five — it was one of his newer acquisitions, developed more recently than most of the others. But when he pressed into the dark element’s comprehension, something responded that hadn’t been there before the Cradle Seed, a depth that the previous rank seven had been sitting above rather than inside.

And then there was the memory of the first tower floor. The being he’d fought who had possessed level five dark aura — the intimate exposure to that level of dark element in real combat, his body and his awareness having been thoroughly acquainted with what that depth felt like from the outside. The experience had done something he hadn’t consciously registered at the time. A blueprint, lodged somewhere below deliberate memory.
CRACK.

The dark aura broke through with a sharp internal sound that he felt more than heard, and the element settled into him at the new level with a completeness that the other breakthroughs had shared. Present. Permanent. Part of him rather than available to him.
Dark element,he thought, opening his eyes briefly to register the moment.Level five.

He felt the control that came with it — a profundity in how he could work with darkness that hadn’t existed at level four. Shadows responded. Concealment deepened. The gap between intent and execution in dark element applications essentially vanished.
He closed his eyes and kept going.
Eventually he stopped.

Not because he’d achieved everything — space, holy, and illusion remained at level four, the wall unchanged. But because the work that could be done here was done, and continuing to push against the same resistance was diminishing returns rather than progress.
He messaged his clone through their shared awareness.
How long outside?
Just under a day,came back immediately.Settlement is stable. Dragon still in coma. No significant events.
Three years of training. One day outside.

Leon stood up, stretched, and felt the accumulated development of three years sitting in him — not as fatigue, which the 1000x time had compressed into something his physiology handled without difficulty, but as presence. He was significantly stronger than he’d been when he sat down.
The Cradle Seed made this possible,he thought again.Without that affinity improvement, three years wouldn’t have been enough.
He reached into his soul-connected inventory.

The mythical armor came out in its glass casing, the same protective shell that had incinerated the ancient entity’s hand on contact during their time in the dimensional world. It sat in his palm warm and steady, the armor inside visible through the crystalline exterior — crimson scales edged with molten gold, the dragon emblem on the chest plate, the whole set radiating quiet, absolute authority.
He looked at it for a long moment.
Let’s see if I’m ready for you,he thought.

chapters.title: Chapter 557: Mythical Armor—1
paragraphs: Leon looked at the mythical armor in its protective casing and made a decision.
Everything I have,he thought.Every single thing.
He set the casing down in the center of the glass field, stepped back a hundred meters, and started.

First pass — his epic-ranked sword channeling everything he had into a single focused strike, holy energy and spatial compression combined. The blow landed and produced a sound like reality objecting.
CRACK!
He inspected the casing.
A hairline scratch. Already fading.
So that’s how it is,he thought.

He tried again. Different approach — ice and lightning fused, the combination that had served him well against the hardest targets he’d faced. He drove it into the casing with the precision of someone who understood exactly what they were targeting.
Another scratch. Fading faster than the first.

He spent the next several hours working through everything systematically. Every skill he possessed. Every technique he’d developed across the tower, the dimensional world training, the years compressed into days. Individual elements first, then combinations, then combinations of combinations, each attempt producing marginally more effect than the previous and each effect healing before he could build on it.
It’s not working,he thought, watching another scratch fade to nothing.Not even close to working.
He activated Elemental Surge.

The boost hit him like a wave — his affinity ranks climbing from their natural level through seven, past the uncertain territory of seven-plus, arriving at something that could only be described as rank eight temporarily. Every element responded at that level simultaneously, and for the duration of the skill’s window Leon felt what it meant to exist at that depth of elemental mastery.
This,he thought, his whole body humming with the combined resonance of every element at rank eight,is what it means to be a god of elements.

The feeling was not metaphorical. Every element in the air around him bent toward his awareness without effort. Space folded at a thought. Fire existed because he decided it existed. Lightning was his nervous system externalized. The entire elemental spectrum responded to him the way his own hands responded to him — without intermediary, without effort, without any gap between intent and reality.
He channeled all of it into his sword.

The blade transformed — not the metal changing but the space the metal occupied filling with something that exceeded what metal should be able to contain. Every element layered simultaneously, white holy energy woven through the combination as stabilizer, the whole construct blazing with a light that had no single color because it contained all of them.
He threw everything into the casing.

The strikes continued for hours more, each one drawing deeper than the last, the toll accumulating in ways his body registered with increasing honesty. Blood vessels in his hands burst and sealed, burst and sealed, holy energy working continuously to keep him functional as the mana expenditure climbed toward numbers that should have been impossible to sustain.
His body was not happy about any of this.
One more,he thought, tasting blood again.One real one.
He stepped back. Several hundred kilometers, teleporting in rapid succession, each jump covering more distance than the last as his newly expanded spatial range demonstrated itself.
Above him, he built the attack.

Not a sword exactly — a concept that happened to be shaped like a sword, enormous, spanning the sky above the glass field, every element he possessed poured into its construction without reservation. Thirty thousand mana. Everything. His blood vessels were announcing their displeasure loudly and he ignored them, holy energy and his Primordial Void Heart working in tandem to keep him standing while he put the last of what he had into the construct above him.
His hands were trembling. Both of them. Blood on his lips, on his chin, on his clothes.
This is it,he thought.Everything I have right now in this world in this body at this moment.
He launched it.
BOOOOOOOOOOM!

The sound wasn’t a sound. It was a physical event, a pressure wave that traveled outward from the impact point at speeds that made the concept of running from it irrelevant. Leon teleported the moment he released the construct — once, twice, three times in rapid succession, each jump several kilometers, putting as much distance between himself and the impact as his depleted mana could manage.
It wasn’t enough.

The shockwave caught him at twenty kilometers and hit like a wall made of compressed air and force and the aftermath of thirty thousand mana detonating against a surface that hadn’t wanted to accept it. His ribs announced themselves with a sound he felt rather than heard — not broken, but the kind of cracked that left no ambiguity about how close to broken was.
He was airborne for a moment and then not, the ground finding him rather than the other way around.
He coughed blood, which was becoming a familiar sensation, and let the holy energy work.

Five hundred kilometers away, in the settlement, James was mid-sermon when the ground moved beneath the congregation’s feet and a sound arrived that had no business existing at that distance. The new converts — Pyrans and humans both, Pope James having made considerable progress with his mission — looked around with expressions ranging from alarmed to curious.
James looked up from his text with the serene expression of a man whose faith had specific and well-tested dimensions.
"Our God is working," he said, and returned to his sermon without further comment. The congregation settled. This was simply what living in Leon’s world sometimes involved.

His wife Mia, sitting in the front row with their daughter on her lap, caught his eye with a look that communicated considerable skepticism about his calm. He gave her the small private smile that he reserved for her specifically.
She shook her head and looked forward.
Leon healed, stood, and floated to the crater.

Several kilometers wide. Deep enough that filling it with water would produce a lake of meaningful size. The glass field around it had been transformed — the crystalline ground compressed and rearranged, the impact having done more to the landscape than any of his previous training combined.
He looked at the casing at the crater’s center.

A circular crack sat in the transparent encasing. Small — the size of a bullet entry point, the geometry of it almost delicate against the scale of what had produced it. Around the crack, a visible healing process was underway, the material knitting itself back together in real time.
He stared at it.
That’s the first time I’ve actually damaged it,he realized.Every previous attempt was too shallow for it to bother responding to.
He watched the healing complete itself. The crack sealed. The casing returned to its previous flawless state as though nothing had touched it.
Leon’s mouth hung open slightly.

He’d put thirty thousand mana into a single attack. Had cracked his own ribs from the shockwave at twenty kilometers. Had spent an entire subjective day attempting every technique and skill combination he possessed.
And he had produced a crack the size of a coin that had healed in thirty seconds.
I cannot open this,he thought, with the flat clarity of someone arriving at an honest conclusion rather than a defeated one.Not now. Not with what I currently am.
He reached for the casing to store it back in his inventory.
The spatial fluctuation happened right beside him.

chapters.title: Chapter 558: Mythical Armor—2
paragraphs: Leon recognized the fluctuation immediately.

Xyra materialized beside him, her silver hair drifting in the absence of any wind, and stood looking at the destruction around them without speaking. Her gaze moved across the crater first — several kilometers wide, the glass field transformed beyond recognition — then to the scattered evidence of every failed attempt he’d made across the past subjective day, and finally to the casing sitting undamaged at the crater’s center.
She said nothing.
Leon stood beside her and felt the silence become increasingly uncomfortable with each passing second.
Why is she here,he thought.And why is she just staring.
He lasted approximately thirty seconds before he couldn’t stand it anymore.
"Why are you here?" he asked. "And why are you looking at me like that?"
She didn’t answer the question. Instead she looked at him directly and said: "Give me your hand."
Leon hesitated for exactly one second — processing the request, finding no obvious reason to refuse, reminding himself of the contract — and extended his right hand toward her.
Pain detonated through his wrist.

Sharp, clean, complete — the specific pain of something that had happened too fast to be prevented and had already finished happening before his nervous system fully registered the beginning of it. He looked down.
His hand was severed at the wrist.

Clean cut, the kind of precision that left no ragged edges, blood beginning to spray in the rhythmic way that meant something serious had just happened to something important. His hand sat a single inch from his wrist, separated, the gap between them impossibly neat.
She can’t harm me,his mind started.The contract says she can’t—
Then his hand was back.

Not healed — back. Restored. The cut was gone, the blood was gone, his wrist was completely intact and had apparently always been completely intact. The entire event had occurred and been undone in less time than it took him to form the thought about the contract.
He stared at his hand.
What,he thought.
"Look there," Xyra said.
Her voice was calm. She was pointing at the crater’s center, where the mythical armor’s casing sat.
A crackling sound was coming from it.

Leon looked and felt the pieces assemble in his mind simultaneously. On the surface of the transparent casing — which had resisted thirty thousand mana and a full day of his absolute best efforts without producing anything more significant than a coin-sized crack that healed in thirty seconds — a fracture was spreading.
On its surface, a small amount of liquid was visible. Deep red with a slight golden undertone.
His blood.

The single drop of blood that Xyra had obtained from the clean cut she’d made and immediately reversed had landed on the casing, and the casing was breaking. Not healing — breaking, the fractures spreading outward from where the blood had contacted it with the momentum of something that had been waiting for exactly this and had now received it.
The casing shattered.

Clean, complete, final — it came apart like thin glass struck by a precise force, the pieces dissolving into nothing before they could even fall, and the mythical armor sat in the open air of the crater for the first time since Leon had acquired it.
Leon stared at it.
Then he stared at the space where the casing had been.
Then he looked at his hand, which remained entirely intact.
A day,he thought.I spent an entire subjective day. Thirty thousand mana. Cracked ribs. Blood. And she just—
"Leon."
He looked at her.
"Do you feel stupid right now?"

The question was delivered without cruelty and without particular softness. Just honest. She genuinely wanted to know, or genuinely already knew and was giving him the opportunity to acknowledge it himself.
He felt his face do something involuntary. His head lowered slightly.
"Yes," he said, to the ground somewhere near his feet.

Xyra continued without letting the moment breathe too long. She told him what she thought of his approach — the brute forcing, the complete absence of coming to ask her first, the pattern she’d observed across everything she’d watched him do in which he threw himself at problems headfirst and relied on his luck and his constitution to survive the consequences. She’d watched him do this repeatedly from her cage. She’d watched him do it after. The fact that he was alive was not a testament to good judgment. It was a testament to luck that she found genuinely remarkable and slightly infuriating to witness.
Leon listened to all of this with his head still angled slightly downward and the expression of someone absorbing accurate information about themselves.
She also told him about the armor.

It had consciousness, she said. She’d felt it from a significant distance — a presence inside the mythical armor that was aware of its surroundings and had been aware of everything Leon had been doing for the past fourteen subjective hours. The consciousness had watched him. Had not attacked him, despite having the capability to do so and despite the significant provocation of someone spending an entire day slamming various forms of energy against its housing.

Two reasons for that restraint. The first was recognition — the armor had known, from whatever sense a conscious mythical armor used to know things, that the person attacking its casing was the same person who owned it. The second was, in Xyra’s estimation, something closer to entertainment. Fourteen hours of increasingly desperate attempts from the armor’s owner had apparently constituted sufficient spectacle that attacking had seemed like an interruption.
It was watching me,Leon thought.The entire time. Finding it funny.
He wasn’t entirely sure how to feel about that.

"You don’t need to think about repayment," Xyra said then, her tone shifting into something that was still matter-of-fact but carried a different quality underneath it. "I’ll help you when you need it. We have all the time in the world — neither of us is going anywhere."
As she said the last part, her silver eyes moved over him with an unhurried deliberateness that made the statement feel like it was carrying more than its literal meaning.
"But," she added, and her voice gained an edge that made the back of his neck do something, "if I find you doing something this reckless again without coming to me first, there will be consequences."
She left the nature of those consequences entirely unspecified, which was somehow worse than a specific threat.
Leon nodded at her with the reliable frequency of a mechanical toy.
"Good," she said, apparently satisfied, and looked at the mythical armor now sitting exposed in the crater.
Leon followed her gaze.

The armor was exactly what he remembered from that first glimpse — crimson scales edged with molten gold, the dragon emblem on the chest plate alive with something that wasn’t quite light. The greaves and gauntlets and helm all present, all waiting, radiating the quiet authority of something that had existed for a very long time and expected to continue existing for considerably longer.
It was the most beautiful and the most dangerous thing he’d ever looked at that wasn’t Xyra.
Now what,he thought, looking at the conscious mythical armor that had spent fourteen hours watching him make a fool of himself.

chapters.title: Chapter 559: Mythical Armor—3
paragraphs: Now that Leon had acknowledged his stupidity with sufficient sincerity, Xyra appeared satisfied.
"Try to merge with the armor," she said. "It will be fine."
Leon looked at her.

She had just finished telling him — at length and with considerable directness — that he was reckless, that his habit of throwing himself at problems without thinking was going to get him killed someday, and that the only reason it hadn’t yet was luck she found personally insulting to witness. And now she was telling him to walk up to a conscious mythical armor that had watched him make a fool of himself for fourteen hours and try to merge with it.
He looked at her for slightly too long.
Her silver eyes narrowed.
"Are you doubting me?" Her voice carried a specific quality that he’d learned to recognize. "You’re really asking for a spanking. I said it will be fine. Go."
Leon moved immediately.

The word spanking had a remarkable effect on his decision-making speed. He walked toward the armor without further deliberation, approaching across the crater floor, his hand extending toward it slowly — cautiously, with the careful movement of someone who had just watched the casing that had survived thirty thousand mana shatter from a single drop of blood.
The armor didn’t wait for him to finish the approach.
It moved.

Lightning fast — faster than his spatial awareness gave him useful warning about, the mythical armor simply deciding that his pace was unacceptable and resolving the distance itself. It hit him like liquid mercury at high velocity, and the first thing that happened was that everything he was wearing ceased to exist.

Clothes, light armor, everything — gone in the same instant the mythical armor made contact, burned away so completely that there was no residue, not even ash. The molten metal — because that was what it felt like, liquid and impossibly hot — began crawling across his skin with the purposeful movement of something that knew exactly where it was going.
It was the most painful thing he had ever experienced.

Leon had high pain tolerance. He knew this about himself with some confidence, having established the reference points through a series of genuinely terrible experiences. The race change. The fight with the ancient entity. The dimensional world battle that had left bones exposed. He had calibrated his understanding of pain against those events and considered himself informed on the subject.
This was worse than all of them.

The molten heat moving across every surface of his body — every surface, none of them spared, his brain receiving the information from all of them simultaneously — produced sounds from him that he had not planned to make. Not quiet sounds. Genuine, involuntary, completely undignified sounds, because the pain was at a level where social considerations stopped being relevant.
He heard himself and didn’t stop because stopping required a decision and decisions required cognitive resources he was currently allocating entirely to remaining upright.
From a distance, Xyra watched with the relaxed attention of someone viewing something she found very interesting.
Then the molten armor began trying to enter his body.

The pain increased by an order of magnitude that he would not have previously considered possible. It was trying to integrate — pushing through his skin, finding the pathways between muscle and bone, looking for wherever it needed to go to become what it was supposed to become. His blood was flowing in places and sealing in others, his holy energy and his Primordial Void Heart working frantically to keep him functional while something mythical rank rewrote the terms of his physical existence.
He screamed.

Not continuously — in bursts, between the grinding effort of staying on his feet, his teeth clamped together in the intervals between the sounds his body was making without his permission. The experience he’d had with soul-level pain during the tower gave him just enough reference point to hold himself upright rather than collapsing. Just enough. The margin was not comfortable.
This is worse,he thought, in the fragments of coherent thought available to him.This is genuinely worse than that.
Two minutes.

Approximately two minutes of subjective time that felt like several hours, during which Leon experienced the full range of what it meant to have a conscious mythical armor decide to integrate with a host it had apparently selected during a fourteen-hour circus performance and chosen not to incinerate.
Then it stopped.
The heat was gone. The liquid metal was gone. The pain was gone — completely, instantly, the way pain stopped when its cause stopped rather than gradually.
Leon looked down at himself.

No armor. No clothes. No anything covering him except for golden patterns that traced across his skin in designs he recognized from the armor’s surface — the dragon emblem on his chest, scales suggested in the markings along his forearms and shoulders, intricate detail work running down to his hands. The patterns glowed faintly, warm rather than hot now, and he felt no pain from them despite their appearance.
His legs had approximately enough structural integrity left to lower him toward the ground in something that resembled a controlled descent before giving up entirely.

As the ground came up toward him, his vision caught something in the corner of his awareness — the translucent golden screen of his system flickering to life, multiple notifications stacked on top of each other, the text moving across his fading vision with the patient insistence of something that considered itself important regardless of timing.
He ignored all of it completely.
Later,he thought, with the absolute conviction of someone whose body had just been rewritten by a mythical consciousness and who had exactly zero remaining capacity for reading notifications.

The screen stayed visible for a moment longer, as though mildly offended by being dismissed, and then Xyra’s arms caught him and the notifications slid to the peripheral edge of his awareness where they would wait until he had the energy to look at them.
He didn’t reach the ground.

Xyra was beside him before he could fall, moving with a speed that didn’t announce itself, her arms catching him with a steadiness that made his current state of complete exhaustion feel adequately supported. He found himself leaning against her, which he lacked the energy to have opinions about.

She looked at him with an expression that was softer than her usual register — the ethereal beauty of her face carrying something that was genuine concern underneath its composure, her silver eyes moving across him with an attention that was checking rather than enjoying.
"Are you alright?" she asked, her voice quiet in a way he hadn’t heard from her before.

The softness of the question, combined with the face it was delivered from, combined with the way she was holding him — if he hadn’t known her, Leon thought distantly, he would have been completely undone by this moment. Completely. Without defense. He would have looked at her and felt something that would have required significant time to recover from.
He knew her.

Which meant the softness made him nervous rather than vulnerable, and the beauty made him cautious rather than charmed, and the concern — genuine as he believed it was — arrived in his awareness wrapped in the context of everything else she was.
"Fine," he said, his voice somewhat less steady than he would have preferred. "I’m fine."
She looked at him for a moment longer.
Then the smile appeared — small, knowing, the expression of someone who had observed something they found satisfying and wasn’t bothering to conceal it.
Leon decided he was well enough to stand on his own and began the process of making that true.

chapters.title: Chapter 560: Impressive Armor
paragraphs: Getting away from Xyra was not as simple as stepping back.

Leon moved to create distance and her hand moved with him, a casual and completely unapologetic contact that made him go very still for exactly one second before continuing his retreat at a slightly faster pace.

"You owe me," she said, her silver eyes carrying the specific satisfaction of someone who had just collected a down payment on a larger debt. "Next time the repayment is going to be considerably more substantial."
Leon processed this information.
"Noted," he said, with the tone of someone who had decided that engaging further was not strategically sound.

She looked at him for one more moment — the unhurried assessment of someone who had all the time in the world and was content to use it — and then disappeared. Clean teleportation, no announcement, simply present and then not.
Leon stood alone in the crater.
Considerably more substantial,he thought, looking at the empty space where she’d been.What does that even mean for her specifically.
He decided not to follow that thought to its conclusion and turned his attention to something considerably safer.

The golden patterns on his skin caught the dimensional world’s ambient light in a way that shifted depending on how he moved — not quite glowing, not quite not glowing, the markings sitting at the threshold between those two states. He’d been aware of them since the integration finished but hadn’t properly examined them yet. The dragon emblem on his chest was the largest and most detailed. The scale-like patterns along his forearms had a precision that suggested intention rather than decoration.
He felt no heat from any of it. No discomfort. No weight. The patterns existed on him the way his own skin existed — completely, neutrally present.
Control,he thought, reaching for the heat experimentally.
It responded.

Not like channeling an element through mana — more direct than that, more immediate, the heat existing in the patterns already and simply needing direction rather than generation. He pushed it outward in a controlled test, directing it toward a rare-ranked spear he’d pulled from his inventory.
The spear melted.

Not slowly — the metal softened and lost its shape within seconds, the rare-ranked material unable to manage what the armor was producing even at a fraction of what Leon suspected was available. He pulled the heat back and the remaining metal solidified into a misshapen lump on the crater floor.
Interesting,he thought.

He pushed further, directing the heat at an epic-ranked piece he’d kept in inventory — one of the spare weapons from the pre-dungeon distribution, solid and well-made, the best the cosmic shop had offered at that tier.
Nothing.
He increased the intensity.
Still nothing. The epic-ranked weapon absorbed the heat without visible response, the material quality simply sufficient to handle what he was producing.
There’s a ceiling,he realized.Rare rank is the limit of what the heat alone can do. Epic is beyond it.
He filed that honestly. The heat function was an addition, not the core of what he was working with. He set it aside and focused on what the armor actually was.
He willed it.

The golden patterns responded — the markings lifting slightly from his skin and spreading, the liquid-metal quality returning but differently from the integration process. Controlled this time, directed by his intent, the armor forming over his body in a smooth continuous motion rather than the overwhelming crash of the initial merging.
It looked nothing like the armor in the casing.

That armor had been regal. Crimson scales and molten gold edging, the dragon emblem blazing, the entire set radiating the authority of something ancient and significant. What covered him now was gold but different gold — bronze mixed through it, the color muted, the surface texture simpler. Thin where the original had been substantial. The design was surprisingly modern despite the mythical origin, closer to a fitted suit than traditional armor, covering everything without bulk or restriction.
He looked down at himself and felt the faint dissatisfaction of someone who had seen the premium version and was currently working with something two to three tiers below it.
It’s not the full armor,he thought.This is what I can access right now.

What he didn’t know — couldn’t know, since the armor’s consciousness was present but not yet communicating with him directly — was that the design wasn’t random. The consciousness had reached into his memory during the integration and selected the aesthetic based on what it found there, the modern fitted quality reflecting something from his previous life that had lodged in the armor’s understanding of what he was. It had chosen a form suited to him specifically rather than defaulting to its own preferences.
He didn’t know any of this. He just looked at the bronze-gold suit and thought it was actually quite good despite being below the full version, and started testing.
He tested for hours.

The 1000x time field was still active — Xyra had left it running, either intentionally or because canceling it hadn’t occurred to her before she teleported away — and he used every minute of it. Systematic testing, moving through every category of attack he could produce and measuring the armor’s response to each.
Epic-ranked sword strike at full strength with single elemental enhancement.
Light scratch.

The blade made contact, the enhancement added force that should have been meaningful against almost anything at his current tier, and the result was a mark on the armor’s surface that faded within seconds and left a scratch on his skin underneath that was shallow enough to be almost insulting in how minor it was.
That’s impressive,he thought, running his fingers across the fading mark.Genuinely impressive.

He hit it again. Different angle, different enhancement, same result. Then a combination strike — sword plus spatial compression, the two forces working together the way he’d developed during the dimensional world training.
Light scratch. Fading.
He pulled out a rare-ranked weapon and struck with the same configuration.
Nothing. Not even a mark on the armor’s surface, let alone anything reaching his skin underneath.
He stood back and looked at what he’d established.
Rare rank and below: couldn’t penetrate the armor at all, regardless of technique or enhancement combination. The defense was absolute at that tier.

Epic rank: could penetrate, but the result was a light scratch that faded quickly and left minimal damage to the body underneath. The armor wasn’t invulnerable to epic-ranked attacks — it was just dramatically better at handling them than anything he’d previously worn.
And that’s the incomplete version,he thought.Two tiers below what it actually is.

He thought about what full access would look like. If the bronze-gold incomplete form was handling epic-ranked strikes from his own abnormal strength with light scratches that faded in seconds, the full crimson-and-gold version was operating in a category he didn’t currently have reference points for.
I need to get stronger,he thought, not with frustration but with the clear-eyed recognition of someone who had just been shown where the ceiling was and understood what reaching it would require.
He also felt, underneath the analytical assessment, something simpler.

He liked the armor. Genuinely liked it — the way it moved with him, the complete absence of weight or restriction, the fact that it functioned as clothing equally well as protection and meant he’d never need to worry about a fight destroying what he was wearing again.
The consciousness that had designed it based on his own memory had made a good choice.
He didn’t know that yet.
But he appreciated the result anyway.

sentences.text: Getting away from Xyra was not as simple as stepping back.

Leon moved to create distance and her hand moved with him, a casual and completely unapologetic contact that made him go very still for exactly one second before continuing his retreat at a slightly faster pace.
"You owe me," she said, her silver eyes carrying the specific satisfaction of someone who had just collected a down payment on a larger debt.
"Next time the repayment is going to be considerably more substantial."
Leon processed this information.
"Noted," he said, with the tone of someone who had decided that engaging further was not strategically sound.
She looked at him for one more moment — the unhurried assessment of someone who had all the time in the world and was content to use it — and then disappeared.
Clean teleportation, no announcement, simply present and then not.
Leon stood alone in the crater.
Considerably more substantial,he thought, looking at the empty space where she’d been.What does that even mean for her specifically.
He decided not to follow that thought to its conclusion and turned his attention to something considerably safer.

The golden patterns on his skin caught the dimensional world’s ambient light in a way that shifted depending on how he moved — not quite glowing, not quite not glowing, the markings sitting at the threshold between those two states.
He’d been aware of them since the integration finished but hadn’t properly examined them yet.
The dragon emblem on his chest was the largest and most detailed.
The scale-like patterns along his forearms had a precision that suggested intention rather than decoration.
He felt no heat from any of it.
No discomfort.
No weight.
The patterns existed on him the way his own skin existed — completely, neutrally present.
Control,he thought, reaching for the heat experimentally.
It responded.
Not like channeling an element through mana — more direct than that, more immediate, the heat existing in the patterns already and simply needing direction rather than generation.
He pushed it outward in a controlled test, directing it toward a rare-ranked spear he’d pulled from his inventory.
The spear melted.
Not slowly — the metal softened and lost its shape within seconds, the rare-ranked material unable to manage what the armor was producing even at a fraction of what Leon suspected was available.
He pulled the heat back and the remaining metal solidified into a misshapen lump on the crater floor.
Interesting,he thought.

He pushed further, directing the heat at an epic-ranked piece he’d kept in inventory — one of the spare weapons from the pre-dungeon distribution, solid and well-made, the best the cosmic shop had offered at that tier.
Nothing.
He increased the intensity.
Still nothing.
The epic-ranked weapon absorbed the heat without visible response, the material quality simply sufficient to handle what he was producing.
There’s a ceiling,he realized.Rare rank is the limit of what the heat alone can do.
Epic is beyond it.
He filed that honestly.
The heat function was an addition, not the core of what he was working with.
He set it aside and focused on what the armor actually was.
He willed it.
The golden patterns responded — the markings lifting slightly from his skin and spreading, the liquid-metal quality returning but differently from the integration process.
Controlled this time, directed by his intent, the armor forming over his body in a smooth continuous motion rather than the overwhelming crash of the initial merging.
It looked nothing like the armor in the casing.
That armor had been regal.
Crimson scales and molten gold edging, the dragon emblem blazing, the entire set radiating the authority of something ancient and significant.
What covered him now was gold but different gold — bronze mixed through it, the color muted, the surface texture simpler.
Thin where the original had been substantial.
The design was surprisingly modern despite the mythical origin, closer to a fitted suit than traditional armor, covering everything without bulk or restriction.
He looked down at himself and felt the faint dissatisfaction of someone who had seen the premium version and was currently working with something two to three tiers below it.
It’s not the full armor,he thought.This is what I can access right now.
What he didn’t know — couldn’t know, since the armor’s consciousness was present but not yet communicating with him directly — was that the design wasn’t random.

The consciousness had reached into his memory during the integration and selected the aesthetic based on what it found there, the modern fitted quality reflecting something from his previous life that had lodged in the armor’s understanding of what he was.
It had chosen a form suited to him specifically rather than defaulting to its own preferences.
He didn’t know any of this.
He just looked at the bronze-gold suit and thought it was actually quite good despite being below the full version, and started testing.
He tested for hours.
The 1000x time field was still active — Xyra had left it running, either intentionally or because canceling it hadn’t occurred to her before she teleported away — and he used every minute of it.
Systematic testing, moving through every category of attack he could produce and measuring the armor’s response to each.
Epic-ranked sword strike at full strength with single elemental enhancement.
Light scratch.

The blade made contact, the enhancement added force that should have been meaningful against almost anything at his current tier, and the result was a mark on the armor’s surface that faded within seconds and left a scratch on his skin underneath that was shallow enough to be almost insulting in how minor it was.
That’s impressive,he thought, running his fingers across the fading mark.Genuinely impressive.
He hit it again.
Different angle, different enhancement, same result.
Then a combination strike — sword plus spatial compression, the two forces working together the way he’d developed during the dimensional world training.
Light scratch.
Fading.
He pulled out a rare-ranked weapon and struck with the same configuration.
Nothing.
Not even a mark on the armor’s surface, let alone anything reaching his skin underneath.
He stood back and looked at what he’d established.
Rare rank and below: couldn’t penetrate the armor at all, regardless of technique or enhancement combination.
The defense was absolute at that tier.
Epic rank: could penetrate, but the result was a light scratch that faded quickly and left minimal damage to the body underneath.
The armor wasn’t invulnerable to epic-ranked attacks — it was just dramatically better at handling them than anything he’d previously worn.
And that’s the incomplete version,he thought.Two tiers below what it actually is.
He thought about what full access would look like.

If the bronze-gold incomplete form was handling epic-ranked strikes from his own abnormal strength with light scratches that faded in seconds, the full crimson-and-gold version was operating in a category he didn’t currently have reference points for.
I need to get stronger,he thought, not with frustration but with the clear-eyed recognition of someone who had just been shown where the ceiling was and understood what reaching it would require.
He also felt, underneath the analytical assessment, something simpler.
He liked the armor.

Genuinely liked it — the way it moved with him, the complete absence of weight or restriction, the fact that it functioned as clothing equally well as protection and meant he’d never need to worry about a fight destroying what he was wearing again.
The consciousness that had designed it based on his own memory had made a good choice.
He didn’t know that yet.
But he appreciated the result anyway.

chapters.title: Chapter 561: Moving Forward
paragraphs: Seraphine advanced through the dark.

The dungeon had taken almost everything from her. She was back at level one, her skills were gone, and none of the techniques connected to the system would respond. Only the katana in her grip still felt natural.
Months of progress had been peeled away, leaving the foundation underneath.
Stay calm,she told herself.The foundation is enough. It has to be.
The enemy ahead moved too quickly. Nothing at this level should have possessed that kind of speed, but the dungeon clearly had no interest in fair scaling.

Seraphine reacted before thought could slow her down. Her basic comprehension of lightning, drilled into her until it had become instinct, answered without help from the system. Her body followed lessons it had truly learned rather than commands supplied from somewhere else.
She made it through the clash alive.
By almost nothing,she thought as she checked for injuries.Still counts.
Then she continued.

There was no way to know where the others had been sent or how far into the dungeon she had already traveled. She had darkness, a katana, and the difference between knowledge she genuinely possessed and power the system had once provided.
Leon told us to rely on the foundation.
Her grip tightened.
That’s what I’m doing.
Ira’s progress was considerably louder.
"COME AND TRY!"

The dungeon had taken her spear along with the rest of her equipment. It had reduced her to level one and left her with nothing except her body, her understanding of fire, and an unavoidable test of how much of that power belonged to her rather than the system.
Apparently, more of it belonged to her than she had realized.

The flames she summoned were technically level one, but they didn’t behave that way. Her comprehension ran far deeper than the dungeon’s limits seemed prepared for. The fire formed quickly, answered without hesitation, and burned with heat the surrounding environment had clearly failed to predict.
Three enemies moved around her inside the tight chamber where she’d appeared.
Ira grinned at them.
I’m enjoying this.
She knew exactly what that implied about her.
Then she charged.

There was nothing elegant about the attack. Ira drove forward with brute physical aggression and allowed the flames to act according to their nature under the control of someone who understood them and had no desire to hold back.
Two enemies abruptly chose retreat over continuing the fight.
"Yeah," Ira called after them. "That’s what I figured."
Vyra remained composed.

She had been that way since entering the dungeon. Judging by the number of enemies she had already killed, several hours had likely passed. Her level, skills, and access to the system were gone, leaving her in a condition that would have ruined an ordinary person.
Vyra had never been ordinary.
Centuries of accumulated understanding could not be removed by lowering a number. The dungeon had taken her power, but it couldn’t reach the experience behind it.
She regarded the enemies gathered before her.
Children.
There was no cruelty in the thought. It was merely correct.

Vyra passed through them with minimal movement. She fought like someone who had repeated the same work across lifetimes longer than entire civilizations and no longer considered the process difficult.
The floor ahead gave her more reason for interest.

Difficulty had risen sharply during the previous section. There had been no gradual increase. One moment the dungeon had tested her at one level, and the next it had adjusted as though it had studied her performance and concluded that ordinary resistance would not be enough.
Good.
The faintest trace of approval touched her thoughts.
It noticed.
She walked on to meet the next challenge.
Loriel was close to dying.

There was no softer way to describe it. Her survival depended on seconds, not careful choices. The dungeon had placed her in a fight she couldn’t win directly, which suited the limits of her role far too well.
She had prepared to support the others.
There was nobody here to support.

Three enemies surrounded her. She had no weapon, and at level one, the life element offered only weak, slow healing. Nearly all of what she could produce was already being spent on keeping her body functional.
I’m going to die here.
The thought came with the clean certainty of an honest calculation.
A second thought followed.
No. I won’t.

Loriel couldn’t say where the refusal came from. It didn’t arrive as courage or sudden confidence. It simply settled inside her, solid and immovable, because accepting death was no longer an option she was willing to consider.
She studied the three enemies and remembered Leon’s instruction.
Foundation.
What did she actually know about the life element once every system-built technique had been stripped away?
Healing, certainly.
Life force.
The clear boundary separating living things from dead ones.
What can life do besides restore wounds?
At first, no answer came.
Then several pieces connected at once.
Loriel stopped directing the element toward her injuries.
Instead, she attempted something she had never tried before.
Leon reached the tower entrance.
He stopped outside the gate for one second.

His awareness drifted toward the mansion Xyra had constructed beyond the far side of the tower. He didn’t choose to sense it. The place had become a constant pressure at the edge of his perception, the world spirit’s home sitting comfortably within the range of his spatial awareness.
Ignore it. Walk quickly. Don’t look at anyone. Go straight to the third-floor portal.
He entered through the gate.
The familiar hall spread out before him, unchanged in its broad shape. Steady light filled the space, and the circular reception desk remained at its center.
The elf sat behind it.
Her attention appeared to be on a book. Golden eyes moved across the open page with the concentration of someone fully absorbed in what she was reading.
Leon glanced at her.
Then at the book.
The bookmark stuck out from the top of the page instead of the bottom. From where he stood, the cover made the problem even clearer. The writing faced the wrong direction, and the spine was reversed.
She had turned the book upside down and was pretending to read it with complete dedication.
"Weirdo," Leon murmured, barely making a sound.
Without slowing, he turned toward the path leading to the third-floor portal.

The tower had added signs since his previous visit. Directions now marked the hall, apparently created in response to his clearance of the first two floors. Rather than existing from the beginning, the guidance seemed to appear whenever it became relevant.
He located the third-floor portal without trouble.
Then he stood before it.
His thoughts went to Seraphine, Ira, Vyra, and Loriel.
All four were somewhere inside the Class Reawakening Dungeon. He couldn’t see what they faced, couldn’t reach them, and had no way to change what happened now.
Before they entered, he had done everything available to him. He’d given them resources, equipment, training, and whatever guidance he could offer.
There was nothing left except waiting for their return.
Come back.
His gaze remained on the portal.
Every one of you. Please come back.
Leon allowed himself to hold on to the thought for another second.
Then he drew a breath, stepped into the portal, and disappeared through it.
