They strained toward the unmarked passage like compass needles settling on north.
Something tied to the sealed black door waited down that route.
Leon considered all three choices.
The bronze passage would move him closer to clearing the floor.
The silver route promised another treasure and another enhancement for the Gatekeeper.
The black corridor offered no listed reward and served no official objective.
It was also the only path the Tower refused to recognize.
Leon now carried one Tower Key, two unabsorbed Epic treasures, and two unidentified fragments.
The Gatekeeper waiting at the end had already gained Spatial Resistance and Technique Mimicry.
Taking another optional route would strengthen it again.
The bronze path was safer.
It was also the practical choice.
The fragments pulled toward the darkness once more.
Leon’s eyes settled on the unmarked corridor.
This time, he did not look away.

chapters.title: Chapter 569: The Uncounted Passage
paragraphs: Leon worked the fingers of his left hand once. The arm answered without pain or delay.

The Burden of Possession had been punishing only while its law remained attached to him. Once the band opened, the suppression ended and his regeneration did what it had done after far worse injuries. The strain was gone. His mana reserve was not instantly full, but it continued rising with every passing minute.
Under better conditions, he still would have found a quiet place and absorbed the two Epic crystals before following anything this suspicious.
The labyrinth made that a bad choice.
Every cleared room could cause the maze to rearrange itself, and the black fragments in his storage were pulling toward the unmarked passage more strongly than before.

This was the first useful trail he had found. The sealed door had shown itself inside a mirror. The fragments had reacted to a pulse from somewhere across the maze. Now, for once, they were leading him toward a place he could reach.
If he backed off to rest, the labyrinth might shift before he returned. He would still have two puzzle pieces afterward, but the board they belonged to could be gone.
He was physically whole, alert, and unwilling to let the trail disappear.
Leon entered the dark.
As soon as he passed beneath the arch, the opening closed behind him. He sensed it more clearly than he saw it: the space at his back changed, and solid stone replaced the way out.
The Tower gave him no notification.
That was wrong enough on its own. It announced claimed treasure. It announced restraints locking around his wrist. Usually, it found something to say about everything.
Here, it remained silent.
The lack of a message felt louder than one.
Light barely survived inside the passage.

A few steps in, Leon summoned a small flame over his palm to test the darkness. The fire illuminated his hand and a narrow section of floor, then its glow faded away long before it should have. Holy energy reached no farther. Mana met the same limit.
The blackness did not seem to repel the light. It allowed the glow to travel a short distance, then took the rest into itself.

His enhanced senses still worked beyond what his eyes could manage. Spatial perception outlined the corridor clearly enough, so he could continue without stumbling. Even then, losing the simple assurance of sight bothered him more than he would have guessed.
His spatial perception functioning at all was the first odd part.
It spread down the passage and gave him an orderly answer. The corridor ran straight ahead. It had a definite length. Its far end sat at a fixed, measurable distance.
Several minutes of walking revealed the second problem.
That far end remained exactly where it had been when he entered.
Leon reduced his pace.
He had followed a straight route without a single branch or turn. His perception still reported a finite corridor with an endpoint ahead, but the distance to it had not decreased.
He continued for another stretch while tracking it carefully.
Nothing changed.
The path was straight.
The end was finite.
And it never came any closer.
Leon drew his sword. At shoulder height, he carved a shallow diagonal line into the wall on his left, leaving a clean scar in the stone. Then he carried on.
Minutes later, the same mark appeared ahead of him.
He had not turned around.
His perception had confirmed a straight path with every step, yet the diagonal cut he had left behind now waited in front of him on the same left-hand wall. It matched exactly.
Leon stopped beside it.
The answer became obvious.
The passage was looping.
Its far end curved back into its beginning, so moving forward would always bring him around to the place where he had started.

A chill ran over his skin, mostly because his senses had never given him false information. The corridor truly was straight. It truly had a finite length. Space had simply been folded around and joined to itself so neatly that his perception read the whole thing as one continuous line.
Leon extended Void Dominion and searched for the join.
There.
A faint wound in space marked the place where two sections had been fused together.
He tried to pull the seam open.

The attempt stopped against the same absolute resistance he had encountered at the edge of the floor. His authority could identify the flaw, but the Tower’s authority sat above his. Knowing where the join was did not give him the power to break it.
That figured.
A loop would hardly count as a puzzle if every challenger could cut through it. The Tower had placed the trap beyond his ability to overpower, just as it had done with the outer walls.
He would need to solve it properly.
The fragments shifted while he was still considering the problem.
Leon removed both from storage and placed them in his open hand. The two black slivers weighed nothing and swallowed the little light that reached them.
At once, they began pulling.
One angled toward the wall in front of him. The other leaned back along the route he had taken.
By themselves, they pointed in opposite directions.

He brought their broken sides together. Once they settled into the larger, unfinished shape, the conflict vanished. The joined fragments tilted as one and drew his hand toward a single place on the otherwise smooth wall.
Leon followed the pull.

At the indicated point, the stone held a flaw so small it almost did not exist. A hair-thin imperfection interrupted the seamless surface. Without the fragments, he could have walked past it a thousand times and never noticed.
It marked the join in the loop.
Nothing visible should have revealed it, but the fragments had found it immediately.
Leon studied the pieces, and their purpose began to make more sense.
They were not only parts of some key or seal.
They also served as guides.

The fragments could locate hidden spaces and seams that the Tower’s interface refused to recognize. Whatever kept the pieces concealed from the Cosmic System appeared to hide those flaws as well, but the fragments remained able to detect them.
Leon continued toward the seam.
The corridor started working harder to stop him.

Every new loop carried a different trick, each one less reliable than the last. The mark from his sword began changing places. Though he had cut it into the left wall, it later appeared on the right. On another circuit, it waited on the ceiling. After that, he found it low beside the floor.
It remained the same diagonal scar each time. Only its location changed.

The corridor’s length also refused to stay stable. One circuit stretched farther than the last. The next became shorter. The supposed fixed distance to the "end" shifted quietly with every pass until he could no longer use it to judge direction.
Then he heard footsteps coming from ahead.
They matched his own pace exactly, echoing toward him from the direction he was travelling, as if someone farther along the passage were walking in perfect rhythm with him.
On one circuit, Leon rounded a bend and saw a figure far down the corridor.
It was walking away from him.
The shape matched his body, and its stride matched his. As Leon advanced, it retreated into the black at the same speed.
He stopped.
The distant figure stopped as well.
Leon took one step.
It did the same.
His spatial perception insisted that the figure stood ahead of him inside the passage, even though nobody else had entered.
The explanation came after a moment.
The loop had folded his line of sight back across his own route.
He was not watching a duplicate.
He was seeing himself one circuit farther ahead, walking across the same stone under his feet.
Trying to catch the figure would only leave him chasing his own back forever.
Leon allowed it to vanish into the darkness.
Then he ignored what the corridor showed him and placed his trust in the fragments.

chapters.title: Chapter 570: Hall of the Uncounted
paragraphs: Leon gave up on forcing the passage to obey him.

Instead, he kept moving, watched the joined fragments, and used their pull to find each nearly invisible seam. The misplaced sword mark, the false echoes, and the distant image of his own back stopped mattering once he knew what they were. The process took time, but it asked for patience rather than power. His mana continued recovering throughout the search.
At the last seam, the fragments reacted differently.

They no longer pointed toward some tiny flaw in the stone. Their pull settled on a section of wall that appeared completely untouched. No crack. No thin scar. Even with his perception focused on it, Leon found nothing unusual.
The joined shape strained toward the blank stone as if what it sought lay beyond the wall, not along its surface.

Leon stepped closer. He adjusted the two fragments until their broken edges sat together and the unfinished symbol became as complete as the pieces allowed. Then he placed the pattern flat against the wall.
The stone opened.
No notification appeared.

There was only the quiet grind of stone shifting where stone should not have been able to shift. A section of the wall drew inward, folded aside, and revealed a staircase leading down into deeper darkness.
An inscription had been carved across the lintel above the opening. The old letters had worn shallow with time, forcing Leon to read their shape through his senses more than his sight.
THE COUNTED ASCEND.
THE UNCOUNTED DESCEND.
He considered the words, but they explained very little.

Whoever had carved them was unknown. So was when they had been written, or what exactly was being counted. The choice itself was clear enough, though. Leon had already made it when he entered the unmarked passage.
He returned the fragments to storage, kept one hand close to his sword, and descended.
The staircase continued far below the labyrinth.
With every turn, the place felt older.

The difference from the official maze was impossible to miss. The labyrinth above had been maintained perfectly. Its floors were clean, its walls seamless, and every block sat exactly where it belonged.
None of that care reached this stairway.

The farther Leon went, the rougher the stone became. Cracks crossed the walls and split the steps. Thick dust covered the stairs, untouched and deeper than anything he had seen elsewhere on the floor. Some sections of wall had collapsed entirely, leaving piles of rubble that forced him to slow and climb around them.
Whatever this hidden place was, the Tower had abandoned it to time.
His boots left the only tracks behind him.
Nothing followed, but seeing those prints somehow made the stairwell feel less empty. They showed that no challenger had passed this way recently.
Or that anyone who had come before had left by another path.
The air cooled as he descended. It smelled dry and stale, like stone that had remained sealed for centuries.
At the bottom, the Tower still offered no message.
Its silence followed him just as it had around the fragments.

The staircase opened into a wide chamber with a low ceiling. Cracks ran through the room, and a single pale light shone from somewhere overhead. Leon couldn’t locate its source. The weak, colorless glow spread across the chamber and stretched every shadow.
He was not alone.
Figures stood throughout the room.
At first, Leon took them for statues. A closer look confirmed it. Weathered stone people filled the chamber, each carved in the shape of a challenger.
Past challengers.
Their faces were gone.

Time hadn’t worn them away. Someone had deliberately removed them, smoothing every face until no feature or identifying mark remained. None of the figures could be distinguished from another by who they had once been.
Some held keys.
Broken keys.

The bronze shapes had snapped in half and remained gripped in stone hands. Other figures hugged treasure chests against their bodies. A smaller number knelt with their hands reaching toward the center of the floor, where an incomplete black symbol had been carved into the stone.
Leon recognized it immediately.
It was the same symbol formed in part by the fragments in his storage.
The statues had not all met the same end.

One armored challenger held two halves of a key, positioned as though it had broken between his hands. A robed woman clutched a chest with both arms while fractures spread through the stone around her feet. Another had dropped to one knee, one empty hand stretched toward the unfinished symbol.
Whatever had happened in this room, owning something had not protected any of them.
There were no names.
No dates.

Nothing explained who the challengers had been or why they had been left beneath the trial. Only the final poses remained. Broken keys. Treasures held tight. Empty hands reaching for a symbol none of them had completed.
Leon studied the kneeling figures for another moment, then pulled his attention back to the rest of the chamber.
One figure knelt at the center, separate from all the others.
It wasn’t made of stone.

Black armor rested at the heart of the carved symbol, tall even while kneeling. A complete suit held a long spear across its lap. Behind a protective plate in the breastplate sat another black fragment.
The third piece was made from the same light-drinking material as the two Leon carried. Under the pale light, it gave off a dull glint.
Leon stopped well outside the armor’s reach.
He asked the Tower interface to identify it.
Nothing responded.
The Cosmic System gave him no name for the guardian, no trial notice, no danger rating, and no reward. Like the fragments, the armor seemed invisible to every system that should have recognized it.
That silence was warning enough.
The moment he reached for the fragment, the thing holding it would almost certainly wake.
Still, the sight confirmed something important. The hidden route contained more than the two pieces he had already found. However many fragments existed in total, a third now sat within reach.
Leon prepared before touching it.
Void Dominion spread across the chamber as he tested the space.

Down here, beneath the maintained labyrinth, the Tower’s authority felt weaker. Space responded to him again, folding cleanly under his intent. He checked the available exits and found two: the staircase behind him and another closed passage elsewhere in the room.

The time spent solving the loop and descending the stair had allowed his passive mana recovery to replace much of what the mandatory trial had cost. His left arm was whole, his channels were clear, and his conscious bronze-gold armor had no remaining damage.

Void Dominion spread without instability. Leon also kept Leximancy, Elemental Surge, Raijin, and his combined elements ready. An uncounted guardian deserved more caution than the official constructs, not less.
He fixed the exits and the chamber’s geometry in his mind before advancing.
Leon reached toward the fragment.
The armor moved.
Its hand snapped up with far more speed than something that large should have possessed. Metal fingers closed around Leon’s wrist a fraction before he touched the plate.
Cold seeped through his gauntlet.
There was no trace of living warmth in the grip.
The spear slipped from the armor’s lap and landed in its free hand as the figure rose. It unfolded to its full height, standing a head taller than Leon, then planted its feet in the black dust.
Leon tore his wrist free and retreated, bringing his sword up between them.

That brief grip told him more than either silent interface had. The strength behind it had already passed the Ethereal Initiate enemies he could handle with ease. Combined with the speed of the movement, the empty armor felt closer to an Ethereal Lord-class threat. Leon could not assign an exact rank to something the Tower refused to acknowledge, but he would not mistake it for an ordinary Floor Three construct.
The Tower still named nothing.
There was no announcement. No title for the guardian. No rules waiting for him to read.
Only a suit of black armor holding a narrow spear, blocking the fragment embedded in its chest.
Leon needed some name for it, even if the name existed only in his thoughts.
He chose the simplest one that fit.
The Uncounted Warden. Fine. Let’s see what you are.

chapters.title: Chapter 571: The Absence Field
paragraphs: The Warden looked nothing like the other guardians on this floor. Black armor covered a tall, empty shape, with no eye slits or other openings in its blank helmet. A narrow spear made from the same light-eating material rested in its practiced grip.
The third fragment waited behind a plate in its chest. That was where Leon needed to strike.
The Warden advanced.
Leon answered with a test rather than a full attack. He shaped a tight burst of fire and sent it straight at the center of the guardian’s body, watching to see how it reacted.
The flame crossed the chamber and reached the thick darkness around the Warden.
Then it ceased.

Nothing knocked it aside. The armor hadn’t blocked it, and the spell hadn’t lost a contest of power. Its core entered the shadow, and the fire simply stopped existing, as though that part of the room rejected the idea that flame belonged there.
Leon noted it and moved.
One long step brought the Warden into range. Its spear thrust forward, and Leon tried to fold space, shifting himself three feet to the side.
The darkness moved faster.

As the displacement formed, the Warden’s shadow stretched across the stone and reached him. The fold lost its structure the instant the darkness touched it. Space came apart around Leon before the movement could finish and dropped him less than a foot from where he’d begun.
He landed wrong, off balance and still inside the spear’s reach.
The point scraped his side.
His conscious armor managed to turn the thrust, but the spearhead dragged over the plate and split it with a crack.

For the instant the shadow covered it, the armor’s consciousness froze and the crack remained. The spear was made from the same uncounted material as the Warden, allowing it to harm protection that ordinary Floor Three weapons could barely mark. As soon as Leon reached clear light, bronze-gold metal flowed over the split and closed it within seconds.
Leon retreated quickly. By the time he put distance between them, he understood what the shadow was doing.

Anything supernatural failed inside the continuous darkness connected to the Warden. Fire went out, folds collapsed, spatial awareness blurred, and the conscious part of his armor became lifeless. Mana did not weaken inside the field; its flow simply ceased until the shadow passed.
Outside that absence, his abilities worked. Inside it, he had his physical body, sword, and armor.

Power was not the answer. The field had not overpowered his small flame or consumed his fold through greater energy. It had removed both without a contest. A full Elemental Surge would cease at the same boundary and waste far more of his reserves.
His physical strength and integrated combat experience stayed with him. Ordinary objects were not erased, and his armor still protected him even when it could no longer move or heal.
Leon tested one other option while the Warden crossed a strip of pale light.
"Stop."
Leximancy struck the armor and found no living mind, soul, or identity inside the hollow shell for the command to seize. The Warden did not slow.
Unfortunately, the Warden knew how to fight, and the absence field gave it control of the room.

Its spearwork had the discipline of a veteran. Each thrust kept Leon near the edge of the weapon’s ideal reach, punishing every attempt to close the distance. The guardian also used its position to steer him into the shadow, forcing him to fight for every safe patch of stone.
Leon stayed light on his feet and wasted as little movement as possible. He tracked the changing edge of the shadow while keeping himself on illuminated ground.
The Warden’s Ethereal Lord-class force made that difficult even with Leon’s restored body.

Twice, the spear came too fast for a complete parry. The bronze-gold plates endured in the light, but a hit delivered inside the absence field cut another shallow line before he escaped and the damage repaired.
The third attack began high.
Halfway through the thrust, the spearhead dropped toward the seam it had targeted before.
Leon caught it against the flat of his sword. Rather than trying to stop the blow, he turned with it and redirected the force.
Even then, the impact drove him sideways for three steps.
His last foot came down on the edge of the shadow.

The armor locked around him at once, warning him just before the field cut off his mana. Leon threw himself back into the light, and the spear punched through the place his throat had occupied a moment earlier.
The Warden overreached on the next thrust.
A small opening appeared.
Leon slipped past the spearpoint and entered its reach. His sword crossed the black plate covering the fragment.
The strike left a pale line on the armor.
Then the spearshaft slammed into him and forced him away.
It wasn’t much, but the Warden now had a damaged point of its own.
Leon couldn’t win by trading physical blows.
The guardian had greater reach, no sign of tiring, and a field that made half the chamber unusable. Trading at its preferred distance would accomplish nothing.
He needed to attack the field itself.
The shadow was continuous.
So he had to divide it.
Leon began creating light sources.
He didn’t aim them at the Warden. A compact fire orb went near one wall. Holy light anchored itself beside a cracked pillar. Across the room, he suspended a tight knot of lightning.
Every source remained outside the current shadow.

His channels were healthy, and maintaining several small lights cost little. The danger came whenever the field reached a source and erased every bit of energy invested in it. Enough losses could outpace his passive recovery.
The first fire orb was placed too near.
When the Warden shifted, its shadow passed over the orb’s core and erased the spell immediately.
That failure gave Leon the detail he needed. A source died inside the field, but light created beyond it still traveled across the floor.
His next placements were wider.
He set them beyond the shadow’s reach and spread them around the Warden, covering angles the pale overhead light couldn’t touch.
He kept each source compact. Making one brighter would not overpower a conceptual absence. Only placing light at several angles could divide the darkness carrying it.
Multiple lights struck the guardian from different directions.
Its single shadow shortened, split, and broke apart into smaller patches. Narrow strips of lit stone appeared between them.
Leon tested one.
He folded space across the gap.
This time, the displacement held.
He used it immediately.
Leon appeared beside the Warden with his sword already cutting toward the damaged chest plate.
The guardian turned before the blade arrived. Its spearshaft swept toward Leon’s sword arm.
He abandoned the attack and withdrew through the same illuminated route.
The paths were usable.
They were also thin and temporary.
The Warden understood what he was doing.

One thrust of its spear shattered a fire orb. Without that light, the nearest patch of darkness expanded. The guardian shifted its position and used its own body to connect two smaller shadows into one larger pool.
Then it continued forcing Leon towards the darkest side of the chamber, striking repeatedly at the same armor seam whenever the absence field froze it.
Leon replaced the lost flame with a lightning source anchored farther back.
The new angle divided the restored shadow again.
Holding it in place added another steady pull on his reserve.
The Warden attacked before the technique had settled.
Leon ducked beneath the spear, crossed a strip of light, and struck the same pale mark across its chest.
The impact rang through the buried chamber.
Before he could escape cleanly, the return sweep hit his side and threw him into one of the faceless statues.
Stone broke behind him.
One of the statue’s arms fell away.
From then on, Leon had to manage two fights at the same time.
His body handled the spear through instinct and training while his attention replaced destroyed lights and adjusted the positions of the others.
Whenever another path opened through the darkness, he crossed it and attacked the black plate over the fragment.
His second clean strike widened the pale mark into a thin crack.

Each attempt cost another light. The Warden’s spear opened shallow cracks whenever the field froze Leon’s armor, but the bronze-gold plates repaired in the light and his regeneration erased the bruising beneath them. Only the mana lost with each destroyed source accumulated.
Across the chamber, the pale crack across the Warden’s chest continued to grow.
Once the guardian understood the rhythm of his attacks, Leon changed the pattern.
He let the Warden push him toward the room’s darkest corner.
The guardian increased the pressure, driving him beyond the reach of the lights scattered around the chamber. As Leon retreated, its separated shadows began joining again.
Soon, one broad pool of darkness covered the floor.
The absence field swallowed his abilities.
Behind him, the black wall left nowhere else to go.

chapters.title: Chapter 572: The Path Below
paragraphs: Leon had saved one last source of light.
During an earlier exchange, he’d hidden a dormant knot of holy energy behind one of the cracked statues. The Warden committed to the killing thrust, and Leon activated it.
Holy light erupted at the guardian’s back.
Its shadow tore apart from behind.
The new light broke the connected darkness into pieces, opening thin strips of illuminated stone around the Warden’s feet. Leon felt his void return immediately.
There wasn’t enough time for a full teleport.
The spear was already driving at his heart. Leon reached through one of the bright gaps and folded the space running along the weapon’s path. He only managed to shift the thrust by a small amount.
It was enough.
The spearpoint missed his ribs and scraped a line across his armor.
His body moved before thought could slow it.
The Warden had extended too far. Leon stepped past the spear’s effective reach and drove his sword into the hairline fracture on its chest plate.
The black metal refused to give.
The guardian dragged itself backward as the broken patches of shadow stretched toward each other. If they reconnected, the absence field would catch Leon’s blade before he could force it through.
He put his full physical force behind the opening.
Holy energy rushed along the sword. His right arm drove forward, backed by the full strength of his armored body. The point sank deeper into the existing crack.
The plate split just before the shadows joined.
Leon’s blade punched through the core around the fragment, and the holy energy inside it exploded.
A violent tremor ran through the Warden.
Its spear slipped free and hit the dusty floor.
Then the armor lost its shape.
It didn’t fall like a dead body. The entire suit crumbled in place, breaking down into fine black dust. The remains sifted through the pale light and spread across the chamber floor.
Leon stayed braced behind his sword until the Warden’s final hand dissolved.
Only then did he lower the blade.

As the final shadow disappeared, his conscious armor woke across its entire surface. Bronze-gold material flowed over the remaining cracks and sealed them within seconds. The bruising left by the Warden’s blows faded under his regeneration almost as quickly. Around the room, the lights he’d created began going dark one after another as he stopped supplying them.
The chamber faded back into its original pale gloom.
No victory message appeared.
The Tower remained silent.
Where the Warden’s chest plate had been, the third fragment hung in the air for a moment. Then it began to fall.
Leon caught it before it disappeared into the settling dust.
The piece was cold, weightless, and made from the same material that swallowed light as the first two. The Tower gave no response. Neither did the Cosmic System.
He took the other fragments from storage and placed all three together in his palm.

Their broken sides pulled toward one another. The edges shifted, aligned, and locked into place, revealing more of the design than Leon had seen before. Three pieces met along their torn borders, and the pattern spread across them as if it had always been one drawing.
They still did not truly fuse.
When Leon tested them, they separated again into three individual slivers.
But the joined image was large enough to change his earlier assumption.
This wasn’t merely a key.

The pattern had become too detailed for anything so simple. It looked ancient and unusually complicated, something between a key and a seal without being entirely either. Its real function remained hidden in the missing pieces.
Leon still couldn’t tell how many fragments existed or what completing them would accomplish.
He only knew they were meant for more than opening an ordinary lock.
For a brief moment, the unfinished lines seemed to extend beyond the black pieces. Missing sections appeared in the way the surrounding light curved away from empty space.
Leon shifted his palm, and the impression disappeared.
It hadn’t shown him the complete design or how many pieces remained. It had only made one thing clear.
Three fragments were not enough.
The newest piece had something the other two lacked.
A thin groove ran along its reverse side, a shallow channel carved into the black surface. When Leon aligned all three fragments again, that groove joined faint marks on the first two.
He’d assumed those marks were scratches.
Together, they formed part of a directional symbol.
The arrow was incomplete, but the angle was obvious.
It pointed downward.
Leon studied it in silence.
The route wasn’t behind some hidden door in this chamber.
It continued beneath the floor.
This place had only been a stop along the way. Whatever the fragments led toward was deeper still.
Before leaving, Leon searched the chamber.
The remaining carvings on the walls showed challengers taking treasures downward. Several of their names had been deliberately carved away, just as the faces had been erased from the statues.
Another wall held a damaged relief. It showed a maze viewed from above, with a huge sealed doorway beneath it.
The section beyond that door had been destroyed.
The carvings confirmed that the hidden route was old and far larger than Leon had first thought.
They explained nothing else.
Once he claimed the fragment, the exit opened.
Stone pulled back along the far wall where Leon had sensed the sealed passage earlier. Beyond it lay a corridor climbing upward.
The slope continued for a long distance.
Eventually, it returned him to the maintained labyrinth, opening at an unfamiliar junction somewhere else on Floor Three.
The change was immediate.
The walls were seamless once more. The air felt cleaner, and the subtle pressure of the Tower’s authority settled across his senses again.
Behind him, the hidden entrance closed.
When the stone finished moving, it left no crack or seam behind.
Without the three fragments in storage, Leon might have questioned whether the buried hall had existed at all.
The instant he stepped onto the clean, swept floor, the Tower became active again.
Its interface responded all at once. The familiar attention of the trial settled over him as though it had only now noticed his return.
Leon checked his progress.
[Tower Keys Collected: 1/3]
[Optional Treasures Claimed: 2]
[Gatekeeper Enhancements: Spatial Resistance, Technique Mimicry]
There was no record of the black corridor.
Nothing mentioned the buried chamber, the Warden, or the third fragment.
As far as the Tower’s official trial was concerned, the hidden fight had never happened. The Gatekeeper had received no enhancement from it either.
That was useful.
It was also dangerous.
The secret path didn’t make the Gatekeeper stronger, but the Tower provided no guidance there. No instructions, no warnings, and no rating for whatever waited ahead.
If something below killed Leon, he would still be dead.
His body made the cost clear enough.
His body was whole, and his conscious armor had already repaired every crack once the absence field released it.

His spatial control had never been damaged. His mana reserve was lower because the field had erased the energy inside each destroyed light, but passive recovery had already begun replacing what he spent.
He had exchanged mana and risk for another fragment and a direction.
The trade had been worth making.
It hadn’t been free.
Four routes opened from the junction.
One bronze archway carried the carving of a key.
A silver archway bore an open chest.
The remaining two corridors had no markings at all. They were plain black openings leading away from the intersection into darkness.
At first, the fragments remained motionless in storage.
Leon brought them out and connected them again.
The groove across their reverse sides found its direction.
It didn’t point toward either of the unmarked corridors.
The unfinished arrow angled past both passages, through the walls, and directly downward toward the stone beneath Leon’s boots.
He examined the two dark corridors, then lowered his gaze to the floor.
Those passages weren’t the final destination.
They were entrances, separate ways of reaching whatever lay below the maintained labyrinth.
The real path didn’t cross Floor Three.
It descended toward the sealed doorway shown in the broken relief.
Leon stood alone at the junction with one key, two unabsorbed treasures, three black fragments, and a mana reserve still climbing toward full.
He kept his eyes on the stone under his feet.

chapters.title: Chapter 573: Tempered Before the Trial
paragraphs: Leon paused at the four-way intersection, giving the decision one final round of thought before committing.

The two unmarked corridors on either side lay dark and silent, yet the black fragments inside his storage ignored both of them. Their pull angled toward the stone beneath his feet. Those passages might enter other buried sections, but neither pointed toward the destination the three pieces had revealed.

Searching every hidden corridor would waste too much time. The Tower’s official objective made more sense. Each time someone claimed a key, the floor shifted around the central gate. If the buried path ended anywhere, the middle of the floor was where it was most likely to connect.
That reasoning ruled out the silver route as well.
He had already traded Spatial Resistance and Technique Mimicry to the Gatekeeper. Whatever reward waited beyond the silver route, the true cost would still come due inside the Gatekeeper’s chamber.

Under ordinary circumstances, Leon might have inspected every valuable path simply because he could. These circumstances were not ordinary. The uncounted route had already produced a mystery rarer than another Epic treasure, and its fragments directed him toward the central gate. Outside the Tower, the Class Reawakening Dungeon remained active, with no guarantee that time passed at the same rate in both places. He could not wander through every side chamber merely to prove he was capable of clearing it.
This was not retreating from the harder challenge.
It was choosing the one the Tower refused to acknowledge.
So Leon stepped beneath the bronze arch marked by its cleanly carved key.

The passage beyond was almost suspiciously straightforward. No traps waited for him. No twisting loops. None of the maze’s usual attempts to wear him down. It ended after only a short walk at a small antechamber before another trial door.
He stopped there and extended his perception.
Nothing stirred beyond the sealed entrance. The trial had not begun. For the moment, the antechamber offered a rare stretch of quiet.

He still carried two Epic treasures he hadn’t absorbed. Ever since claiming them, he’d been waiting for a place calm enough to use them properly. His body was whole, his spatial channels were clear, and the quiet passage had allowed his mana reserve to recover almost completely.
Even so, bringing those treasures into the Gatekeeper’s chamber untouched would be the worse choice.
Settling onto the floor, he took out the Spatial Tempering Crystal and began.
Energy rushed from the crystal the instant the absorption started.
Just as he’d expected, it sought out his spatial channels first.

The dense tempering force pressed into structures already shaped by Transcendent Void Dominion. It did not repair damage; there was none. Instead, it forced those pathways to endure hostile distortion from within, creating controlled pain as it tested and reinforced them.
His muscles wanted to recoil.
He refused.
Instead of resisting the energy, Leon seized control of its movement. Rather than allowing the crystal to flood his channels, he guided it through each fold-path little by little.
The process was painfully slow.
Whenever the ache sharpened, he eased the flow and allowed that section to adapt before moving on. Gradually, the pathways became more resistant to outside pressure and distortion.
He tested one of his shorter folds at the edge of his awareness.
It came together as cleanly as before, but required slightly less effort to maintain.
When the final surge settled, Leon created another short fold and deliberately pressed conflicting spatial pressure against it from multiple directions.
It held.
The structure remained intact. His channels had become tougher, his control more efficient, and the folds themselves were more resistant to disruption.
The crystal hadn’t granted him new abilities. It had simply reinforced the ones he already possessed.
The Tower’s authority over space was still beyond him, but breaking his techniques through hostile spatial interference would now be considerably harder.

He continued the absorption until every trace of the crystal disappeared into his channels. When the last of it settled, the sharp pain faded. His regeneration cleared the physical aftereffects while he rested before taking out the second treasure.
Leon exhaled, gathered himself, and reached for the second treasure.
The Mirrorheart Tempering Shard behaved completely differently.
Its power ignored his channels.
Instead, silver-black energy spread across his awareness.
For a long, stretched instant, Leon watched himself.
They weren’t memories.
They weren’t visions.
They were reflections, flawed echoes of his own movements replaying again and again at the edge of his mind.

He watched himself begin a sword exchange. He saw the same subtle leading step repeated across one reflection after another until the habit became impossible to ignore. A familiar opening performed twice became an opening an opponent would expect the third time.
Another comparison appeared.
One technique was executed with real intent.
The other copied every movement perfectly.
The difference was obvious.
The imitation preserved the form but lacked the judgment behind it. It carried the outline of the technique while leaving the decision that gave it meaning completely hollow.
Watching it wasn’t pleasant.
Every comfortable habit, every preferred angle, every repeated pattern was displayed with uncomfortable honesty.
Still, Leon understood the purpose behind the tempering.
He let it continue.

When the shard’s power finally settled, those habits stood out with unsettling clarity. Familiar motions now carried a faint warning whenever repetition crept in, and the underlying framework of a technique became easier to notice than the visible movement itself.
The last silver-black trace dissolved into his awareness, leaving no physical shard behind.
The shard hadn’t handed him solutions.
It had simply made recurring questions much harder to overlook.
Against a Gatekeeper that could reproduce whatever Leon revealed, that awareness could easily matter more than gaining another offensive technique.
He drew his sword to test it.
The first draw felt normal.
On the second, he immediately caught the familiar shift of his leading foot and the slight twist in his wrist before the blade cleared the sheath.
By the third attempt, he altered both while keeping the same speed.
The draw wasn’t any stronger than before.
But anyone preparing for the angle shown by the first two attempts would now be wrong.

By the time both absorptions were finished, Leon felt the honest mental fatigue of prolonged concentration, but his body had already recovered from the tempering. His mana reserve had returned to full during the quiet interval, and both arms moved without pain or delay.
He retrieved the three black fragments for another look.
Nothing changed.
Neither crystal drew any response from them. They showed no interest in the power he’d just absorbed.
They continued to lean toward the stone floor with the same quiet insistence as before, pointing downward exactly as they had since the buried hall.
Whatever those fragments sought, it wasn’t Epic treasure.
Leon stored them again, rose to his feet, and pushed open the bronze door.
[Mandatory Key Trial: Measure of Worth]

chapters.title: Chapter 574: Measure of Worth
paragraphs: The chamber on the other side opened into a broad, brightly lit space filled with pedestals.
Every pedestal displayed something valuable. Leon moved through the room at an unhurried pace, inspecting each offering in turn.

The first held a healing elixir that gave off a faint glow, powerful enough to drag a cultivator back from the brink of death. Leon’s own regeneration made it unnecessary for him, but it could still save someone who lacked that advantage. Beside it rested an elemental crystal, raw power rolling from it strongly enough to reach him across the chamber.
Another stand supported a slab of high-grade weapon material, the kind a master smith might spend years trying to obtain.

There was also a compact storage artifact, refined and small, yet worth a fortune by itself. More treasures continued down the line, any one of them good enough to serve as the reward for an entire lesser trial.
The final pedestal stood apart from the rest.

A plain bronze disk lay on top of it. No aura surrounded the metal. It gave off no light and carried none of the pressure that came with power. Someone sweeping the chamber might have mistaken it for rubbish and passed it by.
Words of fire appeared above the row.
[Choose the possession you value most.]
[Only what you choose may leave this chamber.]

Leon called on the Cosmic System and examined every item. A room like this was almost asking him to look for deception. The simple answer would be that all the impressive treasures were fake while the dull bronze disk was the only genuine object. Anyone clever enough to see through that would take the disk and leave pleased with themselves.
Except the System confirmed the opposite.

The healing elixir was real. So was the elemental crystal. The weapon material and storage artifact were genuine as well. Every treasure in the chamber possessed exactly the worth it seemed to possess. Their authenticity wasn’t the trick.
That left the choice itself.
Standing among the pedestals, Leon saw what the trial wanted from him.
It was measuring what he considered valuable, and the rewards had to be real or the decision meant nothing. He could take the elixir. He could choose the elemental crystal.

Either would be an incredible prize, but doing so would force him to leave behind the bronze disk and the key he had come down this route to obtain. Something rare right now wasn’t necessarily the thing that mattered most. Each shining treasure offered him power in return for giving up his actual goal.
Leon ignored them all, reached the last pedestal, and lifted the bronze disk.

As soon as his fingers closed around it, every other pedestal became empty. The treasures vanished from the chamber, either erased or placed somewhere he could no longer reach. Which one hardly mattered. The dull metal in his hand began to change at the same time, stretching and gaining weight until it took on the familiar shape of a bronze key.
[Tower Key Acquired]
[Tower Keys Collected: 2/3]

Nothing appeared about an enhancement. Leon had refused the optional rewards, so the Gatekeeper received no benefit from the second key. He stored it beside the first just as the wall at the far end of the chamber began to shift.

The labyrinth moved around him immediately. This time, it didn’t place another puzzle in front of him or force him through some newly formed detour. The bronze route simply rebuilt itself toward the next trial, almost as if the labyrinth were rewarding him for continuing along the intended path.

While the walls rearranged, the three fragments tugged sharply downward again. The pull lasted only through the movement, insistent and aimed beneath the floor, but nothing opened. No crack appeared in the stone. No hidden doorway or staircase revealed itself. The fragments merely pointed with greater urgency than before, then settled once the labyrinth stopped changing.
Whatever the arrow marked, he was nearer to it now. The strength of the pull made that clear.
There still wasn’t a way down from here.
Leon continued toward the third key.
The next bronze door led into a small circular arena. Its floor was clean, the walls close, and the entire room had plainly been made for a single purpose.
[Mandatory Key Trial: The Borrowed Hand]
One guardian stood at the center.

Like the Tollkeeper, it was formed from bronze, though the resemblance ended there. This construct had a narrow frame built for speed instead of mass and carried a straight bronze sword. When Leon stepped inside, it turned toward him and flowed into a ready stance with far more ease than the heavier guardians had shown.
[Mandatory Guardian: Patternbound Sentinel]

The strength gathered inside its narrow frame carried the effective force and speed of a high Ethereal Initiate, then shifted subtly as the floor’s adaptive calibration measured Leon. It remained far below the uncounted Warden’s Ethereal Lord-class pressure. Its unknown trial mechanic was the real danger.

Leon drew his own sword and approached cautiously. His body and mana were recovered, but exposing greater abilities before understanding a trial called the Borrowed Hand would be careless. He began with ordinary swordsmanship, keeping every movement controlled and efficient while he tested the Sentinel through an initial exchange. If the construct forced the issue, he still had far more power available.
The construct caught his blade without trouble, retreated a step, and began circling.
So far, nothing unusual.

Leon entered a second exchange using the same forward step and high cut. Before the attack had fully formed, the Sentinel was already moving. Its answer wasn’t flawless, but the early reaction made Leon change the angle of his strike, and the construct’s low counter forced him back.
He reset, then repeated the same approach for a third time.
The Sentinel had already learned it.

It shut down the approach before Leon completed it and guided its blade toward the left side he had protected during both earlier exchanges. Leon twisted hard enough to keep the point away from the armor seam, then withdrew and created space between them.
The construct was adapting far too quickly. He needed to work out the method before it landed a proper hit.

They circled while Leon studied it, and the Mirrorheart tempering worked quietly behind his thoughts. The reflections he’d experienced during the absorption had trained his attention for this exact kind of problem.
The Sentinel wasn’t copying his techniques.

It hadn’t taken his cut and thrown it back at him the way the Covetous Reflection had. It didn’t possess his sword style or his individual moves. What it had learned was everything surrounding them: the step he repeated before opening, the angle at which he held his blade, the way he protected his left side, the rhythm of his feet, even the direction he preferred when evading.
It didn’t require the technique itself. It only had to predict what Leon would do next.
And Leon kept giving it the answer.

He tested the idea on purpose. First, he performed a basic sequence. Then he repeated it without changing anything: the same initial step, the same turn of his shoulder, the same opening angle of the sword.
On the first attempt, the Sentinel watched.
During the second, its stance shifted early. It began preparing for the sequence before Leon had finished setting it up, already committing to the counter it expected.
That was enough to prove the pattern.
The first repetition taught it. The second let it prepare. By the third, it would understand the sequence almost completely and answer it with near-perfect timing.
Its danger came from learning the shape of Leon’s habits.
That same commitment could also be used against it. Once it trusted a repeated pattern, a sudden break in that pattern would leave it committed to the wrong response.
Leon began teaching it exactly what he wanted it to learn.

chapters.title: Chapter 575: The Borrowed Hand
paragraphs: Leon ran the sequence for a third time.
Same opening step. Same roll through the shoulder. Same starting angle of the sword, following the line the Sentinel had already learned.
The construct took the bait completely.

Its blade drove in to intercept the attack it expected, committing to the counter before Leon’s cut had fully formed. Leon let the setup remain convincing for one more instant, then abandoned it. His point dropped, his feet shifted off the learned line, and the Sentinel’s sword passed through the place his attack should have occupied.
The pattern had told it what would happen.
The pattern was wrong.

That alone wasn’t enough to end the fight. The construct recovered with frightening speed, dragging its weapon back into guard before Leon could finish it. Still, the exchange had given him what he needed.
From then on, Leon stopped letting it learn anything cleanly.

He kept Leximancy and his largest attacks out of the exchange. The Sentinel was an artificial Tower mechanism with no living will he could confidently bind, while its adaptive shell gathered reinforcement against direct force. More importantly, every visible beginning became information for it. Leon could still escalate if the method failed, but there was no reason to show this guardian his strongest abilities while a cleaner answer remained.

He broke up the timing of his ordinary swordwork, delaying some attacks and releasing others early so no stable rhythm could settle in. Feints became part of nearly every sequence. He would begin something familiar, allow the Sentinel to identify it, then turn the motion into something else before the construct could adjust.

During one exchange, fire gathered along his blade as he started a fire-enhanced cut. The Sentinel saw the flame and moved for the answer it had begun to build. Leon stripped the fire away before the strike landed and came in with bare steel from an angle the flame had helped hide.
Later, he showed the same opening again. The construct prepared for another fire-cut.
Lightning snapped instead.
The sudden change caught the Sentinel shifting its weight in the wrong direction.

Leon gave it movement patterns too. When pressure came toward his left side, he repeatedly slipped away to the right, teaching the guardian that this was his preferred preference. Once the Sentinel began counting on that response, it drove at his left again and committed its blade to cutting off the retreat.
This time Leon didn’t move through space at all.
He stayed where he was, caught the incoming blade physically, and turned it aside while the Sentinel continued trying to intercept an escape that never happened.

The Spatial Tempering Crystal had improved the efficiency of his folds noticeably. On the one careful displacement he allowed himself, he slid half a step through the Sentinel’s guard. The fold stayed tight under the adaptive spatial pressure surrounding the arena and cost less control to maintain.
Leon was grateful for the difference.

He couldn’t keep using space freely. After only a few repetitions, the Sentinel would begin reading that too. Every fold needed to accomplish something before it became another habit the construct could study.

None of the choices came from the System. Leon made them from the fight itself, relying on the sense built over a hundred exchanges. His body knew when the Sentinel had fully committed and when it still had room to change course. He kept working patiently, feeding it false patterns, then punishing the counters those patterns produced.
Bit by bit, the guardian’s ability to read him turned against it.
For the final trap, Leon offered his left side.

He made the opening look deliberate enough to be useful but natural enough to resemble the defensive preference he had taught the Sentinel since the opening exchange. The construct had repeatedly watched him protect that line and retreat to the right.
Now it finally saw the chance it wanted.
The Sentinel thrust straight for the exposed opening with complete commitment, certain it had reached the end of the pattern.
Leon had never intended to leave the target available.

At the last instant, he folded the incoming strike a fraction off course. The tempered displacement held cleanly, carrying the point just past his ribs. While the construct’s blade continued into the space he had abandoned, Leon stepped inside its reach.
The Sentinel tried to correct.
It couldn’t do it quickly enough.
Once it had committed to a learned answer, breaking that motion was the one weakness built into its design.

Holy energy wrapped Leon’s sword as he drove it upward into the exposed core. The blade met real resistance before forcing its way through. Then the core cracked, and the light inside the construct flickered out.
The Sentinel collapsed in on itself and stopped moving.
[Tower Key Acquired]
[Tower Keys Collected: 3/3]
[Route to Central Gate Unsealed]
The third key lifted from the arena floor. Leon claimed it while his breathing settled, unharmed and satisfied.
Three out of three.
At last, Floor Three’s key requirement was finished.
The labyrinth reacted more violently than it had at any earlier point.

Movement spread across the entire floor. Walls traveled over enormous distances. Bronze paths, silver paths, and unmarked corridors all rotated, withdrew, or vanished into the shifting structure. The maze folded in on itself and rebuilt around one purpose.
When the motion ended, almost everything had closed.
A single broad corridor remained, running straight toward the center of Floor Three.
Leon took a moment to breathe and judge his condition.

His body was whole. His conscious armor was intact, and the compact trial had taken only a modest share of a full mana reserve. What remained was mental fatigue from hours of puzzles, hidden mechanisms, and enemies that punished careless habits.
He was ready to fight.
Leon started along the open path.
Nothing interrupted him before he reached the central chamber.
The room beyond was enormous.
At its far end stood the gate, a massive arch built from dark metal and stone. Three keyholes waited in its surface.
Beyond that barrier, Leon could sense the Gatekeeper.
The Tower had already revealed the abilities waiting with it: Spatial Resistance and Technique Mimicry. Those were the costs attached to the two optional treasures he had taken.
The debt had reached the point of collection.
He crossed the chamber with the three keys in hand.
Then the fragments jerked downward.
The pull came harder than ever, a brutal wrench from inside his storage that stopped Leon in the middle of a step. He immediately brought out all three pieces and fitted their broken edges together.
The groove along the reverse locked into the shape of an arrow.
This time it didn’t point toward some uncertain section of the floor or hint at a route somewhere below the labyrinth.
It aimed directly at the base of the central gate.
Straight beneath the arena where Leon stood.
He followed the direction and searched the floor. With his perception sharpened and stabilized by the Spatial Tempering Crystal, he found what the final rearrangement had uncovered.
A circular seam ran through the stone.
It formed a wide ring around the section of floor supporting the gate, a join that hadn’t been visible before the labyrinth shifted. The Tower’s interface still gave no sign that it existed.
By moving the official paths into position for the final trial, the floor had exposed the edge of something hidden beneath its own center.
The uncounted route wasn’t simply somewhere below Floor Three.
It ended here.
Under the final arena.
Under the Gatekeeper’s gate.

The three fragments remained incomplete. They gave Leon no further clue about the whole they belonged to. He still didn’t know how many pieces were missing, what the completed pattern would unlock, or what might be waiting beyond it.
They revealed only the entrance’s location.
The path down lay beneath his feet, at the exact place where the Tower wanted him looking forward.
Leon remained there with the three keys in one hand and the three black fragments pulling toward the floor in the other.
He could place the keys into the gate, open it, and fight the Gatekeeper carrying the power of both treasures he had claimed.
Or he could search the circular seam for a way through and follow the fragments into something the Tower offered no rules, warnings, or system guidance for.
Ahead of him waited the Gatekeeper and the price of his choices.
Below waited whatever the Tower refused to count.

Same starting angle of the sword, following the line the Sentinel had already learned.
The construct took the bait completely.
Its blade drove in to intercept the attack it expected, committing to the counter before Leon’s cut had fully formed.
Leon let the setup remain convincing for one more instant, then abandoned it.
His point dropped, his feet shifted off the learned line, and the Sentinel’s sword passed through the place his attack should have occupied.
The pattern had told it what would happen.
The pattern was wrong.
That alone wasn’t enough to end the fight.
The construct recovered with frightening speed, dragging its weapon back into guard before Leon could finish it.
Still, the exchange had given him what he needed.
From then on, Leon stopped letting it learn anything cleanly.
He kept Leximancy and his largest attacks out of the exchange.
The Sentinel was an artificial Tower mechanism with no living will he could confidently bind, while its adaptive shell gathered reinforcement against direct force.
More importantly, every visible beginning became information for it.
Leon could still escalate if the method failed, but there was no reason to show this guardian his strongest abilities while a cleaner answer remained.
He broke up the timing of his ordinary swordwork, delaying some attacks and releasing others early so no stable rhythm could settle in.
Feints became part of nearly every sequence.
He would begin something familiar, allow the Sentinel to identify it, then turn the motion into something else before the construct could adjust.
During one exchange, fire gathered along his blade as he started a fire-enhanced cut.
The Sentinel saw the flame and moved for the answer it had begun to build.
Leon stripped the fire away before the strike landed and came in with bare steel from an angle the flame had helped hide.
Later, he showed the same opening again.
The construct prepared for another fire-cut.
Lightning snapped instead.
The sudden change caught the Sentinel shifting its weight in the wrong direction.
Leon gave it movement patterns too.
When pressure came toward his left side, he repeatedly slipped away to the right, teaching the guardian that this was his preferred preference.
Once the Sentinel began counting on that response, it drove at his left again and committed its blade to cutting off the retreat.
This time Leon didn’t move through space at all.
He stayed where he was, caught the incoming blade physically, and turned it aside while the Sentinel continued trying to intercept an escape that never happened.
The Spatial Tempering Crystal had improved the efficiency of his folds noticeably.
On the one careful displacement he allowed himself, he slid half a step through the Sentinel’s guard.
The fold stayed tight under the adaptive spatial pressure surrounding the arena and cost less control to maintain.
Leon was grateful for the difference.
He couldn’t keep using space freely.
After only a few repetitions, the Sentinel would begin reading that too.
Every fold needed to accomplish something before it became another habit the construct could study.
None of the choices came from the System.
Leon made them from the fight itself, relying on the sense built over a hundred exchanges.
His body knew when the Sentinel had fully committed and when it still had room to change course.
He kept working patiently, feeding it false patterns, then punishing the counters those patterns produced.
Bit by bit, the guardian’s ability to read him turned against it.
For the final trap, Leon offered his left side.
He made the opening look deliberate enough to be useful but natural enough to resemble the defensive preference he had taught the Sentinel since the opening exchange.
The construct had repeatedly watched him protect that line and retreat to the right.
Now it finally saw the chance it wanted.
The Sentinel thrust straight for the exposed opening with complete commitment, certain it had reached the end of the pattern.
Leon had never intended to leave the target available.
At the last instant, he folded the incoming strike a fraction off course.
The tempered displacement held cleanly, carrying the point just past his ribs.
While the construct’s blade continued into the space he had abandoned, Leon stepped inside its reach.
The Sentinel tried to correct.
It couldn’t do it quickly enough.
Once it had committed to a learned answer, breaking that motion was the one weakness built into its design.
Holy energy wrapped Leon’s sword as he drove it upward into the exposed core.
The blade met real resistance before forcing its way through.
Then the core cracked, and the light inside the construct flickered out.
The Sentinel collapsed in on itself and stopped moving.
[Tower Key Acquired]
[Tower Keys Collected: 3/3]
[Route to Central Gate Unsealed]
The third key lifted from the arena floor.
Leon claimed it while his breathing settled, unharmed and satisfied.
Three out of three.
At last, Floor Three’s key requirement was finished.
The labyrinth reacted more violently than it had at any earlier point.
Movement spread across the entire floor.
Walls traveled over enormous distances.
Bronze paths, silver paths, and unmarked corridors all rotated, withdrew, or vanished into the shifting structure.
The maze folded in on itself and rebuilt around one purpose.
When the motion ended, almost everything had closed.
A single broad corridor remained, running straight toward the center of Floor Three.
Leon took a moment to breathe and judge his condition.
His body was whole.
His conscious armor was intact, and the compact trial had taken only a modest share of a full mana reserve.
What remained was mental fatigue from hours of puzzles, hidden mechanisms, and enemies that punished careless habits.
He was ready to fight.
Leon started along the open path.
Nothing interrupted him before he reached the central chamber.
The room beyond was enormous.
At its far end stood the gate, a massive arch built from dark metal and stone.
Three keyholes waited in its surface.
Beyond that barrier, Leon could sense the Gatekeeper.
The Tower had already revealed the abilities waiting with it: Spatial Resistance and Technique Mimicry.
Those were the costs attached to the two optional treasures he had taken.
The debt had reached the point of collection.
He crossed the chamber with the three keys in hand.
Then the fragments jerked downward.
The pull came harder than ever, a brutal wrench from inside his storage that stopped Leon in the middle of a step.
He immediately brought out all three pieces and fitted their broken edges together.
The groove along the reverse locked into the shape of an arrow.
This time it didn’t point toward some uncertain section of the floor or hint at a route somewhere below the labyrinth.
It aimed directly at the base of the central gate.
Straight beneath the arena where Leon stood.
He followed the direction and searched the floor.
With his perception sharpened and stabilized by the Spatial Tempering Crystal, he found what the final rearrangement had uncovered.
A circular seam ran through the stone.
It formed a wide ring around the section of floor supporting the gate, a join that hadn’t been visible before the labyrinth shifted.
The Tower’s interface still gave no sign that it existed.
By moving the official paths into position for the final trial, the floor had exposed the edge of something hidden beneath its own center.
The uncounted route wasn’t simply somewhere below Floor Three.
It ended here.
Under the final arena.
Under the Gatekeeper’s gate.
The three fragments remained incomplete.
They gave Leon no further clue about the whole they belonged to.
He still didn’t know how many pieces were missing, what the completed pattern would unlock, or what might be waiting beyond it.
They revealed only the entrance’s location.
The path down lay beneath his feet, at the exact place where the Tower wanted him looking forward.
Leon remained there with the three keys in one hand and the three black fragments pulling toward the floor in the other.
He could place the keys into the gate, open it, and fight the Gatekeeper carrying the power of both treasures he had claimed.
Or he could search the circular seam for a way through and follow the fragments into something the Tower offered no rules, warnings, or system guidance for.
Ahead of him waited the Gatekeeper and the price of his choices.
Below waited whatever the Tower refused to count.

chapters.title: Chapter 576: The Vault Beneath
paragraphs: Leon fitted the three Tower Keys into the central gate, one after another, and let it take them.

Each key slid into its hole and locked, and he felt the mechanism draw them deeper, claiming them. When he tested his grip on the last one out of habit, it wouldn’t come free. They’d done what they were made to do, and the gate had no intention of giving them back.
[Tower Keys Accepted]
[Central Gate Unsealed]
The great doors ground apart down their center, and beyond them the dark stirred with a presence — heavy, patient, large enough that his awareness pressed against it and found no edge.
The Gatekeeper.

He knew what it carried; the Tower had told him plainly enough that it held Spatial Resistance and Technique Mimicry. The presence itself offered nothing so precise. Only weight, and the sense of something settled in for a long wait. He didn’t step toward it.

The unlocking hadn’t only opened the doors. Beneath his boots the floor turned — wide stone rings rotating against one another, the gate’s mechanism reaching down into the foundation — and as they moved, the circular seam his fragments had found came fully into the open, a clean ring cut around the base of the gate.

Leon checked his condition before turning away from the open gate. His body was whole, both arms moved without pain or delay, and his conscious bronze-gold armor had repaired every mark left by the previous trials. The rest before the final key trial and his passive recovery afterward had returned his mana to nearly full.

The three black fragments pulled toward a shallow depression set into the exposed mechanism. He drew them out, aligned them edge to edge, and pressed them into the hollow. They filled part of the design and no more, their outer edges running off toward pieces he didn’t have, and for a moment nothing happened.
He looked again at the groove on their reverse side. He’d read it as direction — down, always down.

But the groove was still there now that he’d arrived, still describing something, and he understood it differently on the second look. Not a pointer. A track. The way a lock described a motion rather than a place.
He took hold of the aligned fragments and turned them through the depression, following the groove’s channel, sliding the pieces the way the pattern wanted to move.
Catches released deep in the floor.

The depression sank and split, and the stone beneath the official gate drew back to reveal a spiral staircase winding down into the dark. The Tower said nothing about it — no message, no rules, no acknowledgment that a staircase had just opened under its most important door.
He weighed it. He could fight the Gatekeeper first; it waited right there.

But clearing Floor Three the official way might pull him straight out to the next floor, or seal the maze behind him, and he couldn’t count on this staircase still being here afterward. The hidden route had survived this long by staying hidden. He wasn’t going to gamble it on the hope that the Tower would leave an opening it didn’t officially acknowledge.
He picked the fragments back out of the depression and went down.
The stairs wound tight and steep, and the Tower’s presence thinned as he descended. Past a certain depth the interface stopped answering entirely.

He reached for the Cosmic System and found it just as quiet — not gone, only unwilling or unable to offer a reading on the stone or anything inside it. Below that point he was outside the Tower’s ordinary accounting, in a place neither interface would describe.
The staircase ended and opened onto the vault.

His perception spread into a vast space — cracked pillars marching away into the dark, holding up a ceiling lost somewhere far above his reach. The place was old in the way the Hall of the Uncounted had been old: no maintenance, no swept care, only age and damage and dust.

Broken treasure chests lay scattered with their lids torn off. Discarded weapons rested among them, the arms of challengers who’d come this far and never left. Names had been carved into the stone and then scratched deliberately away, the same erasure he’d seen above.

Shallow channels ran through the floor, all of them converging inward on a central sealed doorway set into a great block of stone. Around that doorway, embedded in four separate stone seals, were four black fragments.
He stopped and looked at them a while.

Four, matching the three he carried, the same light-drinking black, their broken edges catching the dim light the way his did. Seven fragments made the whole. Every broken line on Leon’s three pieces found its continuation among the four in the seals. The complete design was in this room.
Above the seals, worn into the stone in the same old letters as the first hidden stair, ran an inscription.
THE VAULT BENEATH THE COUNTED PATH
He read it and left it. The name told him where he stood and nothing about who had named it, and he’d stopped expecting the old carvings to explain themselves.
He walked toward the central door, and the fragments wrenched free of his hand.
All three at once, pulling out of his grip toward the four in the seals. He let them go.

The seven came together in the air before the door, drawn to one another along their broken edges, aligning and locking piece against piece until the full design stood complete for the first time — a key, unusually complex, made wholly of that black material, teeth within teeth and a bow folded back on itself, drinking the vault’s faint light so it read as a key-shaped absence hanging in the dark.
As it settled, an inscription burned to life across the central seal.
OBSIDIAN KEY
No history came with the name. Just the two words, and the key hanging finished before the door.

The Obsidian Key turned on its own, rotating inside the central mechanism, and the four surrounding seals answered. They unlocked one after another, each with a heavy grinding release — first one, then the next, then the third and fourth, the apparatus coming undone in careful sequence.
Watching four independent seals release around a single door, Leon understood something he’d had backwards.

You didn’t need four separate seals and a seven-piece key scattered across a labyrinth to keep people out. That much security wasn’t the architecture of a treasure room. It was the architecture of a cell.
The seals hadn’t only kept challengers from getting in. They’d kept something from getting out.
The central doors opened.
The completed key withdrew from the mechanism and remained suspended beside the entrance.
