chapters.title: Chapter 577: The Hollow King of Avarice
paragraphs: Beyond them lay a throne chamber, heaped with treasure — not scattered and broken like the vault outside, but gathered, weapons and artifacts and chests of valuables piled around the walls and arranged around a single central seat.
On that seat sat the thing the seals had held.
It was tall and gaunt, wearing royal armor of black and gold gone to damage — cracked plates, a dented crown, the whole of it worn like something that had sat too long.
Through the gaps he saw no body, no flesh or bone, only a hollow darkness that deepened beneath the crown past anything his perception could read.

Broken weapons and dulled treasures orbited the throne, some drifting free and some chained to it, turning slowly around their seated king. Its hands were empty. In the center of its chest, behind a cracked seam in the plate, black-gold energy circulated — the drawn-off power of everything piled around it, cycling through a cavity where a heart should have been.
Words were carved deep into the stone of the throne, and Leon read them as the figure lifted its hollow head.
The Hollow King of Avarice.
He didn’t need a Tower panel to name it. The throne named it, and the thing carried the truth of the title in every stolen treasure and every dulled chain. This was no guardian set to watch a door.
Its combined pressure stood firmly within Ethereal Lord territory, stronger in total output than the Uncounted Warden.
Much of that strength was not its own. Power flowed from the surrounding treasures into the hollow armor, raising the sovereign far beyond the Ethereal Initiates Leon had already surpassed.
It didn’t attack. Its head tilted, the darkness beneath the crown considering him, and when it spoke the voice rose from everywhere at once, a dry resonance out of the treasure piles themselves.

"You took the rewards," it said. "Knowing each would strengthen what waits at your gate. Most who reach me flinched from every treasure the Tower offered, too afraid of the cost. You did not." Something like approval moved through the words. "You understand value."
Leon said nothing, and kept his eyes moving over the chamber — the piled artifacts, the chains, the slow-turning treasures, mapping what sat where.
"I can offer more than the Tower ever will."

The treasures stirred, and clear images rose from them. Greater elemental authority, fire and storm answering him at a scale he hadn’t yet reached. Spatial movement gone perfect and effortless, folds without strain. His conscious armor manifested fuller, more complete than he’d yet worn it.

The whole hoard of the vault, laid out as his. Access to the Tower’s hidden routes at a thought. And knowledge — the uncounted path explained, its makers named, the mystery he’d been chasing simply handed to him.
The offers were good. That was what made him careful. The power in them was real, or close enough, and the King held it out as though it cost nothing.
He reached along the edges of the offer with his own perception, not the System — the System had nothing, and he’d stopped waiting on it.
Under every gift ran the same thread of black-gold energy that bound the orbiting treasures to the throne, the same chains that held them.

Anything he accepted would carry that thread into him. Take the power, and the power would take him — bind him to the vault the way every dulled treasure in the room was bound, make him one more possession turning slowly around a throne he’d never rise from.
"No," Leon said.
The hollow head stilled. "You refuse power. Wealth. Even the answers you came chasing."
"I refuse a leash." He said it flatly.

He had no quarrel with power, and none with treasure — he’d spent the whole floor proving it, taking what he wanted and paying as the prices came. But a gift that made him a possession was worth nothing, and once he’d seen the thread through it, everything the King offered had emptied out.
"Keep all of it."
The chamber went silent. Then the visions collapsed, the treasure-light drawing back into the piles, and the Hollow King rose from its throne.
"Then you are taken the harder way."
It attacked.
Leon met it head-on, because the fastest way to learn a thing was to hit it and see what happened.
The King’s empty hand swept toward a pile and a weapon leapt to it — a long black blade full of borrowed light — and it crossed the distance faster than its size allowed.

Leon didn’t bother with restraint. He answered with real force: a sword strike backed by holy energy, then a lance of white fire that took the King square in the chest and blew a crater through the black-and-gold plate, deep enough to end most things twice over.

The crater filled itself in. Black-gold energy flowed up from the treasure piles into the cracked cavity and out through the armor, and the ruin he’d made sealed over, plates knitting whole while he watched.
Leon tested another path.
"Kneel."
Leximancy struck the Hollow King hard enough to drive one armored knee toward the floor.

Before the command could hold, black-gold power surged through the four strongest threads linking it to the hoard. The burden of the word spread across several anchors instead of remaining fixed on one will, and the King forced itself upright.
The command worked. The structure supporting the King broke its hold.

He tried a cleaner kill. He folded space in a tight, stable arc — the Spatial Tempering held it steady even with the vault pushing back — and took the King’s head from its shoulders with a single pass of his blade.
The head crumbled to dust before it hit the floor, and a new one rose out of the hollow, the darkness beneath the crown simply extending itself back into shape.

Not a lack of force, then. He had force enough. The problem was that breaking the body did nothing to what fed it. As long as the treasures poured power into that chest, cutting the King down was like cutting water.
He reached to fold something larger — to tear open the ground beneath the throne, to distort the whole chamber and rip the King’s foundation out from under it.
The vault refused him.
The ancient structure pushed back against any distortion on that scale, the space around him going stiff and unyielding.

Short folds it allowed. Redirections, local pressure, a step of teleportation within the chamber — those held. Rearranging the room, it would not. He filed that away and stopped wasting strength on it.

The King fought with a cruel intelligence. When he pressed close it dropped the long blade back into the hoard and called a shorter, heavier weapon to rule the near distance. When he backed off to use elements it summoned an artifact and answered with stored elemental power, forcing him to defend.
And it used chains — lengths of golden-black energy lashing out from the throne, catching at his footwork, trying to bind him and drag him toward the seat.
One chain caught his forearm long enough for a stolen blade carrying Ethereal Lord-level force to split the conscious armor at his side. The weapon opened flesh beneath it and spilled blood.
Leon twisted free while the wound closed almost before the pain finished registering. Bronze-gold material flowed over the damaged plate just as quickly. Blood remained. The injury did not.
He was spending power, but his reserves ran deep and his mana trickled back even as he fought. He wasn’t in danger of running dry.

He was in danger of the chains — of the way they reached for more than his body, that thread of ownership riding under every one, trying to fix itself to him rather than merely cut him. Those he made very sure to sever fast.
Then he saw the channels clearly, and the fight changed shape.

Not every treasure fed the King. He’d assumed the whole hoard did, but watching the black-gold energy flow he saw it ran from only certain artifacts — threads connecting a handful of treasures to the cavity in the King’s chest, while the rest of the hoard sat dark and dead. A limited number. He picked out four that mattered, and the Mirrorheart tempering sharpened his eye for the pattern of them — for how the King’s power repeated, and which sources it drew from when.

One pulsed in time with the King’s regeneration, the treasure that rebuilt it. One thrummed whenever the chains lashed out. One flared each time the King loosed stored elemental power. And one held a deep, steady note beneath the others — the anchor, he judged, that held the King’s hollow identity and armored form together at all.
Destroy what feeds the body, not the body. That was the fight.

He tried a cleaner kill.
He folded space in a tight, stable arc — the Spatial Tempering held it steady even with the vault pushing back — and took the King’s head from its shoulders with a single pass of his blade.
The head crumbled to dust before it hit the floor, and a new one rose out of the hollow, the darkness beneath the crown simply extending itself back into shape.
Not a lack of force, then.
He had force enough.
The problem was that breaking the body did nothing to what fed it.
As long as the treasures poured power into that chest, cutting the King down was like cutting water.
He reached to fold something larger — to tear open the ground beneath the throne, to distort the whole chamber and rip the King’s foundation out from under it.
The vault refused him.
The ancient structure pushed back against any distortion on that scale, the space around him going stiff and unyielding.
Short folds it allowed.
Redirections, local pressure, a step of teleportation within the chamber — those held.
Rearranging the room, it would not.
He filed that away and stopped wasting strength on it.
The King fought with a cruel intelligence.
When he pressed close it dropped the long blade back into the hoard and called a shorter, heavier weapon to rule the near distance.
When he backed off to use elements it summoned an artifact and answered with stored elemental power, forcing him to defend.
And it used chains — lengths of golden-black energy lashing out from the throne, catching at his footwork, trying to bind him and drag him toward the seat.
One chain caught his forearm long enough for a stolen blade carrying Ethereal Lord-level force to split the conscious armor at his side.
The weapon opened flesh beneath it and spilled blood.
Leon twisted free while the wound closed almost before the pain finished registering.
Bronze-gold material flowed over the damaged plate just as quickly.
Blood remained.
The injury did not.
He was spending power, but his reserves ran deep and his mana trickled back even as he fought.
He wasn’t in danger of running dry.
He was in danger of the chains — of the way they reached for more than his body, that thread of ownership riding under every one, trying to fix itself to him rather than merely cut him.
Those he made very sure to sever fast.
Then he saw the channels clearly, and the fight changed shape.
Not every treasure fed the King.

He’d assumed the whole hoard did, but watching the black-gold energy flow he saw it ran from only certain artifacts — threads connecting a handful of treasures to the cavity in the King’s chest, while the rest of the hoard sat dark and dead.
A limited number.
He picked out four that mattered, and the Mirrorheart tempering sharpened his eye for the pattern of them — for how the King’s power repeated, and which sources it drew from when.
One pulsed in time with the King’s regeneration, the treasure that rebuilt it.
One thrummed whenever the chains lashed out.
One flared each time the King loosed stored elemental power.
And one held a deep, steady note beneath the others — the anchor, he judged, that held the King’s hollow identity and armored form together at all.
Destroy what feeds the body, not the body.
That was the fight.

chapters.title: Chapter 578: What Fed the King
paragraphs: He went for them across several hard exchanges, not all at once.
The elemental anchor exposed itself most, because the King kept drawing on it, and the King drew the same way each time — a gather, a channel, a release.

The third time it loosed a torrent of stored flame at him, Leon caught the attack’s leading edge with a small precise fold and bent its path, redirecting the fire back along the thread that had summoned it, into the artifact that supplied it.
The anchor cracked and went dark, its thread snapping loose. The stored elemental attacks stopped coming.

The chain anchor he reached by letting a chain reach him. When the next length lashed for his legs he angled his armored forearm into its path and let it bind to the bronze-gold plate — then, instead of cutting free, he took the physical line and traced its power straight back to the source, hauling himself along it toward the treasure that fed it.

He felt the ownership-thread trying to sink into him through the contact and broke free of it a breath before it could set, and as the chain’s recoil swung him past its anchor he drove his sword through the artifact.
It shattered. Every chain in the room fell dead.
The regeneration anchor the King guarded above all, placing its body between Leon and the treasure whenever he moved that way.

So Leon didn’t move that way — he faked it. He launched an all-out assault at the regeneration anchor, committing hard, selling it, and the King spun to interpose itself and shield the source that kept it whole.

In protecting the healing anchor it shifted its guard and let the deep steady note of the Sovereign anchor pulse clear, and Leon marked its position exactly. Then he cut the regeneration anchor while the King was still committed to blocking an attack he’d already dropped, and the treasure split. The next wound he opened in the King’s armor stayed open, black edges gaping where the plate no longer knit itself shut.
Three anchors were gone.

The King had landed several real hits during the exchanges, but every wound had already closed and the conscious armor had repaired each split within seconds. Blood marked where the attacks had reached him. Nothing remained underneath it.

The lasting cost was mana and concentration. The vault resisted every spatial working, making each precise fold more expensive than it would have been outside, and the destroyed chain had taken energy to escape. His reserve remained substantial and continued recovering. Both hearts beat steadily.
The Hollow King, stripped of three powers, abandoned the throne.
It came at him directly, and it was still terrible — the skill and strength were its own, and desperation had made it faster.

It called its strongest stolen weapon, a great black glaive humming with the last of its borrowed light, and drove at him with everything left: no chains, no elements, just a hollow king and a master’s weapon and the single anchor holding it together.

It expected him to go for the chest again. He’d gone for the chest and its anchors the whole fight, and it braced to counter that exact attack, ready to spend the Sovereign anchor’s last energy on one decisive trade.

So Leon showed it the setup and withheld the strike. He began a large technique — holy fire gathering along his blade, a spatial fold visibly building, every sign of a committed thrust at the King’s chest. The King saw it, recognized it, and committed to the counter, the glaive sweeping in on the line that would cut him in half as he lunged.
He didn’t lunge.

He let the fire die and the fold collapse unused, stepped off the braced line with an irregular half-beat of timing, and as the glaive swept through the space his thrust should have carried him into, he made one small controlled fold — nudging the great weapon a hair off true.
It missed him by inches. And the King, having spent its counter into a killing blow that killed nothing, stood open.
Leon drove his sword through the Sovereign anchor.

The steady note that had underpinned everything cut out. The black-and-gold armor lurched, the darkness beneath the crown thinning, the whole form beginning to come apart with nothing left to hold its accumulated identity together.

It made one last lunge — not for his throat but past him, grasping for the Obsidian Key hanging by the door, reaching to seize the key or to throw a final binding thread and drag him down as its replacement.
He met it.

He stepped inside the failing lunge and drove his sword through the cracked cavity in its chest, into the hollow where the borrowed power had circulated, and released everything at once — physical force and a concentrated pulse of holy energy poured through the blade into the emptiness at its center.

The Hollow King collapsed. Its armor, its crown, the dark remnant of a body it had never truly owned — all of it crumbled into fine black-gold dust and sifted down across the throne and the ruined hoard.
No Tower message came. Down here, nothing counted the kill.

The treasures did not all vanish, but most were wreckage — drained hollow, cracked, dulled, or sealed shut, the wealth of the vault reduced to nothing worth carrying by the death of the thing that had fed on it. There was no fortune to gather.

The Obsidian Key hung intact by the door where the King had failed to reach it. Leon crossed to it, his breathing already settling, and took it down. Seven fragments made one, cold and complete in his hand.
Behind him the throne split open. He turned, blade half-up, but nothing came out.

The empty seat had cracked down its center, and in the cavity inside it sat a small sealed reliquary — a plain dark box, closed and locked, giving his senses nothing. He reached for the Cosmic System and got the vault’s silence. But an inscription ran across the lid in the same old letters.
ONLY AFTER THE COUNTED ASCENT
MAY THE UNCOUNTED CLAIM
He understood well enough.

The counted ascent — the official trial, the thing the Tower actually measured. Whatever waited inside wouldn’t open until he cleared Floor Three the proper way. The hidden victory earned him the box; only the official one would unlock it.
He took the reliquary from the broken throne, stored it sealed, and kept the Obsidian Key with it. The builders of the vault, the erased names, and the Hollow King’s origin all remained unknown.
The vault began to come apart around him.

With the King dead it lost whatever had held it stable — dust sifting from the lost ceiling, cracks widening in the pillars, a low grinding settling into the stone. The spiral staircase remained open at the vault’s edge, and he made for it as the chamber sagged behind him.

He climbed. Dried blood remained on his already repaired armor, the only visible evidence of wounds that had closed during the fight. Near the top the Tower’s presence returned, reaching down to find him, thickening with each turn until the familiar sense of being watched settled back over him.
He came out into the central chamber, and the Tower woke.
[Tower Keys Collected: 3/3]
[Optional Treasures Claimed: 2]
[Gatekeeper Enhancements: Spatial Resistance, Technique Mimicry]

That was all. Not a word of the fragments, the Obsidian Key, the vault, the King, or the reliquary in his storage. As far as the Tower knew, he’d unlocked the gate and stood exactly where he’d been, and nothing had happened in between. The floor beneath the gate had closed seamless behind him, uncounted again.
His body kept a truer record.

Blood streaked the repaired bronze-gold armor, but his flesh was whole and his channels remained stable. His mana sat below its peak and continued climbing. The King had taxed his reserve and concentration without leaving a lasting injury.

The official gate stood open ahead, and beyond it the Gatekeeper’s presence waited — patient, heavy, carrying the price of the two treasures Leon had claimed and nothing from the King below. Whatever he’d killed in the vault, the thing ahead was exactly as strong as he’d made it and no stronger.
He steadied his grip on his sword and stepped through the gate.

chapters.title: Chapter 579: Everything It Learned Was Wrong
paragraphs: Dark stone formed a wide circular arena beyond the gate. The Gatekeeper waited in the middle.

Its shape was humanoid, though far larger than any ordinary man, and seamless gray armor covered it from head to foot. One hand gripped a heavy blade. The helm had no eyes or face, only a smooth metal surface that turned toward Leon when he stepped inside.
The doors shut behind him as soon as he crossed the entrance. At the same time, the presence he had sensed through the gate stopped feeling distant and became a firm pressure in the arena.

Adaptive calibration had pushed the Gatekeeper’s physical output into the lower range of Ethereal Lord territory. It still fell short of the fully anchored Hollow King, but it stood well above the Ethereal Initiates Leon could defeat without much trouble. Raw rank was not the only concern, either. Spatial Resistance and Technique Mimicry made the gap far more dangerous.
Leon began with a test.
He formed one compact spear of white fire and sent it forward. The technique was clean, tightly controlled, and deliberately simple. He wanted to see exactly how the mimicry worked.
The Gatekeeper raised its sword and caught the fire against the blade.
Leon felt the instant it absorbed the technique. Somewhere behind the blank helm, its structure registered.
A moment later, the construct lifted its free hand. White flame appeared over its palm in the same shape and with the same formation Leon had used. The Tower supplied the power behind it.
The spear came back faster and harder than his own.
Leon folded aside. The attack passed him and exploded against the arena wall.
So the copies aren’t weak.
The Covetous Reflection had returned reduced imitations. The Gatekeeper did something else. It recreated the full structure and fueled it with Tower power instead of Leon’s affinity.
It had copied the shape of the technique, though not the understanding behind it. It did not know why Leon had chosen that attack or when it should be used.
At this level of output, the shape alone could still kill him.
Next, Leon attempted a displacement. He folded across the arena, aiming to appear on the Gatekeeper’s flank.
The construct did not mimic it.
His working began to unravel as soon as the fold formed near its body. Space around the Gatekeeper refused Leon’s distortion. The passage broke apart and dropped him short of his target.
Spatial Resistance.

He could not displace the construct or complete a fold cleanly against its body. Teleporting straight into a finishing blow would not work. Void Dominion still obeyed him elsewhere in the arena, but the region immediately surrounding the Gatekeeper rejected his control.
Leon measured the protected area and discarded the idea of ending the fight through direct spatial manipulation.
Anything he showed in complete form could be copied and turned against him. Throwing larger attacks at the Gatekeeper would merely give it larger attacks to return.
Its ability still had limits.

Technique Mimicry could not duplicate Leon’s affinities, his dual-heart constitution, his conscious armor, the combat experience he had integrated, or the judgment that connected one move to another. Leximancy offered no answer either. The Tower construct contained no living will for Leon to bind.
So he decided what it was allowed to learn.

Leon used the same compact fire spear again, always with one fixed release. He added a straight lightning cut and a high sword opening, making each technique genuine and complete enough for the Gatekeeper to copy. Between them, he repeatedly retreated to the right and used one short fold that began well beyond the edge of the construct’s Spatial Resistance.
Those pieces were real. Together, they were still nowhere close to the full way Leon fought.
Technique Mimicry collected the active techniques. The Gatekeeper’s combat judgment studied everything around them.

It returned the fire spear using the Tower’s power. At midrange, lightning gathered over its blade whenever Leon approached. Each time he opened high, the construct readied the same rising counter. With every exchange, it grew more certain, building its responses around the narrow version of Leon it had been shown.
None of that made the battle safe.
The Gatekeeper’s sword carried Ethereal Lord-class force. During one clash, it smashed through a shoulder plate and cut into the flesh below.
The injury sealed within seconds. Before the next exchange finished, Leon’s armor had flowed back over the damaged section.
That did not mean he could ignore the hit. A clean thrust through either heart or his core could kill him before regeneration had time to help.
Leon refused to rush.

Mirrorheart awareness showed him each small change as recognition hardened into expectation. The Gatekeeper reproduced single techniques without error, but it had started preparing for the sequence and timing Leon kept placing around them.
Once that expectation settled firmly into place, Leon began the familiar pattern again.
White fire collected above his hand.
The Gatekeeper lifted its blade, already prepared to catch the spear and send it back.
Leon never released one.
He charged through the flare instead. Its brightness concealed his first physical step, letting him enter before the construct adjusted.
The Gatekeeper shifted into the rising sword counter it had learned from him.
Leon delayed himself by half a beat.

The heavy blade swept past before he reached its path. Lightning crawled along Leon’s sword, advertising the straight cut he had used earlier. In answer, the Gatekeeper brought its copied lightning around to intercept.
Just before contact, Leon dismissed the element.
Ordinary steel struck instead.
The Gatekeeper still recovered quickly enough to block him. It forced Leon backward, then pursued with the rightward retreat and fire-spear combination it had learned from his example.
Leon finally brought space into the exchange, though he made no attempt to affect the resistant body.
Beyond the boundary protecting the Gatekeeper, he folded the path of the copied flame. The spear bent around him and drove into the construct’s sword arm.
Tower-fed fire burst across the gray armor, disrupting its follow-up.
Spatial Resistance had never stopped working. It simply did not matter. Leon had not tried to teleport through the defense at all.
He covered the remaining distance with physical speed, breaking the rhythm of his steps as he approached. The Gatekeeper prepared for another high opening.
Leon went low.
He slipped inside the reach of the heavy blade and thrust his sword beneath the smooth helm.

His earlier spatial examination had already marked the location of the core. The point struck that exact place. Holy energy and a concentrated Elemental Surge poured down the weapon and into the single target.
The core shattered.
The Gatekeeper’s enormous body froze. Whatever presence had occupied the space behind its helm vanished in an instant.
It fell backward, crashed against the dark stone, and remained still.
Before it hit the floor, Leon’s latest wounds had already healed, and his armor had finished restoring itself.
Then the Tower spoke.
[ASCENSION TOWER — FLOOR THREE CLEARED]
[Mandatory Objectives Completed: 3/3]
[Optional Treasures Claimed: 2]
[Enhanced Gatekeeper Defeated]
[Hidden Condition Completed]
[Final Evaluation: SSS]

chapters.title: Chapter 580: The First to Return
paragraphs: Leon read it standing over the dead Gatekeeper, and one line snagged him.
Hidden Condition Completed.
The ordinary trial interface had refused to record the vault, yet the final evaluation recognized that he had completed something beneath the counted route.
It still did not name the fragments, the Obsidian Key, or the Hollow King. Whatever judged the finished floor knew more than the system messages guiding him through it.
He didn’t try to solve that. It went onto the pile with every other question the uncounted path had handed him.

The grade itself, he understood. SSS, not the highest mark. He’d cleared all three mandatory trials, taken two optional treasures, beaten a Gatekeeper he’d enhanced twice, handled every adaptive trap the floor threw, and completed a hidden condition on top of it.
But he’d also walked past optional routes, left treasures unclaimed, skipped counted opportunities the floor had offered.

He’d played it ambitious and smart rather than exhaustive, and the Tower graded him exactly for what that was — excellent, and not perfect. He had no complaint. He’d made those choices on purpose, every one.
[SSS Floor Reward Granted]
[Ascension Tower — Sealed Reward Cache (Floor Three) added to storage]
A reward cache settled into his storage, sealed in the Tower’s own fashion, to be opened at leisure rather than here. He left it sealed and turned his attention to the other thing.
The reliquary reacted.

He drew it out, and the sealed box that had refused him below now stirred, its lock answering the completed clear. The Obsidian Key rose from his hand of its own accord, fit itself to the reliquary, and turned. The lid opened.

Inside, resting alone, lay a small disc of the same black light-absorbing material as the Key itself — flat, dark, and worked with a fragment of the same intricate uncounted pattern, unfinished the way everything on this route was unfinished.
No power poured off it.
It simply sat there, drinking the light. Along its rim ran a short inscription.
TOKEN OF THE UNCOUNTED
When Leon lifted the token, part of its black pattern separated from the surface and sank through his gauntlet. It passed into his chest and divided around both hearts without pain.
New words appeared across the reliquary’s inner lid.
MARK OF THE UNCOUNTED
THE MARKED SEE THE CLAIM.
THE MARKED RESIST THE CHAIN.

A hair-thin trace of black-gold ownership power still clung to one gauntlet from the King’s chains. Leon had not noticed it before. The new mark exposed it at once, and a thought from him severed the weakened thread.

The change strengthened his resistance to possession, enslavement, forced contracts, ownership authorities, and binding curses. It was not absolute immunity. A sufficiently stronger authority could still challenge it, but another Hollow King would find him far harder to place on a chain.

The token remained in his palm after granting the mark. Its larger purpose was still unknown. The unfinished pattern tied it to the hidden routes, but it offered no explanation of what it opened or answered to. The Obsidian Key also stayed whole; unlocking the reliquary had not consumed it.
He didn’t get the chance to examine the token or Key further.

The Tower began pushing him out — the arena dissolving at its edges, the familiar pull of a completed floor taking hold, the space around him folding him up and away before he could do more than store them together.
Floor Three released him,
Leon came out of the Ascension Tower into open air and a world he recognized through the very hall he had always gone through ignoring the weird elf once again, and stood a moment reorienting.

Blood remained dried across one side of his already repaired bronze-gold armor. Underneath it, his body was whole — no open wounds, broken limbs, or damaged channels. His mana remained below its peak and continued climbing, while mental fatigue lingered after two dangerous battles in close succession.
Leon took one steadying breath and felt the world settle around him, then without wait teleported to place he was eager to go back to, still bit anxious.
And almost the moment he did, something else moved.

Not far off, the Class Reawakening Dungeon stood where he’d left it — and it was reacting. A surge rolled out of it, a pressure through the air and the ground both, the whole structure pulsing with a discharge of power that hadn’t been there when he’d gone into the Tower. Its entrance flared. Something was coming out.
The synchronicity of it wasn’t lost on him. He’d stepped out of one trial into the exact moment another one broke open.
A figure emerged from the dungeon’s light.
Vyra.
She came out first — and no one else came with her, no one ahead of her, the space around the entrance otherwise empty.

She was exhausted; he could see that at once, in the set of her shoulders and the deliberate control of her movements, the bearing of someone who’d spent everything and was holding herself upright on discipline alone.
But the exhaustion sat over something else, something new.

A pressure clung to her, an authority in the air that hadn’t been there before, clear enough for his senses to catch immediately. He didn’t try to measure it against anything else. Whatever her reawakening had made of her, it had made something formidable, and it had plainly cost her to earn it.
She was still, unmistakably, Vyra. Calm even worn to the bone, her eyes already moving, taking in the ground, taking in him.
She found him, and stopped.

Her gaze went over him the way his had gone over her — the dried blood, the intact armor, the absence of any wound beneath it. He watched her reach the correct conclusion, and something eased very slightly in her when she found only the aftermath of harm already healed.
"You’re bleeding," she said.
"Was," Leon said. "It’s closed. You look like the dungeon didn’t go easy on you."
"It didn’t." A dry edge, familiar. "It decided I was worth making difficult." She held herself straighter, some of the control reasserting over the fatigue. "I take that as a compliment. Eventually."

He almost smiled. There was concern under her flatness — he could hear it, in the way she’d led with his blood before anything about herself — and he knew better than to pull it out into the open where she’d have to stand in it. That both of them were on their feet and talking said enough. Two separate trials, two survivals, and here they were.
Then Vyra turned her head toward the dungeon, still pulsing and active behind her, its light unbroken, its surge not yet spent. The question came quiet and even.
"How many came out before me?"
Leon looked at the still-active dungeon, at the empty ground around its entrance, at the light that meant everyone else was still inside it.
"None," he said.
The word landed, and the small relief of the last minute went out of the air between them. Vyra’s gaze stayed on the dungeon, and Leon’s went with it.

Somewhere behind that light were the rest of them — near nine hundred participants still inside, Seraphine and Ira and Loriel among them, none of them out, none of them accounted for, the dungeon holding all of them still and giving no sign of when it would give any of them back.
The two of them stood out.

chapters.title: Chapter 581: The Ones Who Came Back
paragraphs: The answer left a heavy silence between them.
None of the other nine hundred and sixty-nine participants had returned.
The Class Reawakening Dungeon continued to pulse behind Vyra. Every surge shook the ground and disturbed the mana in the air, but Leon could not tell what was happening inside.
He spread his spatial awareness toward the entrance.
It stopped at the boundary.
The Cosmic System gave him nothing useful either. Whatever laws governed the dungeon kept the trials hidden from everyone outside.
"You should rest," Leon said. "At least let me heal you properly."
"Later."
Vyra remained facing the dungeon.
"Ira is still inside."
"So are Seraphine and Loriel."
"And the others."
Leon placed a hand on Vyra’s shoulder anyway. Life energy entered her body, easing the worst damage in her muscles and channels.
Vyra allowed it for several seconds before stepping away.
"That is enough."
"It isn’t."
"It is enough for me to stand."
Leon did not argue further.

Neither of them asked about the other’s rewards. Leon had just returned from the Ascension Tower, and Vyra clearly carried a new class, but discussing their gains while hundreds of people were still fighting for their lives felt wrong.
They waited.
The dungeon pulsed again.
Its entrance flared white.
A red-skinned figure stumbled through.
"Ira."
She nearly fell the moment her feet touched the ground.

One side of her clothing had burned away, and black scorch marks covered her skin. Several wounds crossed her arms and stomach. The fire within her body was unstable, rising and falling with every breath.
Ira forced herself upright.
She raised her chin and took two steady steps as though she had just returned from an easy training session.
Then she saw Leon.
The strength left her legs.
Leon caught her before she reached the ground.
Ira clutched him with both arms. Her fingers tightened against the back of his armor as if she feared something might drag her into the dungeon again.
"I’ve got you," Leon said.
She did not answer.

He poured life energy through her body. Burned flesh recovered beneath his hand. Mana flowed into her damaged channels and stabilized them, while holy energy destroyed the hostile residue left by the trial.
Ira kept holding him.
Leon lowered his head and kissed her.
Her response was immediate.

Ira pulled him closer and pressed her lips against his with desperate force. Her tongue entered his mouth, meeting his without hesitation. The kiss lasted far longer than anything she would have allowed in front of Vyra under normal circumstances.
Leon did not stop her.
He continued healing her as the trembling in her body slowly faded.
When Ira finally pulled back, she remained close enough that their foreheads almost touched.
"You should have seen me in there," she said between breaths. "The dungeon tried everything. It didn’t stand a chance."
Vyra stared at her niece.
Ira’s clothes were half burned, her hair was a mess, and Leon was still supporting most of her weight.
"Ira."
"What?"
"You nearly collapsed after taking two steps."
"I was tired from winning."
"You are currently unable to stand without Leon."
"I’m letting him hold me because he missed me."
Leon’s mouth twitched.
Vyra’s stare became flatter.
"Of course."
The dungeon entrance brightened again before Ira could invent another excuse.
This time, several people emerged together.
The first man came out carrying a woman whose left leg ended below the knee. Another survivor followed with both arms wrapped around his stomach, trying to hold a terrible wound closed.
More appeared behind them.
Some walked.
Others crawled.
A few were dragged out by those who still had enough strength to help.
Leon released Ira only after confirming that she could stand.
"Stay with Vyra."
"I can help."
"You can help by not falling over."
Ira opened her mouth.
Vyra caught her shoulder.
"You heard him."
Leon was already moving.

He reached the man with the stomach wound first. Life energy entered the injury and stopped the bleeding. Leon rebuilt the damaged organs enough to remove the immediate danger, then moved to the woman missing her leg.
He could not restore a complete limb in a few seconds without exhausting far more energy than necessary, but he closed the wound and stabilized her condition.
More participants emerged.
Leon organized the survivors as he worked.
"Anyone with healing skills, come forward."
Several exhausted people obeyed.
"Handle the smaller injuries. Don’t waste your strength trying to repair anything beyond your ability. Keep them alive until I reach them."
He pointed toward those who could still walk.
"Carry the unconscious away from the entrance. Keep this area clear."
Leon’s combat experience helped him judge which injuries would become fatal first, but the healing itself came from his Life affinity, mana control, and holy energy.
He moved from one person to another.
Collapsed lungs opened.
Bleeding stopped.
Damaged channels stabilized.
Hostile energies left by the trials were burned away.
Once someone was out of immediate danger, Leon teleported them to their settlement. Families and local healers were waiting there.
The first reunions began almost immediately.
A mother screamed her son’s name and threw herself around him before the spatial fold had fully settled. An old man dropped to his knees when his daughter appeared alive.
Not everyone received the person they were waiting for.
Some families kept watching the dungeon.
The number of survivors slowly rose.
So did the number of missing participants.
Leon maintained a count while he worked.
More than twenty people were already unaccounted for.
The dungeon was still active, so the number was not final. That did little to comfort the families waiting nearby.
Another group emerged.
Then another.
Some participants carried new pressure around them, suggesting successful reawakenings.
Others returned without any clear change.
A few looked more defeated than injured. They had survived, but whatever happened inside had broken something that healing could not immediately repair.
Leon did not ask about their classes.
There would be time for that later.
The dungeon surged once more.
This pulse was stronger than the others.
The light inside the entrance twisted, and a lone figure stepped out.
Amethyst hair hung around a blood-covered face.
Cracks ran through her damaged armor.
Seraphine remained standing through nothing but discipline.
Her eyes crossed the clearing.
They found Leon.

chapters.title: Chapter 582: The Last One Out
paragraphs: Leon reached Seraphine before her second step.
She opened her mouth.
"I’m fine."
He kissed her before she could say it.
Seraphine stiffened for a moment.
Then her arms wrapped around him.
Her kiss was different from Ira’s. There was no desperate force behind it. Seraphine allowed herself to relax slowly, surrendering the control that had carried her out of the dungeon.
Her tongue met his.
She leaned into him while Leon’s life energy spread through her body.
The deep cuts beneath her armor began to close. Mana flowed through her exhausted channels, easing the damage left by the trial.
When their lips finally separated, Seraphine kept her forehead against his.
"You came back," Leon said.
"So did you."
"Barely."
Seraphine glanced at the dried blood still covering parts of his repaired armor.
"You look worse than I do."
"The blood isn’t mine anymore."
"That sentence does not make me feel better."
"It should. I’m healed."
A short distance away, Ira crossed her arms.
"That kiss was longer."
Seraphine did not turn.
"You counted?"
"I did not."
"You answered very quickly."
Ira’s face darkened.
"I didn’t need a long kiss because I came out in better condition."
Vyra looked at her niece’s burned clothing.
Seraphine followed her gaze.
"I see."
"Stop doing that."
"Doing what?"
"Agreeing like that."
Despite the banter, the tension did not leave them.
Loriel remained inside.
Leon finished healing Seraphine before returning to the new survivors.
The dungeon continued releasing people in smaller groups. Each wave contained fewer participants than the one before.
Leon healed those in danger and sent them home.
The families who had already reunited left the area. Those still waiting remained near the entrance, refusing food, rest, or comfort.
Hours passed.
The dungeon’s light began to weaken.
Leon updated the count.
Nine hundred and twelve survivors had returned.
Seven people were still missing.
Loriel was one of them.
Another pulse released three participants.
Two more emerged several minutes later.
The entrance began contracting.
Leon stared at the remaining light.
Two people were still missing.
A final man fell out of the dungeon and struck the ground. Leon teleported to him, stabilized his heart, and sent him toward the healers.
One remained.
Loriel.
The dungeon continued closing.
Ira’s earlier energy disappeared.
Seraphine stood with one hand around her sword’s hilt. Her face remained calm, but her fingers had turned white.
Vyra said nothing.
Leon approached the entrance.
He pressed his spatial authority against the boundary again.
Nothing changed.
He tried the Cosmic System.
No response.
He used holy energy, life energy, and mana to search for any connection to Loriel.
The dungeon rejected everything.
The entrance shrank until only a narrow column of light remained.
Leon’s chest tightened.
Not like this.
He could kill enemies several ranks above himself.
He could create worlds, bend space, and survive wounds that should have ended him.
None of it allowed him to reach one person trapped behind this wall.
The last light began collapsing.
Something flew through it.
Leon moved before he recognized the body.
Green hair streamed through the air, soaked dark with blood.
Loriel fell from the closing dungeon.
Leon caught her.
Her body was cold.
Cuts covered nearly every part of her. Several bones had shattered, and a deep wound passed through her abdomen. Her breathing was so faint that even Leon struggled to detect it.
Worse, some kind of destructive life energy continued spreading through her body. It twisted natural growth into something violent, forcing healthy tissue to consume itself.
Leon placed one hand against her chest.
Life energy flooded into her.
"Leon?" Ira asked.
He did not respond.
The spreading damage resisted ordinary healing. Leon changed his approach immediately.
Holy energy entered Loriel’s body and separated the hostile influence from her natural vitality. At the same time, Leon used his Life affinity to keep her organs functioning.
Her heart stopped.
Leon forced it to beat again.
Seraphine dropped beside them.
"What do you need?"
"Nothing. Give me space."
Vyra knelt on the other side.
"The damage is still spreading below her ribs."
"I see it."
"It is moving toward her heart."
"Not anymore."
Leon trapped the hostile energy and burned it away with holy power.
Loriel’s broken ribs returned to their proper position. Her lungs repaired. The terrible wound through her stomach closed layer by layer.
Ira stood nearby, both hands clenched.
"She’s going to survive, right?"
Leon still did not answer.
He repaired Loriel’s mana channels last.
They were different from what he remembered.
Something had changed inside them during the trial. The new structure was wider, deeper, and filled with a strange vitality even while damaged.
Leon did not have time to study it.
He stabilized everything and checked her again.
Loriel’s heart beat steadily.
Her breathing returned.
Her injuries were gone.
She did not wake.
"Loriel."
Leon touched her face.
No response.
For one terrible moment, he wondered if he had repaired her body too late.
He searched deeper.
Her consciousness was still there.
Whole.
Safe.
She had simply exhausted herself so completely that her mind and body had shut down.
Leon finally breathed.
"She’s alive."
Ira sat down hard on the ground.
Seraphine’s hand loosened around her sword.
Vyra closed her eyes for a moment.
Behind them, the dungeon disappeared.
The final count appeared on the temporary record maintained by the officials.
Nine hundred and nineteen survivors.
Fifty-one dead.
The survival rate was far better than the historical records Leon had studied.
It did not feel like a victory.
Fifty-one people had entered after trusting his warning and their own resolve.
Fifty-one families would receive no one back.
Leon gave the settlement leaders instructions to care for the survivors and prepare the names of the dead. Compensation, support, and proper memorials would be handled after the immediate crisis.
Then he lifted Loriel.
"She needs rest."
Leon folded space around Vyra, Ira, Seraphine, and himself.
They disappeared from the empty ground outside the dungeon.

sentences.text: Leon reached Seraphine before her second step.
She opened her mouth.
"I’m fine."
He kissed her before she could say it.
Seraphine stiffened for a moment.
Then her arms wrapped around him.
Her kiss was different from Ira’s.
There was no desperate force behind it.
Seraphine allowed herself to relax slowly, surrendering the control that had carried her out of the dungeon.
Her tongue met his.
She leaned into him while Leon’s life energy spread through her body.
The deep cuts beneath her armor began to close.
Mana flowed through her exhausted channels, easing the damage left by the trial.
When their lips finally separated, Seraphine kept her forehead against his.
"You came back," Leon said.
"So did you."
"Barely."
Seraphine glanced at the dried blood still covering parts of his repaired armor.
"You look worse than I do."
"The blood isn’t mine anymore."
"That sentence does not make me feel better."
"It should.
I’m healed."
A short distance away, Ira crossed her arms.
"That kiss was longer."
Seraphine did not turn.
"You counted?"
"I did not."
"You answered very quickly."
Ira’s face darkened.
"I didn’t need a long kiss because I came out in better condition."
Vyra looked at her niece’s burned clothing.
Seraphine followed her gaze.
"I see."
"Stop doing that."
"Doing what?"
"Agreeing like that."
Despite the banter, the tension did not leave them.
Loriel remained inside.
Leon finished healing Seraphine before returning to the new survivors.
The dungeon continued releasing people in smaller groups.
Each wave contained fewer participants than the one before.
Leon healed those in danger and sent them home.
The families who had already reunited left the area.
Those still waiting remained near the entrance, refusing food, rest, or comfort.
Hours passed.
The dungeon’s light began to weaken.
Leon updated the count.
Nine hundred and twelve survivors had returned.
Seven people were still missing.
Loriel was one of them.
Another pulse released three participants.
Two more emerged several minutes later.
The entrance began contracting.
Leon stared at the remaining light.
Two people were still missing.
A final man fell out of the dungeon and struck the ground.
Leon teleported to him, stabilized his heart, and sent him toward the healers.
One remained.
Loriel.
The dungeon continued closing.
Ira’s earlier energy disappeared.
Seraphine stood with one hand around her sword’s hilt.
Her face remained calm, but her fingers had turned white.
Vyra said nothing.
Leon approached the entrance.
He pressed his spatial authority against the boundary again.
Nothing changed.
He tried the Cosmic System.
No response.
He used holy energy, life energy, and mana to search for any connection to Loriel.
The dungeon rejected everything.
The entrance shrank until only a narrow column of light remained.
Leon’s chest tightened.
Not like this.
He could kill enemies several ranks above himself.
He could create worlds, bend space, and survive wounds that should have ended him.
None of it allowed him to reach one person trapped behind this wall.
The last light began collapsing.
Something flew through it.
Leon moved before he recognized the body.
Green hair streamed through the air, soaked dark with blood.
Loriel fell from the closing dungeon.
Leon caught her.
Her body was cold.
Cuts covered nearly every part of her.
Several bones had shattered, and a deep wound passed through her abdomen.
Her breathing was so faint that even Leon struggled to detect it.
Worse, some kind of destructive life energy continued spreading through her body.
It twisted natural growth into something violent, forcing healthy tissue to consume itself.
Leon placed one hand against her chest.
Life energy flooded into her.
"Leon?" Ira asked.
He did not respond.
The spreading damage resisted ordinary healing.
Leon changed his approach immediately.
Holy energy entered Loriel’s body and separated the hostile influence from her natural vitality.
At the same time, Leon used his Life affinity to keep her organs functioning.
Her heart stopped.
Leon forced it to beat again.
Seraphine dropped beside them.
"What do you need?"
"Nothing.
Give me space."
Vyra knelt on the other side.
"The damage is still spreading below her ribs."
"I see it."
"It is moving toward her heart."
"Not anymore."
Leon trapped the hostile energy and burned it away with holy power.
Loriel’s broken ribs returned to their proper position.
Her lungs repaired.
The terrible wound through her stomach closed layer by layer.
Ira stood nearby, both hands clenched.
"She’s going to survive, right?"
Leon still did not answer.
He repaired Loriel’s mana channels last.
They were different from what he remembered.
Something had changed inside them during the trial.
The new structure was wider, deeper, and filled with a strange vitality even while damaged.
Leon did not have time to study it.
He stabilized everything and checked her again.
Loriel’s heart beat steadily.
Her breathing returned.
Her injuries were gone.
She did not wake.
"Loriel."
Leon touched her face.
No response.
For one terrible moment, he wondered if he had repaired her body too late.
He searched deeper.
Her consciousness was still there.
Whole.
Safe.
She had simply exhausted herself so completely that her mind and body had shut down.
Leon finally breathed.
"She’s alive."
Ira sat down hard on the ground.
Seraphine’s hand loosened around her sword.
Vyra closed her eyes for a moment.
Behind them, the dungeon disappeared.
The final count appeared on the temporary record maintained by the officials.
Nine hundred and nineteen survivors.
Fifty-one dead.
The survival rate was far better than the historical records Leon had studied.
It did not feel like a victory.
Fifty-one people had entered after trusting his warning and their own resolve.
Fifty-one families would receive no one back.
Leon gave the settlement leaders instructions to care for the survivors and prepare the names of the dead.
Compensation, support, and proper memorials would be handled after the immediate crisis.
Then he lifted Loriel.
"She needs rest."
Leon folded space around Vyra, Ira, Seraphine, and himself.
They disappeared from the empty ground outside the dungeon.

chapters.title: Chapter 583: What the Dungeon Gave Them
paragraphs: Loriel rested in one of the bedrooms inside Leon’s house.
Her breathing remained steady.
Leon checked her condition repeatedly over the next several hours. Nothing was wrong with her body anymore. Her exhaustion simply ran too deep for ordinary healing to remove.
Ira and Seraphine refused to leave.
Vyra stayed as well.
The room remained quiet until evening.

By then, every survivor had returned home, and the settlement leaders had received the final list of casualties. Leon had ordered support for the families of the dead, but there was nothing more he could personally do that night.
Loriel still had not awakened.
They moved several chairs near her bed.
No one wanted to discuss rewards at first.
Vyra eventually broke the silence.
"My trial did not test my strength."
Ira looked toward her aunt.
"What did it do?"
"It took my strength away."
Vyra rested her arms across her knees.
"I was placed in command of several groups of Pyrans. None of them possessed their real strength. Neither did I."
"What were you fighting?" Leon asked.
"An army that never stopped."
Vyra explained without exaggeration.
Every battlefield had forced her to choose.

One group would be surrounded while another defended civilians. If she personally saved the first, the second position would collapse. If she remained behind and commanded, people she could have saved with her own hands would die.
"There was no choice that saved everyone," Vyra said.
Ira’s expression became serious.
"What did you do?"
"At first? I tried to do everything."
Vyra had fought at the front, commanded from a distance, rescued the injured, and reinforced every failing line.
It had not worked.
She could not stand everywhere at once.
Each time Vyra tried to carry the entire battlefield alone, more people died because no one else had been allowed to grow into responsibility.
"The final trial placed every surviving group under attack at once," Vyra continued. "I had enough strength to save one."
"Only one?" Seraphine asked.
"That was what it wanted me to believe."
Vyra had finally stopped trying to become the answer to every problem.
She divided authority among the surviving commanders, trusted them with their people, and strengthened them instead of replacing them.
They won together.
A golden panel appeared before her when the trial ended.
[Class Reawakening Complete]
[Class: Pyran Flame Sovereign]
[Class Rank: S]
[Class Rarity: Unique]
Leon stared at the class name.
"Unique?"
"That was the word."
"That is more important than you realize."
Vyra looked at him.
Leon leaned forward.
"A Unique class isn’t simply rare. It was created for you. Your race, your fire, your experience, and the choices you made inside the trial shaped it."
"There can be no other holder?"
"There might never be another person capable of receiving the same class."
Vyra fell silent.
Her new class was not built only for combat. Its authority could guide, strengthen, and unite the Pyrans beneath her.
Leon smiled.
"You did extremely well."
A small amount of pride entered Vyra’s expression.
"I am aware."
Ira immediately raised her hand.
"My turn."
Vyra looked at her.
"You could simply speak."
"That is less dramatic."
Ira stood from her chair and began pacing.
"My trial started in a sea of fire."
"How large was this sea?" Seraphine asked.
"Endless."
Vyra’s eyes narrowed.
"It was very large," Ira corrected. "Practically endless."
She described monsters rising from the flames. Each one had supposedly been larger than the last, until Ira was fighting creatures tall enough to crush mountains.
Seraphine listened with a calm expression.
"You defeated a mountain-sized beast at Level 1?"
"It wasn’t a real mountain."
"So it was smaller."
"Size is not the important part."
Ira continued before anyone could question her again.
The true heart of the trial slowly became clear beneath her heroic version.

She had been forced to protect a small flame while enemies attacked from every direction. Whenever Ira lost control, her own fire joined the inferno around her and endangered the thing she needed to protect.
Burning everything only made the trial harder.
"I could have destroyed all of it," Ira said.
Vyra looked at her.
"Eventually."
Ira had been forced to learn that fire did more than destroy.
It could protect.
It could guide.
It could provide warmth without consuming what it touched.
She had not become gentle. The trial had simply taught her greater control over the same violent power she already loved.
"And after I defeated the final monster with one perfect strike—"
"Three strikes," Vyra said.
Ira ignored her.
"—the dungeon finally admitted that I was incredible."
A panel had appeared.
[Class Reawakening Complete]
[Class: Calamity Flame Lancer]
[Class Rank: S]
[Class Rarity: Rare]
Ira crossed her arms and waited.
Leon grinned.
"That fits you far too well."
"It does."
"An S-rank Rare class is an incredible result, Ira. Especially after entering at Level 1."
Her proud smile softened.
"You mean that?"
"I wouldn’t lie about this. You earned it."
Ira looked pleased for several seconds.
Then she glanced toward Seraphine.
Seraphine remained perfectly calm.
Ira’s smile weakened.
"What?"
"Nothing."
"Why do you look like that?"
"Like what?"
"Like you know something annoying."
Seraphine adjusted her position in the chair.
"My trial was different."
Ira sat down slowly.
Seraphine had been completely alone.
The dungeon removed her equipment, her class skills, and every person she normally fought beside. It then created several versions of her.
One had abandoned Leon when he was still weak.
Another had chosen greater personal strength over loyalty.
A third had become bitter after spending her life protecting people stronger than herself.
"They said my loyalty was dependence," Seraphine explained. "That I could only stand because Leon, you, and the others were beside me."
Ira frowned.
"So you killed them?"
"Eventually."
Seraphine had fought each version while only possessing her own experience, Lightning affinity, Light affinity, and swordsmanship.
The final enemy possessed all the strength Seraphine believed she lacked.
She defeated it by combining her lightning and light into a sword technique created entirely through her own comprehension.
The dungeon rewarded her after the final strike.
[Class Reawakening Complete]
[Class: Stormlight Sword Saint]
[Class Rank: S]
[Class Rarity: Ultra-Rare]
Ira’s mouth opened.
Leon blinked.
Ultra-Rare.
Seraphine had entered the weakest of the three, yet she had achieved a class rarer than Ira’s.
"Stormlight Sword Saint," Leon repeated. "That combines your sword, lightning, and Light affinity."
"Yes."
"That is an exceptional class."
Ira stared at her.
"Ultra-Rare?"
Seraphine nodded.
"But you were weaker than me."
"I was."
"And you still got something rarer?"
"It would appear so."
Ira looked toward Leon as though expecting him to correct reality.
Leon only laughed.
"You all did better than I expected."
He looked at Vyra first.
"A Unique S-rank class."
Then Ira.
"A Rare S-rank class."
Finally, Seraphine.
"An Ultra-Rare S-rank class."
Leon did not hide his pride.
"Every one of you achieved something extraordinary."
Ira’s annoyance faded.
Seraphine smiled.
Vyra inclined her head.
A faint movement came from the bed.
Loriel’s fingers shifted.
Then her eyes fluttered open.

chapters.title: Chapter 584: The Same Rank
paragraphs: Leon reached the bed first.
Loriel’s green eyes opened slowly.
They remained unfocused for several seconds before finding him.
"Leon?"
He pulled her into his arms.
Loriel gave a quiet sound of surprise, but her arms soon rose around him.
Leon held her carefully.
He knew her body was healed. That did not remove the image of her falling from the dungeon covered in blood.
Loriel rested her head against his chest.
"I’m all right," she whispered.
"You almost weren’t."
"I know."
They remained together for several moments.
Seraphine, Ira, and Vyra gathered beside the bed, but none of them teased Leon or Loriel.
Leon finally helped Loriel rest against the pillows again. He remained seated close beside her.
"How do you feel?" Seraphine asked.
"Tired."
"Any pain?" Leon asked.
Loriel moved her arms and legs carefully.
"No. Nothing hurts."
Her gaze returned to Leon.
"You healed me."
"Most of it."
"Most?"
"You did the difficult part by coming out alive."
Loriel gave him a tired smile.
"I heard some of what you were saying."
Ira leaned closer.
"How long were you awake?"
"I wasn’t fully awake. I could hear everyone, but I couldn’t move."
Leon frowned.
"You should have said something."
"I just told you I couldn’t move."
"That is a reasonable excuse."
Loriel’s smile widened slightly.
She looked toward Vyra, Ira, and Seraphine.
"I heard about your classes. Congratulations."
"Thank you," Vyra said.
Ira grinned.
"You should have seen my trial."
"I heard that part too."
Seraphine looked away to hide her smile.
Leon placed a hand over Loriel’s.
"You don’t have to tell us what happened inside your trial."
Loriel became quieter.
"You came out with the worst injuries," Leon continued. "If you don’t want to remember it, don’t."
"I don’t want to explain the painful parts yet."
"You never have to."
"But I can tell you what class I received."
Leon tried to keep his expression calm.
Loriel watched him for several seconds.
"You want to know, right?"
Leon nodded.
Then he nodded again.
Ira laughed.
"You look like a duck."
"I do not."
"You do."
Loriel covered a small laugh with her hand.
Leon ignored them.
He expected Loriel’s class to have improved by at least one rank. Her previous path had focused on healing, but the changes he sensed in her mana channels suggested something much greater.
Perhaps she had received an evolved Saintess class.
Maybe her rarity had increased.
Loriel opened her status.
A golden notification appeared.
[Class Reawakening Complete]
[Class: Child of Life]
[Class Rank: SSS]
[Class Rarity: Ultra-Rare]
Loriel studied the message.
"I received an Ultra-Rare SSS-rank class," she said. "Child of Life. I don’t really know how good that is."
No one answered.
Ira’s mouth hung open.
Seraphine stared at the golden words.
Leon read them again to make sure he had not misunderstood.
SSS rank.
Loriel had awakened a class at the same rank as Elemental Paragon.
That did not mean their classes possessed identical power or potential. Rank was only one part of a class.
It was still an unbelievable result.
"Did I do badly?" Loriel asked.
Leon looked at her.
"Badly?"
"No one is saying anything."
"You did so well that none of us know what to say."
Her eyes widened.
"Really?"
"Loriel, SSS is the highest class rank I know."
Ira finally found her voice.
"The same as Leon?"
Leon nodded.
"My class is also SSS rank."
Vyra’s head turned sharply.
"You never mentioned that."
"It didn’t come up."
"It has come up many times."
"Not in a way that required the exact rank."
Vyra looked from Leon to Loriel.
She already viewed Leon as an existence far outside normal standards. Learning that Loriel possessed a class of the same rank forced her to reconsider the gentle healer entirely.
Loriel noticed Vyra staring.
"Is something wrong?"
"No."
Vyra’s answer came immediately.
"I was thinking that I should not become lazy."
Ira stared at her aunt.
"You? Lazy?"
"The point remains."
Leon looked back at Loriel.
"What else changed?"
"My status looks strange."
"Show me."
Loriel focused on the interface.
A golden screen appeared before her.
She looked through the new sections with growing confusion.
"The whole thing used to be blue."
Leon’s suspicions strengthened.
"Do you see something called Cosmic Chat?"
Loriel searched.
"Yes."
"Cosmic Shop?"
"Yes."
"Does the Shop mention causality?"
"It does." Loriel looked at him. "What does that mean?"
Leon leaned back.
She had gained access to the Cosmic System.
This was only one additional example, so he could not claim that every SSS-rank class holder automatically received it.
However, the connection was too strong to ignore.
Loriel had awakened an SSS-rank class and immediately gained the same golden interface Leon possessed.
"It means your System has changed," he said. "The blue System you used before was much more limited. The golden one is connected to the Cosmic System."
Loriel listened closely.
Leon explained the basics.

The Cosmic Chat connected users across a far wider scale than ordinary world systems. The Cosmic Shop offered items and knowledge unavailable through lesser interfaces. Causality acted as its currency, earned and spent through actions that affected the world and its future.
He avoided overwhelming her with every detail.
"You should not spend anything until I help you understand the prices," Leon added.
Loriel nodded quickly.
"I won’t touch it."
"Good. Some of the Shop’s prices can be misleading if you don’t understand what you’re buying."
Ira crossed her arms.
"So she really has the same kind of System as you?"
"It appears that way."
"Because her class is SSS?"
"Possibly. One example besides myself is not enough to prove it."
Loriel looked at the golden interface again.
She should have seemed excited.
Instead, her expression turned uncertain.
"I hated the trial."
Leon squeezed her hand.
"You don’t need to be grateful for what it did to you."
"It hurt."
"I know."
"I really don’t like pain."
"You have made that very clear."
Loriel gave him a weak glare.
"But this is still good, right?"
"It is more than good."
Leon looked at the class name again.
Child of Life.
Loriel’s former power had treated life as healing.
The new class clearly reached beyond that.
The trial had forced her to experience growth, sacrifice, survival, decay, and the border between life and death. Leon suspected her class would eventually allow her to do far more than close wounds.
He did not ask her to inspect the skills yet.
She needed rest.
Loriel’s eyes were already becoming heavy.
Leon helped her lie down.
"I’ll be nearby."
"You don’t have to keep watching me."
"I know."
"You’re going to do it anyway?"
"Yes."
Loriel smiled and closed her eyes.
Her breathing settled into a natural rhythm.
This time, she was only sleeping.
Vyra remained for a while longer before standing.
"I should examine my own class."
"And rest," Leon said.
"I rested while all of you talked."
"That does not count."
"It does to me."
Vyra paused beside Loriel’s bed.
Her gaze remained on the sleeping healer for a moment before she left the room.
Several more hours passed.
Leon checked Loriel twice more. Her condition remained stable.
The settlement leaders had handled the surviving participants, and preparations had begun for the fifty-one families who had lost someone. Nothing else required Leon’s immediate attention that night.
Seraphine touched his arm.
"Come with us."
"Where?"
"The next room."
Ira was already smiling.
That should have warned him.
Leon followed them into an adjoining bedroom.
Seraphine entered last and closed the door.
The lock clicked.
Leon turned toward her.
Ira planted both hands against his chest and pushed.
Leon allowed himself to fall backward onto the bed.
She climbed onto the mattress after him with a mischievous smile. Seraphine approached from the other side, calmer but no less intent.
The sight of the two women working together was more alarming than anything Leon had faced inside the Tower.
"We survived," Ira said.
"We returned with S-rank classes," Seraphine added.
Ira leaned closer.

chapters.title: Chapter 587: Fifty-One Names
paragraphs: A week had passed inside the dimensional world, which meant Velaria, the outside world, had not yet finished a single day.
Leon spent most of it watching his people become something new.

He saw Vyra on the training grounds at dawn with four dozen Pyrans arranged around her. She did not shout orders. She simply stood among them, testing the reach of her new class, and the flames of every Pyran in the circle burned steadier for it.
She changed their formation and tried again.
The result followed her.

Pyran Flame Sovereign was not merely a stronger flame class. It carried authority, and authority carried responsibility. Vyra seemed to understand that faster than anyone could have explained it. Leon heard her tell one of the younger Pyrans that if her presence changed how well they fought, then learning to use that influence properly was now part of her duty.
Ira went in the opposite direction.

She still answered most problems with overwhelming force, but the training field she used no longer looked as if someone had shelled it. When she thrust her spear, calamity flame crossed the ground in a narrow line and stopped exactly where she intended. The grass on either side remained untouched.
She complained that precision was boring.
Leon noticed she practised it for six hours anyway.

Seraphine had stopped separating her strengths. Before, she had fought with her sword and called upon lightning or light when the blade alone was not enough. Now all three moved together. Radiance ran along the steel. Lightning followed the path of each cut. Her sword carried the storm, and the storm carried the light.

She repeated the same basic forms for hours, building a foundation instead of chasing spectacle. Stormlight Sword Saint was not a title she had said aloud more than once, but she was already trying to become worthy of it.
Loriel worried Leon more than the others reassured him.

Physically, she had recovered. He had made certain of that. Child of Life had opened something inside her perception that she could only describe in fragments, as though the right words had not been invented yet. She could sense the health of a tree from thirty paces away. She could look at two equally tired people and tell which one carried exhaustion that would matter years later.
That was not healing. Not in any ordinary sense.

But she still flinched at sudden sounds. Sometimes, in the afternoon, she went still and stared at nothing until someone gently called her name. Her golden Cosmic System remained present and unexplained, and neither Leon nor Xyra had made any progress in understanding why Loriel possessed it.
Leon did not push her.
On the fifth day, he found her sitting beside a young tree outside the settlement, one palm resting against its trunk.
"What are you doing?" he asked.
"Listening."
"Is it saying anything useful?"
Loriel considered the question with complete seriousness. "It wants more water."
Leon looked at the damp soil around its roots.
Her mouth twitched.
"That was a joke," she admitted.
It was not much, but it was the first one she had made since leaving the dungeon. Leon sat beside her without commenting on it, and for a while they listened to the tree together.

The other survivors adjusted in the ordinary, unequal way of real people. A handful had returned with classes that would transform their families’ futures. Most received something useful rather than miraculous. Some survived without earning anything close to what they had hoped for.
Survival had not guaranteed greatness.
For fifty-one people, it had not been granted at all.
The memorial was held on the seventh day, on flat ground where the newest road ended and the grass began.

All nine hundred and nineteen survivors attended. So did the families of the dead and thousands of the dimensional world’s other inhabitants. Humans and Pyrans filled the field together without anyone needing to arrange them that way.
At the front stood a single slab of polished black stone.

All fifty-one names had been carved into it. Leon had checked every spelling with the families himself. The letters were deep, clean, and protected from ordinary weathering. Long after the new road reached beyond this field and the nearby town became a city, the names would remain.
Leon stood among the mourners rather than above them. When it was time to speak, he used no platform.
"Fifty-one people entered that dungeon and did not come out."
His voice carried across the field, level and clear.
"They were not sacrifices. Nothing was bought with their lives. I will not tell you their deaths were necessary or glorious. They were losses. That is what they were."
Someone in the crowd began to cry. Leon did not search for the source.

"They entered because they wanted to pass limits this world had placed upon them before they were born. They knew there was danger, and they chose to go anyway. That took courage. But courage does not make the cost smaller. Both things are true. They were brave, and they are gone."
He paused, looking at the families gathered before the stone.

"You will be supported for as long as you need it. Housing, land, income, education—whatever can be provided will be provided. I want to say clearly that none of it balances this. A life cannot be repaid, and pretending otherwise would insult the people we are here to remember."
His gaze passed over the survivors, many of whom had returned carrying powers their dead companions would never see.

"The opportunity was mine to offer. The choice to enter belonged to each person who made it. I will not steal that choice from them by claiming it as mine, and I will not pretend I had no part in opening the door. I know what it cost to walk through it. I will carry that."
That was all he had.
Leon stepped back, and the families spoke one after another.

They did not speak about ranks or classes. They spoke about a woman who always burned breakfast because she talked too much while cooking. A man who had promised to build his daughter a larger room. A younger brother who cheated at cards and confessed before anyone caught him. Small things. The kind that proved a person had existed more completely than any list of achievements could.
One young survivor wept openly while his dead friend’s mother spoke. An A-rank class now sat inside him, a reward he had once wanted more than anything, and he looked as though he hated it.
Leon understood the poison in that feeling. He also knew one ceremony would not remove it.

When the final family finished, people did not scatter. The survivors moved toward the families rather than away from them. Some apologized. Some shared memories. Others simply stood nearby because they had no words that would help and understood that leaving would help even less.
By afternoon, the grief had not become comfort.
It had become something quieter: a decision that the dead would remain part of what came next.
Leon stayed until the last family left the stone.
Only then did he look past the memorial toward the growing town, where cranes moved above unfinished roofs and workers laid another stretch of road.
His people needed more than opportunities he personally delivered. They needed roads they could continue walking when he was elsewhere.
He had one left to give them before he went searching for his own.
