chapters.title: Chapter 588: The Road Left Unsearched
paragraphs: Two days after the memorial, Leon planted the Legendary Instance Seed.

He chose prepared land near the principal settlement, far enough from the expanding residential districts that future growth would not crowd it, but close enough for healers, guards, and training officials to reach it quickly.
Half the nearby town seemed to follow him there.

The walk showed him how much had changed. This place had once been a collection of shelters built by people grateful to have walls. Now it was a large town approaching the point where nobody would be able to call it one for much longer.

Construction covered entire districts. Scaffolding climbed across rows of new houses. Smoke rose from completed forges in a workshop quarter that remained only half roofed. Foundations marked the future school, granary, public bathhouse, and administrative hall. The main roads had been paved; crews were extending the secondary streets while another team prepared the outer wall for defensive formations.

The tools, materials, and formations Leon had purchased from the Cosmic Shop had changed what was possible. Tasks that should have required years could be completed in days. Taken together, the improvements pushed development forward at something close to a thousand times the pace their old methods could have achieved.
It still did not make the town finished.

Temporary housing stood two streets from permanent homes still under construction. Ditches waited for drainage lines. Several districts were more stakes and marked earth than buildings. The city this place was becoming could already be seen, but it had not arrived yet.
Leon stopped in the center of the prepared ground and withdrew the reward he had received from Floor Two.
[Legendary Instance Seed]
It rested in his palm, small enough to appear unimpressive until he let it touch the soil.
The earth answered.

Lines of light spread beneath the ground in branching patterns. The Seed sank from sight, and the cleared field trembled as space folded inward around a forming center. Stone rose in a wide ring. Within it, a dark entrance appeared—not an open hole, but a stable boundary leading into something larger than the land around it could physically contain.
System information formed above the entrance, identifying the instance and its basic conditions. Leon read every line before he allowed anyone closer.

The Seed had become what Floor Two promised: a permanent place where the inhabitants could challenge themselves and earn advancement through effort. It would not hand out endless rewards, and it would not remove the need for preparation, discipline, or skill.
Leon did not pretend danger alone made training valuable.

Before anyone entered, he called over the settlement leaders and established rules. The first teams would be experienced fighters chosen to test the instance carefully. Every entrant would register before entering. Healers would remain nearby. No one under the approved strength would be allowed through, and nobody would enter alone until they understood what waited inside. The rules could change once they learned more, but ignorance would not be treated as courage.
One group of younger survivors had already begun arguing over who should lead the first run.
Leon pointed toward the registration table being carried across the field.
"You can start by helping build that."
Their enthusiasm faded with impressive speed.
"Still want to be first?" he asked.
"Less than before," one admitted.
"Good. That means you have begun thinking."

The crowd spread around the new structure, reading its information and discussing teams. Healers inspected the ground selected for their station. A training officer began drafting an entry schedule before Leon asked. Workers argued about whether the road should curve around the instance or lead directly to it.
Leon watched all of it and felt a quiet satisfaction settle in his chest.
They did not need him to manage every detail. That was the point.

The dimensional world had once been land he owned. Then it had become a shelter dependent upon him for resources, protection, and direction. It was no longer either of those things. Thousands of humans and Pyrans lived here now. They had leaders, workers, healers, soldiers, families, an economy, a town becoming a city, and now a permanent path of advancement they could organize for themselves.
His attention could finally turn elsewhere without leaving emptiness behind it.
Leon had wanted to reach a higher-ranked world for a long time.

The desire was not new, and he did not question it now. The abyssal war, the world-rank merger, the Class Reawakening Dungeon, and the Ascension Tower had all been more urgent. So had the lives being built inside this world.
For once, the nearest crisis was not demanding that he delay.
He found Xyra in her mansion near the tower and gave her the question exactly as it existed.
"If someone descended into Velaria from another world, could I follow the connection backward?"
Xyra remained silent long enough to prove she was considering it rather than preparing something impressive to say.

"A passage between worlds leaves traces," she said at last. "Even after the structure collapses, part of its destination may remain imprinted in the space it occupied. A scar remembers the shape of what made it."
"That sounds possible."

"That is the easiest part." Her silver eyes sharpened. "You would need to identify a foreign coordinate from within Velaria’s laws, reverse a route designed for descent, and stabilize a passage between worlds governed by different structures. Carrying this dimensional world through with you would magnify every weakness in the route."
"Can you do it?"
"No, I can’t go outside"
The direct answer did not trouble him.
"I can examine what you find," Xyra continued. "I can tell you why it fails and help maintain this world while you test it. I cannot give you a destination I do not possess."
Leon nodded. "Then I’ll find one."
He left the dimensional world that evening with Seraphine, Ira, Loriel, and Vyra.
Luna met them in Velaria. She had remained outside the dimensional world, and Leon had contacted her before leaving so she could begin arranging access to the oldest Church records.
Their trail began with the Upper Ones.

Now he returned to the question he had left unfinished.

Luna’s name opened doors, but not instantly. The oldest Church of Light and Church of Life records were divided among institutions that distrusted one another and guarded their vaults as fiercely as they guarded relics. She spent hours negotiating while Leon resisted Ira’s repeated suggestion that locked doors were only philosophical obstacles.
By nightfall, three collections had been brought into a single secure archive.

The records contradicted one another on almost everything: how many Upper Ones came, what they looked like, what they said, and whether they were people or gods. Centuries of politics, translation, worship, and deliberate revision lay between Leon and whatever had truly happened.
He did not read them as a historian.
He read them as someone who understood space.
The earliest accounts all agreed on one detail. The Upper Ones appeared at the same place, yet no record described them travelling there. No road. No vessel. No procession from beyond the city.
They were simply present.

Several ancient maps also distorted the same portion of the original settlement. Different hands had drawn them across different eras, yet each left the same absence. The oldest measurements of the artificial domains used the City of Light as their origin point rather than any geographic center.
Then Leon found the line that made the rest fit.
The earliest surviving version described the sky folding downward.
Later copies replaced it with heaven’s glory descending.
He laid the two passages beside each other.
"This was not a miracle," he said.
Seraphine studied the altered wording. "Someone wanted it remembered as one."
"Or wanted the mechanism forgotten."
The maps told him where to begin.
Leon rose from the archive table and extended his spatial perception beneath the oldest foundations of the City of Light.
Far below them, something in the structure of space answered.

sentences.text: Two days after the memorial, Leon planted the Legendary Instance Seed.

He chose prepared land near the principal settlement, far enough from the expanding residential districts that future growth would not crowd it, but close enough for healers, guards, and training officials to reach it quickly.
Half the nearby town seemed to follow him there.
The walk showed him how much had changed.
This place had once been a collection of shelters built by people grateful to have walls.
Now it was a large town approaching the point where nobody would be able to call it one for much longer.
Construction covered entire districts.
Scaffolding climbed across rows of new houses.
Smoke rose from completed forges in a workshop quarter that remained only half roofed.
Foundations marked the future school, granary, public bathhouse, and administrative hall.
The main roads had been paved; crews were extending the secondary streets while another team prepared the outer wall for defensive formations.
The tools, materials, and formations Leon had purchased from the Cosmic Shop had changed what was possible.
Tasks that should have required years could be completed in days.
Taken together, the improvements pushed development forward at something close to a thousand times the pace their old methods could have achieved.
It still did not make the town finished.
Temporary housing stood two streets from permanent homes still under construction.
Ditches waited for drainage lines.
Several districts were more stakes and marked earth than buildings.
The city this place was becoming could already be seen, but it had not arrived yet.

[Legendary Instance Seed]
It rested in his palm, small enough to appear unimpressive until he let it touch the soil.
The earth answered.
Lines of light spread beneath the ground in branching patterns.
The Seed sank from sight, and the cleared field trembled as space folded inward around a forming center.
Stone rose in a wide ring.

System information formed above the entrance, identifying the instance and its basic conditions.

It would not hand out endless rewards, and it would not remove the need for preparation, discipline, or skill.
Leon did not pretend danger alone made training valuable.
Before anyone entered, he called over the settlement leaders and established rules.
The first teams would be experienced fighters chosen to test the instance carefully.
Every entrant would register before entering.
Healers would remain nearby.
No one under the approved strength would be allowed through, and nobody would enter alone until they understood what waited inside.
The rules could change once they learned more, but ignorance would not be treated as courage.
One group of younger survivors had already begun arguing over who should lead the first run.
Leon pointed toward the registration table being carried across the field.
"You can start by helping build that."
Their enthusiasm faded with impressive speed.
"Still want to be first?" he asked.
"Less than before," one admitted.
"Good.
That means you have begun thinking."
The crowd spread around the new structure, reading its information and discussing teams.
Healers inspected the ground selected for their station.
A training officer began drafting an entry schedule before Leon asked.
Workers argued about whether the road should curve around the instance or lead directly to it.
Leon watched all of it and felt a quiet satisfaction settle in his chest.
They did not need him to manage every detail.
That was the point.
The dimensional world had once been land he owned.
Then it had become a shelter dependent upon him for resources, protection, and direction.
It was no longer either of those things.
Thousands of humans and Pyrans lived here now.
They had leaders, workers, healers, soldiers, families, an economy, a town becoming a city, and now a permanent path of advancement they could organize for themselves.
His attention could finally turn elsewhere without leaving emptiness behind it.
Leon had wanted to reach a higher-ranked world for a long time.
The desire was not new, and he did not question it now.
The abyssal war, the world-rank merger, the Class Reawakening Dungeon, and the Ascension Tower had all been more urgent.
So had the lives being built inside this world.
For once, the nearest crisis was not demanding that he delay.
He found Xyra in her mansion near the tower and gave her the question exactly as it existed.

Xyra remained silent long enough to prove she was considering it rather than preparing something impressive to say.
"A passage between worlds leaves traces," she said at last.

A scar remembers the shape of what made it."
"That sounds possible."
"That is the easiest part." Her silver eyes sharpened.

Carrying this dimensional world through with you would magnify every weakness in the route."
"Can you do it?"
"No, I can’t go outside"

"I can tell you why it fails and help maintain this world while you test it.

"Then I’ll find one."

chapters.title: Chapter 589: A World at the Other End
paragraphs: Beneath the City of Light, space had never healed correctly.

The distortion was faint enough that Leon might have missed it years ago. Now he could follow the places where distance bent by fractions, where two points sat closer together than the stone between them allowed.
The trail ran beneath layers of streets, churches, vaults, and ruins built over one another by generations who had never known what lay below.

Luna cleared the oldest storeroom above the disturbance. Leon opened a controlled path through the rock beneath it, moving stone aside rather than destroying it. Seraphine and Ira guarded the passage. Vyra watched for changes in the surrounding mana, while Loriel kept one hand against the wall and listened to the life above them recede as they descended.
The Mark of the Uncounted stirred before they reached the bottom.

Thin claim threads appeared within Leon’s perception. They were ancient and dead, buried through the distortion and stretching outward toward the wider domain structure. The Mark supplied no explanation and offered no way forward. It merely let him see that the spatial damage beneath the city and the artificial domains were parts of the same construction.
That clue was enough.
They found the chamber less than four hours after leaving the archive.

It had been sealed behind a collapse that was too deliberate to be natural. The architecture beyond it predated both Churches. Most of the chamber had been destroyed. Walls were broken, inscriptions had been removed, and carved surfaces had been chiseled smooth by someone patient enough to erase them by hand.
Ira ran her fingers over one ruined panel.
"This is a lot of effort for people with nothing to hide."
"Maybe they disliked decorating," Leon said.
She glanced at him. "That was almost a joke."
"Do not spread it around."
At the center of the chamber stood no gate, altar, or surviving machine.
There was only a scar.

It hung in the air, invisible to ordinary sight but glaring within Leon’s spatial perception: a wound roughly three meters across where something immense had forced the world to connect to a place beyond itself. The passage was gone. The anchors were ruined. Nothing physical could cross it now.
But space remembered.
Leon approached alone at first. He let his perception settle over the scar one layer at a time, careful not to disturb the little that remained.
The structure told its story through absence.

The passage had originated somewhere outside Velaria. The traces embedded in it carried the pressure of foreign laws, too complete to belong to another domain or hidden region within the same world. Its design had been directional. Everything about it had been constructed to allow descent into Velaria, never ascent away from it.
And it had been anchored into the framework of the domains.
Leon went still when he understood that part.

The Lower, Middle, and Higher Domains were not natural divisions. Their ceilings, their restrictions, and the limits they placed upon every person born inside them belonged to a world-scale structure connected to this very chamber.
Someone had built those limits.
Seraphine read the answer on his face. "The domains?"
"Artificial," Leon said. "All of them. This place was one of the framework’s central points."
"Built by the Upper Ones?" Loriel asked.
"Connected to their road. That is all I can prove."

He found the abyssal damage within the same framework—a broken region that the existing crack had exploited. The structure confirmed the connection, but not the history behind it. Leon could not tell whether the Upper Ones had built the domains to protect Velaria, imprison something, control its inhabitants, harvest the world, or serve a purpose none of them had considered.
Vyra studied the stripped walls. "Whoever erased this chamber wanted the method gone, but left the restrictions standing."
"Which means either the restrictions mattered more," Seraphine said, "or whoever erased it could not remove them."
Both possibilities were unpleasant.
Leon continued deeper.

Most of the original coordinate had been destroyed along with the passage. A few fragments remained, embedded so far within the scar that ordinary spatial damage would have erased them. He held each one separately, compared their orientation, and began rebuilding the missing relationships through inference.
Hours passed.

Seraphine remained beside him without speaking. Ira stopped complaining. Loriel and Luna compared old descriptions from the archive against features in the chamber, occasionally finding a word whose religious meaning concealed a technical one. Xyra observed through Leon’s connection to the dimensional world, commenting only when he asked a direct question.
That was a function that he had learned he could use, while she couldn’t interfere in the outside world; she could see the outside through him and provide help with her knowledge.
Near dawn, Leon found what the Upper Ones had failed to remove completely.
A fragment of the original destination coordinate remained intact.
It did not point north, upward, or anywhere a map could hold. It pointed beyond the boundary of the world.
Leon followed it.

The work demanded patience rather than force. He extended his perception along the surviving fragment one thread at a time, reconstructing just enough of each missing section to continue. Again and again the trail vanished into the dark between worlds. Each time, he returned to the last stable point and approached from a different angle.
For eleven hours, there was nothing.
Then something answered.
The response was faint, no more than a pressure moving back along the thread, but Leon knew immediately what he had found.

It was not another domain. It was not a sealed pocket, a distant continent, or a hidden region of Velaria. The laws at the other end were heavier, deeper, and more complete than any his old world possessed. Even the minute trace of energy leaking across the damaged coordinate was purer than the energy his world could naturally produce.
A genuine world existed at the far end.
A higher-ranked world.
He could learn nothing else through the fragment. No name. No civilization. No indication of what had become of the Upper Ones or whether the route still ended anywhere near them.
That could wait.
Leon held the distant coordinate in his perception and allowed himself one quiet breath of satisfaction.

He had found it himself. No system window had handed him a destination. No treasure had pointed the way. He had taken contradictory history, an erased chamber, and the faintest wound in space, then followed them beyond the edge of his world.
Seraphine saw the change in him first.
"You found something."
"A connection to a different world"
Ira’s exhaustion disappeared. "A stronger one?"
"Much stronger, if its ambient laws and energy are any indication."
Loriel looked toward the invisible scar as though she might see through it by wanting hard enough. Luna did not move at all.
"Can you open it?" she asked.
Leon examined the remains of the one-way road.
"I can try."
His first attempt lasted less than three seconds.
The moment he reversed the surviving flow, the ancient structure began tearing itself apart.
Leon released it before the destination fragment broke with the rest.
The chamber returned to silence.
He still had the destination.
What he did not have was a road capable of reaching it.

chapters.title: Chapter 590: The Missing Road
paragraphs: Leon spent the next day proving that power was not the problem.

He began by reconstructing the missing coordinate structure around the fragment he had recovered. Much of it could be inferred from the surviving sections, but an interworld coordinate did not tolerate approximation. One uncertain segment turned the entire route away from its destination.
His first reconstruction pointed into the dark between worlds and ended there.
He dismantled it and began again.

The second approach reversed the surviving descent path instead of replacing it. The passage had been built to carry travellers in one direction. Its anchors were not merely pointed toward Velaria; every layer of their structure depended upon that direction. When Leon inverted the flow, the old foundations pulled against themselves.
He stopped before the strain destroyed the scar.

For the third attempt, he treated the remnant only as a guide and built a new channel around it. That road reached beyond Velaria’s laws. Then it drifted. Constructed entirely from one side, it possessed nothing at the distant end to hold it in place.
"A bridge without a second shore," Seraphine said.
Leon watched the channel slide away from the coordinate and collapse. "A bridge thrown toward where I know the shore should be."
"That sounds worse."
"It is."

His fourth attempt anchored the foreign coordinate from Velaria’s side. It held for four seconds before slipping free. He could perceive the other world, but perception was not contact. He was trying to fix something in place without being able to touch it.

The fifth attempt sent controlled amounts of energy through the surviving connection. A thin current passed. A stronger one followed. When he increased it to the level needed to support an actual passage, the incomplete coordinate structure buckled under the load.
Leon caught the collapse and rebuilt the damaged sections.

None of the failures injured him. His mana recovered during the intervals between tests, replenishing at its established pace until expenditure never became a lasting limitation. His channels remained stable. His perception did not falter.
That made the answer harder to avoid.

He was strong enough to understand the problem. He possessed the spatial control to test possible solutions without destroying himself or the ancient scar. But strength could not replace a structure that no longer existed.
And every weakness became worse when he included the dimensional world.

He intended to carry a bound rank-three world across the passage. The settlements, the Ascension Tower, Xyra, the Pyrans, the sleeping dragon, and everything else connected to it would add pressure far beyond that of five people crossing. His best channel would have torn apart the moment he tried to push that weight through it.
Xyra examined the results through their connection. She identified the failure in each attempt, but she did not produce a sixth solution from knowledge she did not possess.

"You have enough raw energy," she said in his mind "You have recovered a valid destination, and your understanding is sufficient to guide a crossing of once-built bridge. What you lack is a structure capable of rebuilding and anchoring the road itself."
Leon sat in the center of the ruined chamber, the foreign coordinate held carefully at the edge of his perception.
A structure that could rebuild a road.
Not greater spatial power. Not another attempt to force incomplete anchors to perform a task for which they had never been designed.
A tool.
Then he remembered the sealed cache in his storage.

He had carried it out of the Ascension Tower after Floor Three and left it unopened. At the time, there had been wounded people waiting outside the Tower and a Class Reawakening Dungeon still active. Later came the reunion, the dead, and the responsibilities inside his world. Another treasure had never been the most urgent thing in front of him.
Now it might be.
Leon withdrew the cache.
[Ascension Tower — Sealed Reward Cache (Floor Three)]
It was the reward he had received after earning an SSS evaluation on the floor. SSS described the evaluation, not the rank of whatever waited inside.
He broke the seal.

The cache unfolded into light. When the radiance faded, a dark metallic object rested in his palm, shaped like the central stone of an arch and covered in lines that shifted whenever he tried to focus upon them.
[Worldway Keystone — Mythical]
Leon read its function once.
Then again.

The Keystone could not discover another world. It could not invent a destination coordinate or create a road where no connection had ever existed. It required a genuine surviving link and a valid coordinate.
He had already found both.

Once supplied with them, the Keystone could reconstruct missing sections of an interworld route, reverse a one-way passage, stabilize it during a crossing, and record its endpoints so the same road could later be reopened at an enormous energy cost.
Without the scar and the coordinate Leon had recovered, it would have been useless for reaching this particular world.
With them, it was the missing structure.
Ira stared at the Keystone. "You were carrying that the entire time?"
"I did not know what was inside."
"Still. I feel like this should teach us something about opening rewards sooner."
"It teaches us that the reward would have done nothing before I found a destination."
"That lesson is less entertaining."
Leon placed the Keystone against the spatial scar.
It recognized the surviving connection immediately. The lines across its surface ignited, reached into the wound, and then stopped.
It did not build the route for him.
It waited for direction.

Leon guided it through the old structure section by section. He supplied his understanding of the original descent path. The Keystone restored missing foundations beneath each reversed segment, turning a route that had only run downward into one capable of holding in both directions.

Xyra monitored the dimensional world and warned him whenever the growing connection placed pressure upon its boundary. Seraphine, Ira, Vyra, Loriel, and Luna remained in the chamber, watching the dead scar become a road again.
The work took most of the night.
Near the end, the Mark of the Uncounted flared.
A foreign claim reached toward the forming passage from the direction of the abyssal crack. It was thin and searching, feeling along the damaged framework for a place to attach itself.
Leon saw it because of the Mark. Cutting it was his own act.
He severed the claim before it touched the new route, then closed the opening it had used through the surrounding framework. Only when no trace remained did he continue.
Beyond the distant abyssal crack, the enormous red eye opened.
It did not attack. It simply watched, its attention fixed upon Leon with patient recognition.
No evidence told him when the being had first attached itself to the damaged framework or what it wanted from the Upper Ones’ road. He refused to turn ignorance into a conclusion.
The eye remained open.
Leon returned his focus to the Keystone.
An hour later, the passage stabilized.

Energy from the higher-ranked world flowed into Velaria in a thin, steady current. The air around the restored road seemed to gain weight. Seraphine’s posture tightened. Loriel reached out before catching herself. Ira released a quiet, appreciative curse.
Leon felt the distant world holding at the other end.
Real and reachable right in front of him.

The route remained open only long enough for him to complete the test. Then, under his direction, the Keystone folded it closed. The chamber returned to stillness, leaving the restored structure dormant around the original scar.
[Worldway route established.]
[Endpoints recorded.]
[Passage dormant.]
The abyssal eye had no open road to follow.
Leon looked at the silent Keystone and knew the search was over.
It was time to leave Velaria.

Xyra examined the results through their connection.
She identified the failure in each attempt, but she did not produce a sixth solution from knowledge she did not possess.
"You have enough raw energy," she said in his mind "You have recovered a valid destination, and your understanding is sufficient to guide a crossing of once-built bridge.
What you lack is a structure capable of rebuilding and anchoring the road itself."
Leon sat in the center of the ruined chamber, the foreign coordinate held carefully at the edge of his perception.
A structure that could rebuild a road.
Not greater spatial power.
Not another attempt to force incomplete anchors to perform a task for which they had never been designed.
A tool.
Then he remembered the sealed cache in his storage.
He had carried it out of the Ascension Tower after Floor Three and left it unopened.
At the time, there had been wounded people waiting outside the Tower and a Class Reawakening Dungeon still active.
Later came the reunion, the dead, and the responsibilities inside his world.
Another treasure had never been the most urgent thing in front of him.
Now it might be.
Leon withdrew the cache.
[Ascension Tower — Sealed Reward Cache (Floor Three)]
It was the reward he had received after earning an SSS evaluation on the floor.
SSS described the evaluation, not the rank of whatever waited inside.
He broke the seal.
The cache unfolded into light.
When the radiance faded, a dark metallic object rested in his palm, shaped like the central stone of an arch and covered in lines that shifted whenever he tried to focus upon them.
[Worldway Keystone — Mythical]
Leon read its function once.
Then again.
The Keystone could not discover another world.
It could not invent a destination coordinate or create a road where no connection had ever existed.
It required a genuine surviving link and a valid coordinate.
He had already found both.

Once supplied with them, the Keystone could reconstruct missing sections of an interworld route, reverse a one-way passage, stabilize it during a crossing, and record its endpoints so the same road could later be reopened at an enormous energy cost.
Without the scar and the coordinate Leon had recovered, it would have been useless for reaching this particular world.
With them, it was the missing structure.
Ira stared at the Keystone.
"You were carrying that the entire time?"
"I did not know what was inside."
"Still.
I feel like this should teach us something about opening rewards sooner."
"It teaches us that the reward would have done nothing before I found a destination."
"That lesson is less entertaining."
Leon placed the Keystone against the spatial scar.
It recognized the surviving connection immediately.
The lines across its surface ignited, reached into the wound, and then stopped.
It did not build the route for him.
It waited for direction.
Leon guided it through the old structure section by section.
He supplied his understanding of the original descent path.
The Keystone restored missing foundations beneath each reversed segment, turning a route that had only run downward into one capable of holding in both directions.
Xyra monitored the dimensional world and warned him whenever the growing connection placed pressure upon its boundary.
Seraphine, Ira, Vyra, Loriel, and Luna remained in the chamber, watching the dead scar become a road again.
The work took most of the night.
Near the end, the Mark of the Uncounted flared.
A foreign claim reached toward the forming passage from the direction of the abyssal crack.
It was thin and searching, feeling along the damaged framework for a place to attach itself.
Leon saw it because of the Mark.
Cutting it was his own act.
He severed the claim before it touched the new route, then closed the opening it had used through the surrounding framework.
Only when no trace remained did he continue.
Beyond the distant abyssal crack, the enormous red eye opened.
It did not attack.
It simply watched, its attention fixed upon Leon with patient recognition.
No evidence told him when the being had first attached itself to the damaged framework or what it wanted from the Upper Ones’ road.
He refused to turn ignorance into a conclusion.
The eye remained open.
Leon returned his focus to the Keystone.
An hour later, the passage stabilized.
Energy from the higher-ranked world flowed into Velaria in a thin, steady current.
The air around the restored road seemed to gain weight.
Seraphine’s posture tightened.
Loriel reached out before catching herself.
Ira released a quiet, appreciative curse.
Leon felt the distant world holding at the other end.
Real and reachable right in front of him.
The route remained open only long enough for him to complete the test.
Then, under his direction, the Keystone folded it closed.
The chamber returned to stillness, leaving the restored structure dormant around the original scar.
[Worldway route established.]
[Endpoints recorded.]
[Passage dormant.]
The abyssal eye had no open road to follow.
Leon looked at the silent Keystone and knew the search was over.
It was time to leave Velaria.

chapters.title: Chapter 591: Beyond the Ceiling
paragraphs: Less than three Velarian days had passed since Leon left his dimensional world.
Inside it, nearly a month had gone by.
The difference was visible the moment he returned.

Two streets that had been marked earth when he left were now paved. The school had walls; besides the basic knowledge, its main focus was to teach them to be stronger or learn skills they would like from the people who specialize in the world. Most were interested in fighting and those cool magic skills, as he had expected.

One section of the outer defenses had been completed, and the temporary healer’s station beside the Legendary Instance had become a permanent building. The first controlled teams had already entered under the rules Leon established, and the settlement leaders selected by Vyra had adjusted the schedule based on what those teams learned.
The instance had not solved their future for them.
It had given them something around which to build one.
Leon called the inhabitants together and told them what was happening.

He did not soften it. The road led to a higher-ranked world. He had tested the immediate destination and stabilized the route, but crossing a world boundary still carried risks he could not name in advance.
He also made one point clear.
"I am not leaving you behind."

The rank-three dimensional world was bound to him. Its settlements, inhabitants, resources, Ascension Tower, sleeping dragon, and every unfinished mystery within it would travel with him. Xyra would maintain its internal stability while Leon carried it across.
Questions followed for more than an hour.

Some concerned the pressure of the crossing. Others asked whether the world’s sky would change, whether the natural dungeons would remain stable, and whether the higher world could detect them. Leon answered what he knew and admitted what he did not.
Eventually, one of the construction leaders raised a hand.
"Will the crossing damage the new roads?"
Leon looked at him.
"That is what you are most concerned about?"
"We finished two this week."
"Xyra will maintain internal stability."
The man relaxed. "Then I have no further questions."
Laughter moved through the crowd—not because the danger was trivial, but because life inside this world had become real enough for roads to matter.

The settlement leaders began preparing immediately. Healers checked the most vulnerable inhabitants. The Pyrans organized under Vyra’s direction. Xyra spread her awareness throughout the dimensional world and tightened its internal structure around every unstable region.
The others had already made their choices.
Seraphine stood beside Leon after the gathering ended, looking toward the town.
"We agreed a long time ago that we would not live beneath a ceiling," she said.
"We did."
"Then there was never a choice to make."
Ira reacted as though the question itself offended her.
"There is an entire stronger world through that road. Did you imagine I would stay here while you went first?"
"I imagined you would complain about not going first."
She considered that. "I can do both."
Vyra’s answer was simpler. The Pyrans lived in Leon’s world now, and Pyran Flame Sovereign had bound her future more closely to theirs. Where they went, she went.
Loriel took longer.
"I still don’t understand what happened to me in the dungeon," she said. "Child of Life, the golden System—any of it. Staying somewhere familiar won’t make the answers appear."
Her fingers tightened once against her sleeve.
"I don’t like pain. I’ve decided that isn’t the same as wanting to stay small."
Leon nodded. "It isn’t."
Before the final crossing, Seraphine had one more responsibility waiting in Velaria.
She and Leon returned to the Lower World together.

Her estate stood exactly where she had left it, its walls clean, its gardens maintained, and warm light shining through its windows. Months earlier, she had gathered her people there and placed them under Kaela’s command. At the time, Leon’s dimensional world had still been undeveloped—a place with immense potential, but nowhere near the comfortable home it had since become. Her estate had proper rooms, abundant food, familiar surroundings, and every luxury Seraphine could provide.
Leaving them there had not meant forgetting them.
She had done it because she cared about them.
She had also never imagined that, only months later, she would be preparing to leave Velaria entirely.

Kaela was already waiting in the entrance hall when they arrived. Seraphine’s first and most trusted knight, she had continued managing the estate and protecting everyone within it exactly as Seraphine had asked.
She lowered herself onto one knee.
"My lady."
"Stand, Kaela."
Kaela rose. Her eyes moved over Seraphine once, confirming for herself that she was unharmed, before shifting briefly toward Leon.
"You would not have returned together without a reason," she said.
"No," Seraphine replied. "Gather everyone."

The knights, servants, informants, and others who had followed Seraphine over the years assembled in the largest hall. Some looked worried. Others watched Leon with open curiosity. All of them understood from Seraphine’s expression that this was not an ordinary visit.
She told them the truth.

She explained that Leon had found a road leading beyond Velaria, that the destination was a genuine higher-ranked world, and that they intended to cross it. She did not promise perfect safety. She did not claim to understand what awaited them. She only explained that Leon’s dimensional world would travel with him and that anyone inside it would leave Velaria as well.
"When I asked you to remain here," Seraphine said, "I believed this estate was the best place I could give you. I did not know my path would carry me beyond this world so soon."
Her gaze passed across the gathered faces.

"I will not disappear and leave you to discover it afterward. Leon’s world now has a growing city, defenses, healers, training grounds, and space for every person here. If you wish to come with us, you may enter before we depart."
She paused.
"If you wish to remain in Velaria, this estate and everything within it will continue to belong to you. No one will be punished for choosing the life they already know."
Silence followed.
Kaela broke it first.
"You left me here because someone you trusted needed to protect them," she said.
Seraphine met her eyes. "Yes."

"Then I remained because that was the duty you gave me." Kaela stepped forward and placed one fist over her heart. "But if that duty is finished, my place is with you. I was your first knight. I have no intention of becoming the first one you leave behind."
Something in Seraphine’s expression softened.
"Even if the road leads to a world stronger than anything we know?"
"Especially then."

Several of the knights voiced their agreement immediately. The others followed—not from a command Seraphine had issued, but because they had already chosen her through dangers far smaller than this one.

Not every answer came quickly. A few people asked about the new city, its laws, and whether families would remain together. Leon answered each question plainly. He described what already existed, what remained unfinished, and the risks of the crossing without hiding any of them.
By the time the discussion ended, every person in the hall had chosen to go.

Leon opened the way into his dimensional world within the estate grounds. People carried personal belongings, records, weapons, and the things they refused to abandon. Kaela remained at the entrance until the last of Seraphine’s people crossed, fulfilling her old responsibility before finally stepping through herself.
Seraphine entered last.

She stood for a moment within the growing town and watched her people being received by its leaders. Proper housing was arranged rather than improvised shelter. Families remained together. Kaela immediately began asking practical questions about defenses and where her knights could be useful.
Only then did the tension Seraphine had carried since deciding to leave ease from her shoulders.
She had not known, when she left them in the comfort of her estate, that her life would change this much.
But she would not cross beyond the world and pretend the people who had trusted her were no longer part of it.

Once they were settled, Leon and the others returned to Velaria for the crossing. Loriel found Luna alone in a quiet courtyard behind the Church of Life. Luna stood beneath an old tree with her hands folded, her expression composed in the careful way it became when composure required effort.
Loriel stopped beside her.
"I’m going."
"I know."
"You could tell me not to."
Luna looked at her then. "Would you stay?"
Loriel’s eyes lowered. "No."
"Then asking would only make both of us unhappy."
For several seconds, neither spoke.
Then Luna reached out and drew her into an embrace.
Loriel held herself stiff for the first heartbeat. After that she folded against Luna and clung to her.
"You do not have to prove that the dungeon failed to frighten you," Luna murmured. "It did. You are allowed to be afraid and still go."
"What if I come back different?"
"You will." Luna’s hand rested against the back of her green hair. "Everyone does. Just make certain the change belongs to you."
Loriel laughed once through the tears gathering in her eyes. "That sounds like something Leon would say."
"Do not insult me during our farewell."
That earned a real laugh.
When they separated, Luna placed both hands around Loriel’s hands.
"Come back when the road allows it. Not before it is safe. Not because you feel guilty for leaving. Come back because you have something you want to show me."
Loriel nodded. "I will."

Luna remained in Velaria. Someone Leon trusted needed to monitor the dormant endpoint, preserve the chamber, and serve as their connection to the world they were leaving. The Keystone had recorded both ends, so the farewell was not permanent. Reopening the road would be difficult and enormously expensive, but difficult was not the same as impossible.
At the buried chamber, Leon activated the Worldway Keystone again.
The restored passage opened slowly. He checked every layer of the route before extending his perception through it to the far side.
Stable ground waited beyond. Nothing immediately hostile moved within the limited region he could inspect. There was no battle, no collapsing terrain, and no obvious trap.
The passage revealed only a few hundred meters. Whatever existed beyond that remained unknown.

Leon closed every connection between the road and the damaged abyssal framework. The claim he had severed did not return. The red eye watched from beyond its own crack, but there was no path between it and the route.
Xyra’s voice reached him through their bond.
"The dimensional world is stable."
Leon looked at Seraphine, Ira, Loriel, and Vyra.
"The destination is clear. That is all I can promise."
Ira stepped beside him. "That will do."
They entered together.
The world vanished.

For one long moment, there was only pressure and the enormous silence between worlds. The Keystone held both endpoints while Leon guided them along the repaired road. Behind his physical body, bound more deeply than flesh, the weight of an entire rank-three world moved with him.
Xyra held its settlements steady. The town, the instance, the Ascension Tower, the sleeping dragon, and thousands of lives crossed through the dark without feeling the road beneath them.
Then the pressure broke.
Leon stepped onto solid ground.

The air entered his lungs, dense with energy of a quality Velaria had never naturally possessed. His body responded at once, drawing it through channels prepared to receive power, but the reaction remained his—automatic cultivation, not a loss of control.
Ira drew a sharp breath. Loriel lifted both hands to her mouth. Seraphine stared upward.
The sky was wrong.

Not merely a different color. It held a depth and scale Velaria’s atmosphere could never have supported. Vast formations moved at impossible heights, slow enough to resemble continents drifting through the upper air.

On the distant horizon stood something so immense Leon could not tell whether it was terrain, a structure, or a living existence. It should have vanished beneath the curve of the world. The fact that it remained visible told him more about the scale of this place than any system description could.
[World boundary crossed.]
[Foreign world laws detected. Adaptation in progress.]
[Worldway transit complete.]
[Passage closed. Endpoints retained.]
Behind them, the road folded shut. The higher-world endpoint returned to dormancy, leaving no open passage for the abyssal entity—or anything else—to follow.
Far away, something noticed them.
Leon felt the shift in attention move across the landscape, vast and unhurried, turning toward the place where the Upper Ones’ ancient road had awakened after ages of silence.
It did not approach.
It simply became aware.
Leon remained still beneath the weight of that distant attention, surrounded by people who had chosen to cross with him and carrying thousands more within a world of his own.
He had once been reborn into a world that placed a ceiling above every life within it.
Now, carrying a world of his own, Leon stepped beyond that ceiling.
— END OF VOLUME ONE —

chapters.title: Chapter 592: The Weight of a Higher World
paragraphs: The distant attention remained upon them.

It did not draw closer or press against Leon’s senses. It simply existed somewhere beyond anything he could see, vast and unhurried, aware that the Upper Ones’ ancient road had opened after ages of silence.

Leon stood beneath that attention without moving. Seraphine, Ira, Loriel, and Vyra remained around him, still adjusting to air dense with energy Velaria could never have produced. Above them, formations large enough to resemble drifting continents moved through the impossible heights of the sky. Farther away, the immense shape on the horizon remained impossible to identify as terrain, a structure, or something alive.
Only after memorizing those details did Leon lower his gaze.

Three moons hung above the old-iron sky. One was enormous and silver, bright enough to flatten the shadows across the ground. A smaller moon wore a pale green ring, while the third had broken apart sometime in the distant past, its fragments trailing across the heavens in a crooked band.
"Nobody move yet," Leon said.

The Worldway had already closed behind them, its endpoint returned to dormancy, but the ground still remembered what had happened. Leon knelt and pressed his palm against black stone veined with threads of metal. Space churned beneath the surface where the passage had folded reality, leaving a bruise that anyone familiar with spatial law could read like a footprint in wet clay.

He spent four minutes smoothing the torn edges and folding the residue into itself. The final compressed knot went deep beneath the stone, where the ambient energy could wear it away. Even that small task cost more than it should have. Space here was denser, layered and complete, resisting his touch like clay that had already begun to set.

When the last visible trace disappeared, Leon searched the area again. The residue belonged to them. There was no second signature, no damaged edge suggesting that anything had followed, and the dormant road offered the abyssal entity no path into this world.
The distant awareness did not move.
Leon could not locate it, fight it, or avoid something he knew so little about, so he reached inward instead.
The connection to his dimensional world was intact. Relief loosened his shoulders before he could stop it, and through that bond, in pieces, the world reported itself to him.

Xyra was steady. Her attention brushed his, tired and enormously relieved, then withdrew as she continued holding the internal laws level. The principal settlement remained where it belonged. He felt the weight of thousands of people continuing their lives beneath familiar roofs, the half-built school, the granary, and the Ascension Tower standing where it always had. The Pyran settlement and every other inhabited region remained stable.
Farther down, deep and slow, the red dragon slept on.
[Bound Dimensional World: Rank Three]
[Internal integrity: Stable]
[External anchor: Established — Unknown World]
Leon read the final line twice. Even the System offered no name for the world beneath his feet.

He tested the passage next. He could still open a way into the dimensional world, step through it, return outside, or send someone in without leaving a permanent entrance behind. The crossing had changed none of those functions.

The other direction was different. When he reached toward Velaria, the buried chamber, and the woman guarding the dormant endpoint, he found no active connection. The coordinates still existed within the Keystone, but until the road was reopened, there was only absence.
Luna.
He let the thought pass. Holding it would not shorten the distance.
"Well?" Ira asked.
"Everyone is alive. Everything came through." Leon rose and looked once toward the empty ground behind them. "Nothing followed us."
"Then can we breathe? I’d like it on record that this air is disgusting."
"It isn’t disgusting." Loriel had crouched beside a bristled shrub growing from a crack in the stone, and her voice had gone strange. "Leon. This plant."
"What about it?"

Loriel held her hand just above the bristles without touching them. "I don’t know. Something this small shouldn’t contain so much vitality, but that isn’t the strangest part." Her brows drew together. "The energy inside it is moving through the roots and stem in a pattern I’ve never felt before."
Seraphine finally sheathed the sword she had drawn during their arrival. She walked a dozen paces from the group, set her feet, and rested one hand on the hilt.
"Let me try something."
She drew and cut upward.

Stormlight left the blade as it always had, white shot through with a line of blue, the sound arriving a fraction after the light. It struck a stone ridge and blew a wedge from it. Dust rose and hung in the heavy air.
The ridge stood thirty paces away. Seraphine had aimed at one three times farther out.
She stared at the distance her attack had failed to cross. "It didn’t weaken. It kept everything. It just... stopped."
"Move," Ira said, already stepping forward. "Watch this."

She set her spear, spun it once, and drove a compressed line of Calamity flame across the basin. The fire was correct, the same brutal orange-white she had wielded since taking the class, shaped with the same control. Yet the air refused to part for it. The farther the flame traveled, the harder it had to push for every meter, until it died forty paces away in a burst that scorched the stone black and left the smell of struck iron.
Ira stared at the mark. "That was a third of what it should have done."

Vyra had remained quiet. Now she raised one hand, palm upward, and closed her eyes. Pyran flame answered instantly, rising from her skin in a broad, obedient sheet as she reached beyond her own body to draw ambient power into it.
Nothing answered.

The foreign energy did not resist her. It simply continued flowing as though her authority did not exist. Vyra opened her eyes, and whatever had entered her expression disappeared before anyone could read it.
"My own flame is fine," she said. "Everything past my own flame is a wall."

Leon crouched and drew a slow circle through the grit. Unlike Velaria’s loose mana, the energy here was already refined into something beyond his knowledge. It moved through patterns with purpose, as though meant to enter living bodies along structures that Seraphine, Ira, Loriel, and Vyra did not possess.

His own case was different. The channels created by his Divinordial body accepted the energy, and the Primordial Void Heart drew it in without hesitation, just as it had during the first breath after the crossing. However, his power did not circulate in the same deliberate pathways woven through the world around him. He could absorb the energy by force of his existing foundation, but he lacked the native method that would make its use natural.
The difference was not enough to make him helpless. It was enough to matter.
He was still examining it when Loriel said, "Leon."
Her hand had gone flat against the stone beside the shrub. All color had left her face.
"Something is coming under us." She swallowed. "It’s huge."

Leon felt it half a second later—not sound, but pressure transmitted through the rock. A long displacement moved toward them from the north with the unhurried confidence of something that had never needed to hurry.
"Off the stone," he said. "Now."
Two hundred paces away, the ground rose in a line.

It surfaced like a spine through water, throwing black soil and shattered rock into the heavy air. Petrified trees leaned, cracked at their bases, and collapsed as the line changed direction toward the fading spatial disturbance and the energy they had released.
The ridge came apart.

Something armored in star-metal rose from beneath it. Segment after segment followed, plates the color of broken swords catching the light of three moons, until its immense length blotted out the horizon behind it.
Mandibles the size of gates opened and tasted the air.

chapters.title: Chapter 593: Born Beneath Higher Laws
paragraphs: The System caught up a half breath later.
[Star-Iron Devouring Centipede — Level 94]
[Rank: Ethereal Initiate]
[Affinity: Metal, Earth]
[Warning: Existence is not wholly contained within observed body]
Leon read the last line and had no time to think about it, because the head came down.
"Scatter!" he shouted, and the ground where they had been standing ceased to be ground.

Mandibles tore into the basin and threw it upward. Leon folded Loriel forty paces east before the debris arrived, then bent the largest fragments away from Ira, who was already searching the creature’s underside for a seam. Whatever the trial had cost them, none of the four retreated.

Seraphine went first, taking the air in three strides with stormlight running down her sword. A blow that would have opened a fortress gate in Velaria entered an overlapping joint by only a third of its length before stopping.

Something moved under the armor. Beneath the plates, threaded through the meat of the thing, power ran in channels, and where her blade bit, the flow bent toward it and thickened, and the wound closed on the steel like a fist.
Seraphine tore her sword free and dropped away before the segment could roll and crush her.
"It’spushing back from inside!" she called.
"I saw it." Leon was already moving.
Ira found a seam near the ninth segment. Instead of pouring out power, she compressed Calamity flame into a needle and drove it into the same opening three times.

Black smoke came out. The creature made a sound like a mountain grinding its teeth, and its whole body rippled — and the ripple carried powertoward the wound, from four segments away, and the smoke stopped.

"That’s not healing," Loriel said, some distance behind them. Her voice was steady, which impressed him more than anything else. "Leon, it isn’t healing; it’smoving. It’s bringing life from somewhere else in its body and spending it there."
"How much does it have?"
"I can’t— it’s like asking how much water is in a river."
Vyra hit it next.

She targeted the metal-touched shimmer gathering along the plates whenever the creature prepared to move quickly. Though the world’s energy ignored her, flame still obeyed. White-hearted Pyran fire flooded its flank until the shimmer scattered.
The centipede’s next lunge came in slower and crooked, and Seraphine used the half second that bought her to cut a plate free entirely.
For about ninety seconds, they were doing well.

Leon folded distances for Seraphine, moved Loriel away from debris, and kept hardened space between Ira and the nearest segments. A lattice of frozen earth-and-metal spikes sank through the basin floor to stop the creature from diving beneath them.
And while he did all of it, he watched the circulation.

The channels ran the length of its body in bundles and crossed at the joints, which brightened whenever it was injured. A lifetime of consuming star-metal and this world’s energy had created a system that made his companions’ strongest attacks seem small.
It was not merely tougher than a Velarian beast of the same level. Every part of its greater strength belonged to one cultivated whole.
Then it stopped being interested in playing.
The creature reared, two-thirds of its length coming off the ground, and every plate along its body stood up like the scales of a pinecone opening.
The metallic storm came out sideways.

Vyra took most of it. Her flames rose to meet it and were shredded and blown backward, and she went with them, skidding thirty paces on her heels with both forearms crossed in front of her face. Seraphine’s guard came up in time and broke anyway — the stormlight barrier held a full second, longer than it had any right to, then burst, and she was thrown into a stone shelf hard enough that Leon heard it.
Ira had committed to a thrust. It went in deep enough to matter, and then the segment rolled, and the tail came around, and she was airborne before she could withdraw.

Leon caught her out of the air with a fold of space, put her down, and got a shield of layered force between Loriel and the shrapnel front, and in the process he let a plate-edge open a long line across his own back that closed before the blood finished leaving it.

Loriel was on her knees, both palms out, holding all three of them together with green light and nothing else, and she was burning through herself to do it. Level thirty-one. She had been Sage two weeks ago.
That was the moment Leon understood the problem, and it was not the problem he had expected.

He could kill this thing. He was already fairly sure he could kill it. The issue was that killing it required his whole attention, and his whole attention was currently divided four ways, and every second he spent shielding was a second he was not spending learning where its power came from.

Out in the basin, the centipede curled itself into a spiral. The plates along its entire length began to glow — dull red at first, then white — and the metal veins in the stone beneath it lit up in sympathy, spreading outward in a web that reached almost to where Loriel was kneeling.
It was not preparing an attack. It was preparing to erase the ground.
"Everyone in," Leon said.
Seraphine had already pushed herself off the stone shelf. "No."
"Seraphine."

"Wecrossedfor this." She was breathing badly. There was blood at her hairline, and she had not noticed. "We crossed so you wouldn’t be standing somewhere like this on your own. If we go inside now, then what was any of it—"
She stopped.
Her gaze moved across the shell around Ira, the barrier over Loriel, and Leon standing between them while the centipede gathered enough power to erase the basin.
Her jaw set. "How long do you need?"
"Not long."
"Then don’t be long." She got an arm under Ira, who was swearing at nobody in particular and trying to stand on a leg that would not take her weight. "Vyra. Loriel.Now."

Vyra did not argue. That cost her something — Leon saw it — but she took Loriel by the shoulders and moved her, and whatever pride the fall from her peak had wounded, she kept it out of the way of the decision.
Leon opened the way, the portal leading back to the dimensional world.
It was a controlled aperture, small, edged in silver, and it should have been beneath the notice of a creature made mostly of appetite and armor.
The centipede’s head came around instantly.

It stopped gathering. It stopped everything. Every antenna along its front third turned toward the opening with an attention that was almost sickening in its clarity, and Leon felt the thinglook— not at the light, but through it, at the sky beyond, at the fields and the roofs and the thousands of small burning lives inside.
An entire world. Right there. Unarmored.
It lunged.

Seraphine went through with Ira. Vyra went through, pushing Loriel ahead of her, and the great armored head came down the basin faster than anything of that mass should be able to move, mandibles wide, star-metal shrieking against star-metal.
Leon stepped into the gap.

He set one hand against the inside of the left mandible and put everything he had into a single lateral push — space compressed to a wedge, hardened, and driven sideways at the exact angle the creature’s own momentum could not correct. The impact went through his arm, his shoulder, his ribs. His feet cut two furrows twenty paces long through solid black stone.
The head slewed aside and hammered into the basin wall.
Behind him, the aperture closed to a seam, to a thread, to nothing.
Leon lowered his hand. Somewhere under the ringing in his ears he could feel four presences on the other side of that connection, safe, furious, alive.
He rolled his shoulder once, and turned around.
Between him and everything he had carried out of Velaria, there was now only a centipede.

chapters.title: Chapter 594: Leon Is Still Leon
paragraphs: The first thing Leon did was stop defending. The four barriers he had maintained around the others dissolved at once, freeing the attention he had spent eleven minutes dividing among them.
The centipede pulled its head from the basin wall and charged.

Leon knew several attacks that could turn the valley into a crater, but he did not know who else inhabited this wilderness or what such destruction would announce. Instead, he let the creature drive him backward and watched. Its mandibles closed on empty air. The tail swept through a fold of space he had already left behind.

A lance of compressed cold entered a seam. Power arrived from the neighboring segment after four seconds, and the wound closed two seconds later. Leon repeated the strike, received the same result, then hit the eleventh segment, the ninth, and the eleventh again.
The second wound in the eleventh segment healed more slowly.
There.

The creature could redistribute its power, but its reserves were finite. Some lay within its body, while more flowed from the star-metal veins beneath the basin. Leon dropped two hundred meters of metal-rich rock away from its forward third, and the glow beneath its plates dimmed.

He opened dozens of shallow wounds along its flanks. None threatened its life, but its instincts repaired every one, spending power until Leon stopped attacking the wounds and struck the crossings instead.

The circulating bundles met beneath the joints. A spear of hardened space entered the junction below the fourth segment and twisted, tearing something its neighboring sections could not repair. Leon repeated the process at the seventh and fifteenth.
When the centipede whipped around, part of its body failed to follow. Its first sound that was not rage shook the basin, and it dove toward the earth.

Leon pulled the lattice he had sunk earlier from the ground, raising a cage of stone and cold. It could not hold the creature, but breaking it cost four seconds. He used those seconds to move down its length and sever one junction after another. By the time the centipede tore free, two-thirds of its body had fallen silent, the mineral veins were buried, and the roads carrying power forward had been cut.
Its head rose unsteadily, white plates fading to dull iron.

Leon extended his perception and found the existence the System had warned him about: a knot of anchored intent buried a hundred meters beneath the basin, ready to rebuild the creature after the death of its flesh.
He struck the anchor and the centipede’s head at the same moment.
Only one impact made a sound. The armored length collapsed across the basin and did not move again.
Leon stood in the quiet for a moment, breathing this world’s heavy air, one arm hanging where the mandible had done more damage than he had let anyone see.
[Star-Iron Devouring Centipede — Slain]
[You have earned...]

He stored the entire corpse—plates, mandibles, and the core still glowing sullenly in its chest cavity—but not near any settlement or living ecosystem. Leon sealed it inside an empty storage region cut off from the inhabited lands until he understood whether its severed anchor was truly the only danger it carried. Whatever else this world was, it was rich, and a hundred meters of armored monster was not something a wise man left in a basin for someone else to find.
Then he sat down on a rock and talked to four angry women from inside the dimensional world through his connection.
"—could have held longer," Ira was saying.
"You couldn’t stand up."
"I could havestoodup."
"Ira." He rubbed his eyes. "It gathered enough power to glass the whole basin. I could survive that. Loriel could not."
"I know," Loriel said quietly. "I felt it building."
"Knowing why doesn’t make it sit any better." Seraphine’s voice, flat and tired. "We came for this, Leon. Not to sit in a garden while you walk into an unknown world alone."

"I’m not asking you to sit in a garden. I’m asking for time." He looked out at the basin, at the black stone and the fallen petrified trees and the three moons that had barely moved. "There’s something here that the living things in this world have and none of us do. Their energy runs through a structure — roads, channels, something inside the body. That creature had it. Loriel felt the same kind of pattern inside the weed near our arrival. Until we know what it is and whether we can build one, you have to spend several times as much power for far less effect."
"And you’ll find that out how?"

"By finding people. Cities. Somebody who was taught this as a child and thinks it’s boring." He stood, tested the arm, found it mostly working. "I’ll come back the moment I have anything worth having. That’s not a promise to be careful. It’s a promise to come back."
"It’s a bad promise," Vyra said.
"It’s the one I’ve got."
He let the connection go quiet, and started getting ready.
They were not weak, but things right now were too mysterious and dangerous.

His armor sank from bronze-gold to lie dark beneath his skin. He suppressed his aura in layers, reduced the elemental crown to an ember, and changed into unembroidered gray clothes and plain boots. A cloth pack held a knife, a waterskin, and three days of ordinary food, because a man carrying nothing was more suspicious than one with a bad pack.

At a shallow stream an hour north, he checked his work in the water. There was no glow at his collarbone or shimmer along his arms. The gray clothes hung naturally, their hems worn in the right places, while his armor, elemental crown, and the deeper pressure of his aura had disappeared from sight.

Leon knew his appearance had changed along with the rest of his body. What he did not know was that his Divinordial refinement and Primordial Heart gave it a vitality and perfection that suppression could not hide. He had never needed to measure its effect on a stranger, while those closest to him had watched the transformation happen gradually until it was simply how Leon looked.
He saw no crown, no armor, and no advertised wealth or power. For the purpose of passing as an unimportant traveler, he judged the disguise adequate and moved on.

For nearly three days, Leon followed whatever suggested civilization: worn stone, a collapsed road beneath drifted grit, streams flowing somewhere useful, and the directions flying beasts seemed to avoid.

On the first afternoon, he found a cultivator’s bones in a gully. The ribs looked reinforced, but there was no cloth, ring, boot, pack, or blade remaining. Someone had even taken the pins from the dead person’s hair.

Near noon the next day, Leon crested a rise and saw six travelers on the road below, mounted on beasts with too many legs. Ahead of them, a man dragged himself along the roadside with one leg bent in a direction no leg should bend. The group passed without slowing. One rider adjusted his reins only to give the injured man a wider berth.
Leon went down the slope.
The man heard him coming, rolled over, and got a rusted knife up in both shaking hands.
"Stayback." His voice cracked in the middle of it. There was nothing in his face but certainty — not fear of a stranger, but a flat expectation of what a stranger in this place was for.
Leon stopped ten paces out, set the waterskin and half his food down on the stone, backed away, and walked up the slope without looking behind him.

Leon noted both encounters without deciding what the entire world was from them. A few days of travel could reveal what a road was like, not every person who lived beyond it, and he had built enough of a civilization himself to know how badly a stranger could misread one.
But he stopped leaving his back to open ground.
On the third night, the wilderness went quiet.

Not gradually. Between one step and the next, the small clicking things in the rocks stopped clicking, and the wind that had been moving through the petrified trees continued to move without making any sound at all.
Leon kept walking at exactly the same pace.
The silver moon was high and his shadow lay long and sharp across the pale stone ahead of him. He watched it for a hundred paces without appearing to watch anything.
At the hundred and first, his shadow’s left arm swung a fraction of a second after his own.

And in the middle of it, curled just below where his heart would be, something had been drawn that he had not put there. It was small. It was a mark of some kind, three strokes and a hook, and while he looked at it, it grew perceptibly darker.

The four barriers he had maintained around the others dissolved at once, freeing the attention he had spent eleven minutes dividing among them.

Instead, he let the creature drive him backward and watched.
Its mandibles closed on empty air.
The tail swept through a fold of space he had already left behind.

There.

chapters.title: Chapter 595: A Line of Pale Light
paragraphs: Leon did not stop walking. Whatever had placed the mark inside his shadow was waiting to learn when he noticed, and any reaction would reveal the reach of his perception.

The mark was formed from shadow and spatial energy woven together in a way he did not yet understand. A faint tension joined it to the darkness beneath a nearby shelf, then disappeared into deeper shadow. Leon touched it with his senses, felt it pull taut like a fishing line, and withdrew.

For the next hour, he lied with his body. He let a false limp appear, knelt too long at a stream, and exposed his back to a stand of black rock. Nothing attacked, but when he rose, the rock’s shadow had shifted against the moonlight and the mark below his heart had darkened.
It wants the mark deeper before it starts.

Leon chose a shallow bowl of pale stone with broken ridges on three sides and few natural shadows. While pretending to make camp badly, he sank a cold lattice into the ground and left four points of hardened space along the northern approach. His fire created the final lie: a man who needed light to see the dark.
He lay against the rock and slowed his breathing.
The attack came in the fourth hour.

It descended from overhead, pouring through the ridge’s shadow toward the back of his neck. Leon had positioned the fire so that shadow fell exactly there. He moved a quarter second early and struck where its throat would appear.

Half the blow passed through a body that was not fully solid. The rest broke its descent sideways, revealing a long, sleek beast with a coat blacker than the night around it and pale crescents where its eyes should have been.

It landed and rushed him through the darkness on the ground. Leon answered with compressed frost, avoiding fire or light that might be seen beyond the ridges. His blade struck the point where the moving shadow joined the stone. The beast stuttered as its momentum arrived before the rest of it, and Leon’s next attack opened its flank.
Steaming blood touched the ground. The creature withdrew twenty paces and stared at him, no longer treating him as helpless prey.
[Moonless Shadow Leopard — Level 114]
[Rank: Ethereal Lord]
[Affinity: Shadow, Space]
The leopard stood twenty levels and a full rank above the centipede. Worse, it used its Shadow and Space affinities with an instinctive precision Leon had only begun to understand on a decent level.

He could escape into his world, but the mark beneath his heart remained. Opening a dimensional passage before a creature built to enter places through shadow could lead it straight toward thousands of people whose defenses were not made for an Ethereal Lord.
That choice disappeared.

The leopard tested him with two lunges from opposite shadows. Leon avoided both, but the beast withdrew before he could punish either attempt. Then every shadow in the bowl deepened, and the ridge’s darkness spread across the stone.

Leon set his feet and gathered power into the Void Heart. The spatial fold he intended had worked only twice before. It would expose his presence for fifty kilometers and likely leave him injured, but it could carry him through the attack.
The darkness came at him from six directions.

Pale fabric stirred on the western ridge where no wind moved. A woman stood half-concealed among the stone, watching the killing strike close around him. She remained still until Leon raised his head toward the converging dark and moonlight fell across his face.
Her sword moved before the rest of her did.
A line of pale light crossed the bowl.

It arrived without sound or warning, a stroke of edged moonlight drawn across the world a foot before his chest. The mark vanished from Leon’s shadow without pain. Every shadow in the bowl flattened, exposing the leopard on bare stone, and a shallow white wound opened parallel to the one Leon had made.
The beast screamed.
Leon turned his head.

The woman stood on the western ridge in pale gray-blue robes that moonlight seemed unable to touch. A silver crescent rested at her collar, while a crescent-shaped jade at her waist held a thin line of light pointing south across the Desolation. Her sword looked plain until Leon noticed how completely the surrounding energy avoided it.

The cut had crossed the bowl before she finished stepping into view. The leopard saw her insignia, backed away with its tail low, then vanished beneath the rocks. The pressure of its hunt disappeared with it.
The woman descended and stopped six paces from Leon. Her gaze rested on him longer than the situation required. Then her expression closed, and her voice emerged colder than he expected.
"You built a fire," she said. "In the Desolation. At night. With a Moonless hunting nearby."
"I did."
"Do you know what one is?"
"It’s fast, travels through shadow, and marks its prey before attacking. I learned that tonight." Leon inclined his head. "Thank you for cutting the mark. I couldn’t remove it."
That earned him a long, unimpressed silence.
"You wounded it."
"Once. With cold."
"Show me your sect token."
"I don’t have one."
"Your registration jade."
"I don’t have that either."
Her gaze moved across his plain clothes, boots, and cloth pack. She believed none of them, though Leon could not tell which detail had betrayed him.
"Qingyue," she said. "Of Jade Moon Palace."
She stopped there, clearly expecting the name to be sufficient. Leon had no idea what Jade Moon Palace was, so he gave her a polite nod.
"You’ve never heard of it," she said.
"No."
"Where are you from?"

"A sealed inheritance space. I was inside a long time—I’m not sure how long. The entrance collapsed, and I emerged two days south of here." He allowed some weariness into his voice. "I don’t know the region or its roads. I’ve been following the water north."
Qingyue’s eyes moved to the crescent jade at her waist. The pale line within it trembled, still pointing toward the ground Leon had crossed.
"The space collapsed when you emerged?"
"Completely."
Qingyue studied the way he stood, breathed, and held his hands. Her attention settled twice near his chest, but Leon kept both hearts beating at the pace of a tired traveler until she moved on.
"Your energy doesn’t circulate," she said at last.
"Doesn’t it?"
"No." She did not elaborate. "An inheritance space would explain some of it. Not all of it."
"I can only tell you what happened to me."
"You have told me much less than that." She sheathed her sword with a small sound. "Your explanation is poor, but better than the other possibilities. That is the only reason we are still speaking."

She looked south once more, toward the disturbance her jade had been following, then at Leon. A moment later, she turned north, past the broken rim of the bowl, to where a faint smudge of light sat low on the horizon—so faint that Leon had mistaken it for a difference in the rock.

"Alone, without a sect or token, and unable to recognize a Moonless before it marks you, you will be dead within a month. Probably a week." Her tone remained cold. "That is not advice. It is what will happen."
Leon looked at the smudge on the horizon.
"Which way is the nearest city?"
She started walking.
She neither invited him nor ordered him away. She crossed the bowl at an unhurried pace, and the moonlight still refused to touch her as it touched everything else.
Leon stayed where he was for several breaths. He put the fire out with a handful of grit and picked up his pack.
Then he followed.
He was perhaps thirty paces behind her when her head turned a fraction — not enough to look at him. Just enough to confirm the distance.
She kept walking.
