chapters.title: Chapter 596: No Witnesses
paragraphs: Qingyue moved north across the broken stone at a pace that left little room for conversation. She never told Leon to keep up, but the test was obvious within the first few steps.

Ridges swept toward them and vanished behind them almost as soon as Leon noticed them. Loose stone cracked beneath Qingyue’s feet, yet her upper body hardly moved. She travelled with the ease of someone who had long ago stopped measuring journeys by days.

Leon had no intention of chasing her true limit. Qingyue was at least comparable to the Moonless Shadow Leopard, and likely much stronger. The speed she had chosen, however, was one he could maintain all day.
He closed the thirty paces between them and settled beside her without letting his breathing change.
Sixteen kilometers later, she glanced at him. Her gaze lingered on his calm face, then she turned forward and increased her speed by about a fifth.
Leon matched her again.
This time, she kept the same pace.

The increase placed a little more pressure on his legs, though it came nowhere close to straining him. He kept that from his face. Matching her chosen pace already revealed enough, and Qingyue’s brief sideways glance told him she understood that.
"Your inheritance taught you to move like that," she said after a while.
"Some of it."
"Which part?"
"The part that kept me alive."

The land gradually changed around them. The black, glassy basins of the deep Desolation gave way to gray stone and stubborn patches of scrub. Even the wind was losing its metallic taste. Twice, Qingyue stopped and held a flat crescent of pale jade on her palm. The light inside it pointed south both times.
"How long were you sealed inside?" she asked.
"I stopped counting."
"That is not an answer."
"It’s the one I have."
"Did the others in your inheritance cultivate as strangely as you do?"
"There weren’t any others," Leon said. "Not by the end."
The answer carried enough truth to silence her. She asked nothing else for the next hour.

Leon watched the changing land. Around midday, they passed a line of weathered stone markers and reached a reinforced road. The material beneath its surface made his spatial sense skip when he stepped over it. Deep paired ruts showed frequent wagon traffic, while old fire scars and a stripped axle spoke of the dangers along the route.

The road looked maintained, but never safe. Tracks veered around old patches of scorched stone, and someone had carved warning marks into one of the roadside pillars before weather wore them nearly smooth.
They were nearing the edge of the Desolation.

Leon smelled blood roughly a kilometer before the caravan came into view. Burned qi and the remnants of shattered formations hung over the road, mixed with a sweet medicinal scent leaking from broken cargo. Eight presences moved ahead, all of them alert.
Qingyue sensed them at nearly the same moment. She slowed to a walk, though her sword remained sheathed.
They rounded the shoulder of a hill and saw what remained of a merchant caravan.

There had been eleven wagons. Four burned along the roadside while men searched the other seven, breaking open storage containers and sorting cultivation goods into piles. Nine guards already lay dead.

Around forty survivors had been forced into the gap between two wagons. Merchants, servants, children, and badly wounded guards huddled together under the watch of two robbers. Both men faced the prisoners with weapons ready.
Several captives were too injured to sit upright. Others pressed pieces of torn cloth against wounds while trying to keep the children quiet. Whatever fight the guards had offered was already over.
Leon focused on the attackers.
[Archon — Level 84]
[Archon — Level 81]

The readings continued as his attention moved across the road. Seven Archons in total. Their leader stood beside the largest wagon with his hands behind his back. His presence was much denser, pressing against the air around him.
[Ethereal Initiate — Level 96]
One Ethereal among seven Archons made the group dangerous enough to destroy an ordinary caravan. It also explained the confidence with which they worked.

A young woman moved among the captives, holding the survivors together through sheer composure. A moderate cut crossed her left shoulder, bleeding through a sleeve she had torn to bandage someone else. She guided three children behind a wagon wheel so they could not see the bodies. When a servant began sobbing, she put a waterskin in his hands and sent him to help an old man with a crushed leg. The task steadied him.
She never spared a glance for the wagons holding her family’s fortune.
Near the front of the group, an older merchant in fine robes knelt before the leader with both hands open.

"Take the cargo, the registry seals, the route contracts—everything. I will not report the loss. I will not name you." His voice cracked, but he forced it steady. "There are children here. Take everything and leave them."
The leader regarded him with mild interest and gave no answer.

Leon studied the other robbers. Each man had taken a position near the prisoners, and one had cleaned his blade without sheathing it. Their purpose was clear. Once the cargo was sorted, they would kill every witness.
The older merchant seemed to understand as well. His eyes kept moving between the raised weapons and the children, searching for an argument that might still reach men who had already decided.
Qingyue stopped half a pace behind Leon. Her attention rested on him, waiting to see what he would do.
Below them, the merchant tried again. "Please. My daughter. The children—"
The nearest robber stepped behind him and raised a broad blade as casually as a woodsman lifting an axe.
Leon moved.
He crossed the slope without a sound and caught the robber’s wrist as the blade fell. With a twist, he forced the strike aside and pulled the merchant clear.
His free hand drove through the robber’s chest.
Lightning burst through flesh, heart, and cultivation core. The Archon died before his body struck the road.
Silence lasted half a breath. Then the remaining attackers turned toward Leon.
He gave them no chance to organize.

Lightning carried him across twenty paces. The two men guarding the prisoners were the immediate threat, so he killed the first in passing and tore through the second before the man could aim his weapon. Archons lacked cosmic anchors. Destroying their bodies and cores killed them permanently.

Ice surged from the road between the survivors and the attackers. Leon raised one wall three meters high, then angled another from its edge. The captives were boxed between the wagons with a single entrance, and Leon planted himself inside it.
Four Archons rushed him together.
Behind them, the lone Ethereal Initiate finally began to move.

sentences.text: Qingyue moved north across the broken stone at a pace that left little room for conversation.
She never told Leon to keep up, but the test was obvious within the first few steps.
Ridges swept toward them and vanished behind them almost as soon as Leon noticed them.
Loose stone cracked beneath Qingyue’s feet, yet her upper body hardly moved.
She travelled with the ease of someone who had long ago stopped measuring journeys by days.
Leon had no intention of chasing her true limit.
Qingyue was at least comparable to the Moonless Shadow Leopard, and likely much stronger.
The speed she had chosen, however, was one he could maintain all day.
He closed the thirty paces between them and settled beside her without letting his breathing change.
Sixteen kilometers later, she glanced at him.
Her gaze lingered on his calm face, then she turned forward and increased her speed by about a fifth.
Leon matched her again.
This time, she kept the same pace.
The increase placed a little more pressure on his legs, though it came nowhere close to straining him.
He kept that from his face.
Matching her chosen pace already revealed enough, and Qingyue’s brief sideways glance told him she understood that.
"Your inheritance taught you to move like that," she said after a while.
"Some of it."
"Which part?"
"The part that kept me alive."
The land gradually changed around them.
The black, glassy basins of the deep Desolation gave way to gray stone and stubborn patches of scrub.
Even the wind was losing its metallic taste.
Twice, Qingyue stopped and held a flat crescent of pale jade on her palm.
The light inside it pointed south both times.
"How long were you sealed inside?" she asked.
"I stopped counting."
"That is not an answer."
"It’s the one I have."
"Did the others in your inheritance cultivate as strangely as you do?"
"There weren’t any others," Leon said.
"Not by the end."
The answer carried enough truth to silence her.
She asked nothing else for the next hour.
Leon watched the changing land.
Around midday, they passed a line of weathered stone markers and reached a reinforced road.
The material beneath its surface made his spatial sense skip when he stepped over it.
Deep paired ruts showed frequent wagon traffic, while old fire scars and a stripped axle spoke of the dangers along the route.
The road looked maintained, but never safe.
Tracks veered around old patches of scorched stone, and someone had carved warning marks into one of the roadside pillars before weather wore them nearly smooth.
They were nearing the edge of the Desolation.
Leon smelled blood roughly a kilometer before the caravan came into view.
Burned qi and the remnants of shattered formations hung over the road, mixed with a sweet medicinal scent leaking from broken cargo.
Eight presences moved ahead, all of them alert.
Qingyue sensed them at nearly the same moment.
She slowed to a walk, though her sword remained sheathed.
They rounded the shoulder of a hill and saw what remained of a merchant caravan.
There had been eleven wagons.
Four burned along the roadside while men searched the other seven, breaking open storage containers and sorting cultivation goods into piles.
Nine guards already lay dead.
Around forty survivors had been forced into the gap between two wagons.
Merchants, servants, children, and badly wounded guards huddled together under the watch of two robbers.
Both men faced the prisoners with weapons ready.
Several captives were too injured to sit upright.
Others pressed pieces of torn cloth against wounds while trying to keep the children quiet.
Whatever fight the guards had offered was already over.
Leon focused on the attackers.
[Archon — Level 84]
[Archon — Level 81]
The readings continued as his attention moved across the road.
Seven Archons in total.
Their leader stood beside the largest wagon with his hands behind his back.
His presence was much denser, pressing against the air around him.
[Ethereal Initiate — Level 96]
One Ethereal among seven Archons made the group dangerous enough to destroy an ordinary caravan.
It also explained the confidence with which they worked.
A young woman moved among the captives, holding the survivors together through sheer composure.
A moderate cut crossed her left shoulder, bleeding through a sleeve she had torn to bandage someone else.
She guided three children behind a wagon wheel so they could not see the bodies.
When a servant began sobbing, she put a waterskin in his hands and sent him to help an old man with a crushed leg.

She never spared a glance for the wagons holding her family’s fortune.
Near the front of the group, an older merchant in fine robes knelt before the leader with both hands open.

I will not name you." His voice cracked, but he forced it steady.
"There are children here.
Take everything and leave them."
The leader regarded him with mild interest and gave no answer.
Leon studied the other robbers.
Each man had taken a position near the prisoners, and one had cleaned his blade without sheathing it.
Their purpose was clear.
Once the cargo was sorted, they would kill every witness.
The older merchant seemed to understand as well.
His eyes kept moving between the raised weapons and the children, searching for an argument that might still reach men who had already decided.
Qingyue stopped half a pace behind Leon.
Her attention rested on him, waiting to see what he would do.
Below them, the merchant tried again.
"Please.
My daughter.
The children—"
The nearest robber stepped behind him and raised a broad blade as casually as a woodsman lifting an axe.
Leon moved.
He crossed the slope without a sound and caught the robber’s wrist as the blade fell.
With a twist, he forced the strike aside and pulled the merchant clear.
His free hand drove through the robber’s chest.

He gave them no chance to organize.

chapters.title: Chapter 597: What He Chose to Reveal
paragraphs: Leon met the four Archons at the entrance to the ice corridor.
An ice spear pierced the first man through the chest and shattered his core. Leon struck the second robber’s legs with lightning, dropping him long enough to close the distance and finish him.

Their combined assault had enough force to tear apart the wagons behind him, but the narrow corridor prevented them from surrounding him. Every time two tried to advance together, Leon’s ice forced one into the other’s path.

The third hurled a compressed lance of qi past Leon’s shoulder toward the prisoners. Leon stepped into its path. The attack opened his forearm, but the ice wall behind him remained untouched. Before the man could form another lance, Leon killed him.
The final Archon turned and ran. He made it forty paces before ice closed around his ankles and fixed him to the road.
Behind Leon, the young woman kept her voice low and steady as she told everyone to stay down and hold the wounded still.
Then the pressure over the road deepened.
The Ethereal Initiate walked forward. Heat from the burning wagons bent around him, and hairline cracks spread across Leon’s walls before he came within ten paces.
"Seven Archons," the man said. "You cut through them as though their years of cultivation meant nothing."

Qi gathered in his raised hand. It was denser than anything the others had wielded, folded repeatedly and seated deep within his body. He drew from the ground and air with a fluency that forced Leon to revise his estimate of the coming strike.
Qingyue remained on the slope, watching with her sword still sheathed.
The first exchange drove Leon eleven paces backward and shattered part of the wall beside him.

He recovered his footing with a shallow cut across his ribs. The leader lacked the overwhelming force of the Moonless Shadow Leopard, but his foundation had been refined over many years. Every strike carried layers of compressed qi, making him far more durable than a Velarian with similar raw power.

The difference from the Archons was immediate. Their attacks had relied on power and technique. The Ethereal Initiate’s energy responded almost like another limb, changing direction after release and gathering around damaged flesh before Leon could exploit the opening.
Leon settled into his stance and began testing those layers.

Lightning closed the distance and punished openings at the man’s wrists and knees. Ice controlled the ground between them. Slanted barriers forced the Ethereal Initiate to turn, while patches of frost stole his footing whenever he committed too much weight. Leon kept every deflection angled away from the survivors.

The leader crossed the distance twice with steps that covered far more ground than they should have. Leon gave no sign that he had noticed. He adjusted his timing until the man arrived in front of an ice barrier and had to smash through it.
"You are hiding something," the leader said, his breathing heavier now.

Leon ignored the accusation and watched the qi beneath his opponent’s skin. Whenever the man was wounded, energy rose from deep within his foundation and repaired the damage. Even a slash that opened his shoulder began closing within seconds. The centipede had used a crude version of the same principle. Here, the process was smaller, controlled, and directed by intelligence.

Leon also felt the faint pull beyond the man’s body. His consciousness was tied to something much larger and more distant. Killing him would require more than breaking flesh and core, but Leon kept that understanding to himself.
The next exchange gave the leader a clean opening. His hooked strike slipped beneath Leon’s guard while Leon shaped another wall, cutting deep into his left side.
Leon pressed a hand to the wound and released his Light affinity.

A clean glow spread beneath his palm. The bleeding stopped, and the torn flesh drew together. His deeper restoration remained concealed; the visible healing was impressive, but still believable as a third affinity.

The leader’s expression tightened. Leon had already shown lightning, ice, and light while dismantling his entire group. He had expected an inexperienced prodigy. Instead, every ability served a clear purpose.
Qingyue now watched Leon’s hands more closely than the fight itself. She had understood the same thing. He was choosing exactly how much to reveal.

Leon continued with the same three affinities. Lightning provided speed and damage, ice gave him defense and control, and light closed the wounds he could not avoid. Together, they were rare enough to draw attention without exposing the rest of his power.
Realizing the fight was turning against him, the Ethereal Initiate broke away.

He slipped through the damaged edge of the wall and plunged into the survivors. Someone screamed. A moment later, he emerged with a boy of six or seven trapped beneath one arm and a spike of gathered qi hovering beside the child’s throat.
"Stop."
Leon lowered his hands.
The young woman rose, her face pale, and held one hand behind her to keep the other survivors from rushing forward.
The leader studied Leon’s expression. "Yes. You are that kind."

At the edge of Leon’s perception, Qingyue’s fingers settled on her sword. A fine thread of pale sword intent had already curved around the qi spike. If the man tried to kill the child, she would cut the attack apart before it reached him. With the boy protected, she waited for Leon’s response.
The leader had read Leon correctly, yet it gave him no advantage.
Leon reached for the space around the boy and folded it.

A soft breath of displaced air passed through the road. The child vanished from the robber’s grasp and reappeared four paces away beside the young woman, blinking but unharmed. She pulled him close so quickly that the cut across her shoulder opened again.
The leader stared at his empty arm.

Leon attacked before he recovered. Lightning destroyed the Ethereal Initiate’s body, but his awareness immediately pulled at the anchor spread through the cosmic background. Cold raced along that connection and froze the returning flow of energy. Leon then folded the surrounding space inward, crushing the anchored intent before it could form another body.
For an instant, a pale outline tried to gather where the man had stood. It broke apart as the severed connection collapsed, and the pressure hanging over the road vanished with it.
The man died within a single heartbeat. Leon gave him the quick death he had intended; dragging it out would help no one.
The last Archon finally tore one leg free of the ice and fled toward the rocks. Leon struck him with lightning and shattered his core before the body hit the ground.
Seven Archons and one Ethereal Initiate had attacked the caravan. None remained.
The road fell quiet, leaving Leon surrounded by the wounded.

chapters.title: Chapter 598: Forty-One Alive
paragraphs: Leon went straight to the people most likely to die.

A guard lay pinned beneath a wagon axle with a punctured lung. A servant woman’s belly had been opened. A boy of fourteen had stopped bleeding for the wrong reason. Leon healed those three completely, light pouring from his hands until several nearby survivors backed away in awe.
Then he stopped healing and began stabilizing.

He set bones, closed dangerous bleeding, and dulled enough pain for wounded men to stop fighting the people helping them. Ordinary cuts and bruises remained for medicine and time. A man who restored forty people to perfect health in one afternoon would become a story long before he reached the city, and Leon had already revealed more than he wanted.

The young woman worked through the wreckage from the opposite direction. She sent uninjured servants to collect scattered medicine chests, ordered guards to inspect the wagons, and gave one grieving merchant the task of recording the dead. Twice she swayed. Both times, she steadied herself against a wheel and continued.
Leon reached her last.
"Sit down."
"There are others—"
"There aren’t. You’re the last person still bleeding."

She studied him, then sat on a crate and allowed him to examine her shoulder. The cut was messy and painful, but shallow enough to remain moderate. She had worsened it by working and reopened it when she caught the rescued child.
Leon closed the wound with light. He left the soreness and exhaustion alone. Removing those as well would have displayed a degree of healing he preferred to keep hidden.
"You treated the guards first," she said.
"They were dying."
"Most people would have begun with my father."
"Your father wasn’t dying."
She watched his face with the same quiet attention Qingyue used, though Leon suspected her calculations concerned different things.
The older merchant approached with two servants trying and failing to support him. He freed his arms and bowed deeply.

"Shen Baoyuan, of the Shen house in Moonfall. This is my daughter, Yanning." His voice remained steady until he looked at her healed shoulder. "There were fifty-three of us this morning. There are forty-one now, and all forty-one are alive because you came over that hill. I do not know what to offer a man like you."
"Nothing yet," Leon said. "How many wagons can move?"

"Three now. A fourth can be repaired by morning. We are three days from Moonfall Frontier City." Baoyuan glanced toward the bodies on the road. "If you and the lady will travel with us, I would rather not test our fortune twice."
Leon looked toward Qingyue.
She had descended from the slope and now stood beside one of the fractured ice walls, studying what remained of it. Her silence felt analytical rather than indifferent.
"Moonfall is where I’m going," Leon said.

"Then it is settled," Yanning replied before her father could. She had already risen from the crate. "The fourth wagon will be ready by dawn. We also carry spare clothing. You’ll want something local before we reach the gate."
She had spent the last few hours working through a bleeding shoulder and had resumed organizing the caravan seconds after Leon closed it.
Leon liked competent people.

They camped beside the wreckage. Repairs continued through half the night while the dead were prepared beneath covered cloth. Nobody celebrated surviving. The absence of the twelve who had not survived occupied too much space.
At dawn, the Shen house buried them.

After the stripped bones and staked corpse Leon had found upon entering this world, and the nine men left exposed on an old battlefield, he had not known what customs to expect. Here, at least, expedience did not erase duty to their own dead.
The survivors dug twelve graves. Yanning personally marked the burial place with a formation stake and recorded every name in a ledger before the first body was lowered.
Leon helped dig. Nobody asked him to. Qingyue stood at the edge of the road, watching with an expression he could not read.
By the time the four wagons began moving, the sun had cleared the hills.
Shen Baoyuan made the repayment before they had travelled two kilometers. He opened a strongbox on the tail of the lead wagon in front of witnesses.
First came a heavy purse of ordinary silver and a smaller pouch that the merchant handled more carefully.
"Low-grade spirit stones," Baoyuan explained when Leon examined it. "For cultivators’ goods."

Next came provisions, a waterskin, and clothing in a plain dark blue-gray cut. Finally, Baoyuan offered a flat piece of dark wood with the Shen mark burned into one side and a thread of sealed qi woven through it.

"One serious favor, at any time, for as long as my house stands. We are not a great family. We cannot shield you from a sect, a great clan, or the magistrates if you give them cause. But within our legitimate reach—goods, coin, routes, papers, introductions, or a discreet place to stay—this token will be answered. If I am absent, my daughter will answer it."

Baoyuan rested two fingers on the token before releasing it. "You also have no local papers. When we reach Moonfall, my house will guarantee that you entered the region in our company and explain why you arrived without a registration jade. It will not grant you permanent standing, but it should get you through the gate without being treated as a criminal."
That assistance was worth more to Leon than either purse. Money could be earned. A credible explanation for a man who had appeared from nowhere was much harder to obtain.
Leon accepted everything.

A man who saved forty-one lives and refused all repayment would become a legend or a liar. A man who accepted money, supplies, and a useful favor looked more like a wandering cultivator who had encountered a profitable disaster.
The caravan moved slowly, which suited him.
Yanning joined him beside the lead wagon before midday.
"Do the clothes fit?"
"Well enough."

"Good. They won’t hide your face, but they should stop every gate guard and merchant from identifying you as a foreigner before you speak." She waited one step before adding, "Silver is for inns, meals, baths, and ordinary tools. Spirit stones are for anything a cultivator sells—pills, materials, formation work, or information. Don’t offer silver in the eastern market. They will take it, and they will remember that you didn’t know better."
The advice was practical. The question hidden beneath it was not.
"And if I need to sell something?" Leon asked.
"Come to me first. Even if the Shen house cannot buy it, I will know who can—and which buyers ask fewer questions than they should."
She made the offer sound like ordinary business. The brief warmth in her expression suggested that business was not the only reason.
Leon answered what she asked and nothing more.
Yanning smiled slightly, as though that answer had told her something too.

The question hidden beneath it was not.
"And if I need to sell something?" Leon asked.
"Come to me first.
Even if the Shen house cannot buy it, I will know who can—and which buyers ask fewer questions than they should."
She made the offer sound like ordinary business.
The brief warmth in her expression suggested that business was not the only reason.
Leon answered what she asked and nothing more.
Yanning smiled slightly, as though that answer had told her something too.

chapters.title: Chapter 599: The Gates of Moonfall
paragraphs: Yanning found six legitimate reasons to speak with Leon during the three-day journey.

She explained the local currency and the districts where outsiders were most often cheated. She checked whether his supplies were adequate, warned him about the city gate, and described the temporary registration available to wandering cultivators without sect or clan records.
Each useful conversation contained a question.
"Your inheritance," she asked on the second afternoon. "Did it belong to a sect or a private cultivator?"
"I don’t know."
"You spent years inside and never learned whose it was?"
"I know what was in the rooms. I don’t know whose name was on the door."

She accepted that answer, then approached the same subject four hours later from a different angle. Leon developed a real respect for her technique. She never repeated a question in the same shape. Instead, she built each inquiry out of the business at hand and set the hook somewhere new.
He gave her narrow truths and nothing wide. He did not mention Velaria, the dimensional world inside him, his class, or how little he understood about this world.

Yanning was also checking on him for reasons that had less to do with information. He was the least injured person in the caravan by an enormous margin, yet she asked about his side twice on the second day. On the third morning, she happened to be near the fire when he woke despite having no task there.
Leon filed it under commerce. Building a relationship with someone powerful and unknown was sensible, and she was doing it well.
Qingyue noticed everything he missed.

She walked several paces from the opposite side of the road, occasionally consulting the crescent jade that continued pointing south. Her attention moved between Yanning and Leon often enough to make her conclusions obvious, though she kept them to herself.
She spoke to Leon privately only twice.
The first time, she said, "You told her the water flows north."
"It does."
"You have said many true things since I found you." Qingyue glanced toward him. "Not one of them tells anyone who you are. You are very careful for a man too isolated to know what a Moonless is."
"Careful people survive isolation."
"Convenient."
The second conversation came on the final evening, after the fires burned low.
"Why?" Qingyue asked.
Leon looked up from the road map Yanning had lent him. "Why what?"
"Why interfere? You owed them nothing. You could have crossed the far side of the hill, and nobody in this world would ever have known."
He considered the question because she deserved an honest answer rather than a noble one.
"They had already decided to kill the children. I could stop it. Walking away wouldn’t have been caution. It would have been me deciding those children were worth less than my privacy."
Qingyue studied him across the fire.
"That is a Jade Moon answer," she said, making it impossible to tell whether she meant it as praise.
She went to sleep soon afterward.
Other facts reached Leon in fragments from the guards, servants, and Yanning’s explanations.

The seven lesser robbers had been Void Immortals. Their leader had been an Early Earth Immortal. Leon aligned the local terms with what the System had shown him. Void Immortal and Ethereal Initiate described the same stage. Earth Immortal corresponded to Ethereal Lord.

The new terminology did not change his estimate of Qingyue. The Level 114 leopard had withdrawn upon seeing her insignia, and Leon had already assumed she was at least comparable to it and possibly much stronger. Now he merely possessed the local names for the beginning of that road.
He also learned that unregistered wandering cultivators were common enough to have their own designation and mistrusted enough that nobody used it kindly.
Moonfall Frontier City appeared late on the third afternoon.

It stood against a spur of gray mountain with the Desolation behind it. Leon stopped for a moment because the city was old. Its walls ran for kilometers, filled with formations that turned through the stone in slow, layered patterns. They had been built by people who expected centuries of attacks and had planned accordingly.

Beasts on the approach road hauled loads no animal in Velaria could have shifted. A caravan queue stretched half a kilometer from the eastern gate. Above the northern quarter, an enormous flat platform drifted at rooftop height with lanterns hanging beneath it.
"The city’s ore lift," Yanning said, following his gaze. "It crosses this road near dusk. Don’t stand beneath it."

The Shen name moved their four wagons past the queue. A gate officer in dark armor came out at a jog, took one look at the four wagons where eleven had departed, and began asking questions in the clipped tone of a man who had heard too many versions of the same disaster.
Shen Baoyuan answered plainly. He named Leon and described what had happened on the road without embellishment.
The officer studied Leon. "No identity token. No clan record. No registration."
"No."
"Where are you from?"
"An inheritance space south of here. It collapsed."
"Of course it did. That is what they all say, and occasionally one of them is even telling the truth."

Qingyue stepped forward and turned her collar enough for the silver crescent of Jade Moon Palace to catch the light. She said she had encountered Leon in the Desolation, that his account was implausible but not impossible, and that it deserved investigation rather than immediate punishment. She would bring him through the gate herself instead of leaving him outside it.
The officer’s posture changed at the sight of her insignia. He bowed—not deeply, but more than he had bowed to Shen Baoyuan—and the remaining process took less than a quarter of an hour.

Registration required Leon’s name, a drop of blood, and a controlled pulse of qi pressed into a thin jade tablet. It recorded a stable signature and confirmed that the person standing at the gate matched the person receiving the token. It did not reach deeply enough to find his second heart, the world within him, or anyone sleeping inside it.
"Name."
"Leon."
"Family name."
"No family."
The officer wrote it down without comment, which told Leon that the answer was not rare here.
The temporary jade he received was small, thin, and slightly warm. A registration mark covered one face, while a fading formation on the other showed that it would eventually need to be renewed.
Leon held it a moment longer than necessary.

Days ago, he had left a world he had rebuilt from a wasteland while carrying a civilization inside his chest. He had arrived here as a man who did not officially exist. Now he possessed just enough identity to buy, sell, learn, and sleep beneath a roof. It was temporary and built upon a story that was mostly false, but it was a beginning.
"Don’t lose it," the officer said. "Renew it before the mark fades."

Moonfall’s gates rose twelve meters high and showed repairs from at least four different centuries. Leon followed the Shen wagons through them into smoke, noise, and streets crowded with more people than he had seen in one place since the City of Light.
Yanning fell into step beside him beneath the gate arch.

"Our compound is in the third ward. We have a guest wing, and my father will be insulted if you choose an inn. If you prefer one anyway, I can find you a place where the doors actually lock." Her voice remained professional, but the warmth beneath it had become difficult for anyone except Leon to miss. "Either way, come to me before buying anything expensive. I would prefer your first Moonfall merchant not cheat you badly enough to embarrass the rest of us."
"Understood."
Satisfied, she went ahead to direct the wagons.
Qingyue had stopped a few paces inside the gate. She looked south over the wall, the flat crescent of jade open on her palm and still turned toward whatever had drawn her into the Desolation.
Then she closed her hand around it and looked at Leon instead.
"You’ll be here for a while," she said.
It was neither a question nor an offer.
"For a while."
"Good."
Qingyue turned and walked deeper into the city.

chapters.title: Chapter 600: A Surprise Worth Waiting For
paragraphs: The Shen compound stood in Moonfall’s third ward behind gray walls topped by a respectable defensive formation. Warehouses occupied most of the outer grounds, with offices on one side and a caravan yard large enough to hold twenty wagons.
Only four entered that afternoon.

The caravan yard had been prepared for eleven. Seven empty unloading lanes waited beneath the warehouse awnings, each with workers and tally boards assigned to it. One by one, the workers lowered the boards when they understood those wagons were not delayed somewhere behind the others.

Families and servants had been waiting since noon. The moment they saw the wagons, they began counting. Relief spread across some faces. Others kept searching the gaps between the vehicles for people who would never appear.
A woman in a cook’s apron moved along the line, repeating one name until a guard gently caught her arms and answered. She sat down in the dirt and did not move again for a long time.
Around her, the household kept working. Clerks recorded the surviving cargo. Stable hands unhitched exhausted beasts. Water heated over a hurriedly built fire while the wounded were taken inside.
Leon remained near the gate and stayed out of their way.
Yanning found him twenty minutes later. Her sleeves were rolled up, and ink stained two of her fingers.
"The guest wing is in the eastern courtyard," she said. "Your room is ready. There’s a bathhouse at the end of the corridor, and I had food sent over."
She handed him a folded map of the compound. Four areas had been marked.
"Places I should avoid?" Leon asked.
"Two storehouses have unreliable formations. The third building is where the night guards sleep during the day."
"And the fourth?"
"My family’s residential court. My grandmother is eighty-one, and if she finds you, she’ll decide you haven’t eaten enough in your entire life."
Leon glanced at the map again. "That sounds less dangerous than the other three."
"You haven’t met her."
The faint tiredness in Yanning’s expression eased for a moment. Then someone called her from the offices, and she turned back toward the work.
Shen Baoyuan intercepted Leon before he reached the guest wing. The older merchant was limping, his voice rough from hours of speaking, but he still insisted Leon remain in the compound.
"Stay as long as you need," Baoyuan said. "Yanning can help if you wish to buy anything in the city. Moonfall is not kind to newcomers."
Leon accepted. Refusing would only force the man to argue when he had a household in mourning.
The room was clean and comfortable without being extravagant. Fresh clothes waited beside a washbasin. A tray on the table held rice, roasted vegetables, sliced meat, and a covered bowl of broth.
The Shens were grateful, but they did not pretend he had become family overnight. They offered shelter, privacy, and practical help. Leon preferred that to grand declarations.

He ate only after checking that the injured caravan guards had been given rooms. By then, evening had settled over the compound. Voices continued in the offices, and runners carried messages through the courtyard to the families of those buried on the road.
Yanning returned once to ask whether the clothes fit and whether anyone had tried to charge him for his meal.
"Do guests usually pay the kitchen?" Leon asked.
"No. One of our older cooks occasionally decides unfamiliar people are caravan inspectors and sends them a bill."
"That seems risky."
"She has worked here longer than I’ve been alive. Nobody has successfully dismissed her."
Yanning left before he could tell whether she was joking.
Qingyue did not enter the estate.
She met Leon outside the eastern gate before sunrise the next morning. A travel bundle rested across her back, and the crescent jade in her hand still pointed south, toward the Three-Moon Desolation.
"You’re leaving," Leon said.
"The disturbance I came to investigate has not stopped." Qingyue closed her fingers around the jade. "Walking with the caravan cost me several days. I need to finish what brought me here."
"How long will it take?"
"I don’t know."
It was an honest answer, which made asking again pointless.
Qingyue adjusted the sword at her side. "If you’re still in Moonfall when I return, I’ll have a surprise for you."
Leon studied her face. "You aren’t going to explain that."
"No." A trace of amusement touched her eyes. "If you leave before I return, our paths separate. You should not remain here only because of something I said."
"I already planned to learn about the city."
"Then perhaps I’ll find you when I come back."
She left without a longer farewell.
Leon watched her cross the morning street and disappear beyond a row of closed shops.
A surprise from someone strong enough to make an Earth Immortal beast retreat on sight.
Whatever she intended, it was unlikely to be ordinary. He had already decided against rushing back into the Desolation. Now he had another reason to stay where Qingyue could find him.
Two hours later, Qingyue passed through Moonfall’s southern gate and finally allowed herself to consider what she might offer him.

Four rare affinities were impressive. They were not enough to make Leon unique in the higher world. Qingyue knew cultivators born with ancient physiques, inherited sword intent, or bloodlines that allowed them to fight far above their stage. Great sects gathered such people deliberately.
Leon’s talent had earned her attention. His decisions during the journey had held it.

He had killed seven Dao Palace cultivators and one Early Void Immortal on the road. He could have crossed the hill and continued toward Moonfall without revealing anything, yet he had intervened when the robbers prepared to murder their hostages. Afterward, he treated the wounded according to urgency. A dying guard received his attention before the merchant’s daughter.
He also knew how to hide. Every affinity he revealed served a purpose, and Qingyue doubted she had seen all of them.

During the four days they had spent close together, she had examined his energy whenever she could do so without announcing it. She found no demonic trace, corruption, or instability. He was secretive, but his foundation was clean. His actions had given her no reason to believe he was malicious.
That mattered more than another rare affinity.

If he remained in Moonfall until she returned, she would give him a chance to enter Jade Moon Palace. The Palace would decide whether his talent justified recruitment, and Leon would decide whether he wanted the opportunity. Qingyue promised nothing beyond opening the door.

She had not mentioned that plan to him because she still had a mission to complete, and because an opportunity offered too early could sound like an obligation. Leon did not owe Jade Moon Palace service for her help at the gate. If he chose to follow her later, she wanted the choice made with open eyes.

There was also more she needed to learn. His cultivation method did not resemble any inheritance she knew. His story remained full of missing pieces. Clean energy and good decisions over four days earned him consideration, not blind trust.
She increased her speed once the city fell behind her. Soon she was running south fast enough for the road to blur beneath her feet.
Back at the Shen compound, Leon unfolded a city map on the desk in his room.
The Desolation would still be waiting in a week. For now, he needed prices, language, cultivation principles, and a clearer picture of the powers ruling this world.
He marked the exchange street, the pill market, the formation district, and the public archive.
Six days would be enough to begin.
